questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeals that overturn by age
questions.question: A Malaysian state's flood-relief model rejects claims; appeals overturn 35% of its rejections for applicants aged over 65, against 7% for others. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner investigate the model's errors for this age group
options.B: Add appeal staff so older applicants' appeals are decided sooner
options.C: Lower the model's rejection threshold for applicants aged over 65
options.D: Add age as a model input so it learns older applicants better

questions.key_concept: Appeal reversal rates by group are a warning signal of model error; investigate the cause, not just the appeals backlog.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the gap between the two reversal rates measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Appeals overturn older applicants' rejections at five times the rate for others, which signals that the model makes more errors for that group, and wrongly rejected people who do not appeal are never counted. The model owner should investigate the cause so fewer wrong rejections happen. Faster appeals help those who appeal, but leave the model rejecting older applicants wrongly in the first place.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it helps older applicants sooner. But it treats each wrong rejection after the fact while the model keeps making them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would cut rejections for that group. But changing a threshold before knowing the cause may trade one error for another, untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets the group. But it changes the model before the cause is known, and using age directly may itself be unlawful.

tips: Eliminate: C and D both change the model before the cause is known, and adding age as an input may itself be unlawful.
Final two: A beats B because the reversal gap signals model errors for older applicants; faster appeals help those who appeal while wrong rejections continue.
Exam cue: appeal outcomes are monitoring data. A group whose rejections are overturned more often points to model error for that group.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Transcripts without actions
questions.question: An Indian bus-ticketing platform's AI support agent can rebook trips, waive fees and issue refunds; its log keeps each chat transcript but not the actions it took. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep chat transcripts until the refund dispute period ends
options.B: Have the agent summarize its actions at the end of each chat
options.C: Log each tool call the agent makes, with its result
options.D: Review a monthly sample of transcripts for unusual refunds

questions.key_concept: An agent's chat transcript shows what it said, not what it did; its tool calls and their results must be logged.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a dispute about a refund would need to show.
questions.correct_explanation: A transcript shows what the agent said, not what it did; an agent can state one thing and call a refund tool with different values. Logging each tool call with its result records the actions themselves, so refunds and waivers can be traced and disputes settled. Keeping transcripts longer only preserves more of the same incomplete record.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disputes need records. But transcripts kept longer still omit the refunds and waivers the agent actually made.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because summaries are readable. But they are generated text, a lead to verify, not a record of the calls the agent made.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because review can catch abuse. But transcripts do not show the refunds made, so the sample cannot see them.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the agent's own account of its actions, and D samples records that do not contain the actions.
Final two: C beats A because only tool-call logs record what the agent did; transcripts kept longer preserve the same record of words, not actions.
Exam cue: for AI agents, log actions as well as conversations. What the agent said and what it did can differ.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A hosted grader updated without notice
questions.question: A Panamanian health insurer compares each member-assistant release with the last one, using pass rates from a hosted grading model. The grader's vendor updates it without notice. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Pass rates may fall below the level needed for release approval
options.B: Pass-rate changes may come from the grader, not the assistant
options.C: The grader may favor answers written in its own vendor's style
options.D: The assistant's own answers may vary from one run to the next

questions.key_concept: A grading model is a measuring instrument; if it changes silently, results across releases are not comparable, so its version must be pinned and recorded.
questions.pre_read: Ask what must stay fixed for two pass rates to be comparable.
questions.correct_explanation: A grading model is a measuring instrument, and each silent vendor update can make it stricter or more lenient, so a rise or fall in pass rates between releases may reflect the grader, not the assistant. Release decisions then rest on comparisons that mean little. The assistant's answers do vary run to run, but repeated runs measure that spread so it can be allowed for; a silently updated grader moves every score.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because release gates use pass rates. But a falling rate is what testing should reveal; the doubt is whether the rate measures the assistant at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI graders can favor familiar styles. But nothing suggests such bias here, while the silent updates are a stated fact that shifts every score.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generated answers vary. But repeated runs measure that variation so it can be allowed for; a grader that changes silently shifts every score.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a lower pass rate as the risk rather than asking whether it is valid, and C assumes a style bias the facts never raise.
Final two: B beats D because repeated runs measure run-to-run variation so it can be allowed for, but a silently updated grader moves every score; compare releases only with a fixed, recorded grader.
Exam cue: when AI grades AI, the grader is a measuring instrument. Pin and record its version, or score changes between releases cannot be trusted.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Summaries accepted on word overlap
questions.question: A Bangladeshi news agency accepted its article-summary model because summaries shared 60% of their words with editors' own summaries, above the target. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The vendor, not the agency, may have set the target
options.B: Editors' summaries may differ in length from the model's
options.C: Sharing 60% of words may be too low a bar for news
options.D: Summaries can share many words yet misstate the facts

questions.key_concept: Word-overlap scores for generated text measure shared wording, not factual accuracy, so they cannot show alone that a summary is correct.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of wrong summary would still pass this test.
questions.correct_explanation: Word overlap rewards summaries that reuse the editors' words, but a summary can share most of them and still reverse a figure, a name or who did what. The acceptance measure does not test what matters for news: factual accuracy. Raising the overlap target would demand more shared words while still never checking whether the facts are right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because owners should set targets. But nothing says the vendor set it, and any target on this measure still ignores accuracy.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because length affects overlap. But length differences are minor next to a measure that never checks facts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because higher bars seem safer. But more shared words still says nothing about whether the summary's facts are right.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a fact the question never gives, and B is a minor effect on the score, not a gap in what it tests.
Final two: D beats C because overlap measures shared words, not facts; a higher target asks for more of the wrong evidence.
Exam cue: check that an acceptance measure tests what harms people if wrong. For generated text, fluency and overlap are not accuracy.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Synthetic voices for older callers
questions.question: An Icelandic health line's speech-recognition menu had too few recordings of callers aged over 80, so its fairness test used synthetic voices made to sound older. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Synthetic voices may not show how older callers really speak
options.B: The test may hold too few cases to give reliable results
options.C: The synthetic voices may infringe the rights of a voice actor
options.D: Older callers may prefer to speak with staff in any case

questions.key_concept: Fairness results on synthetic data reflect the generator's idea of a group, not the real group, until checked on real cases.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose voices the test really measured.
questions.correct_explanation: Synthetic voices come from a model's idea of older speech, which may miss real features such as tremor, breathing or slower pace, so good results may not hold for real callers aged over 80. The test answers a question about the generator, not the group. Sample size is a common limit, but synthetic voices can be made in any number; their realism is the gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because group tests are often too small. But synthetic voices can be produced in any number; their realism, not their count, is in doubt.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because voice cloning raises rights questions. But nothing suggests a real person's voice was copied, and it would not affect the test's validity.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some callers prefer people. But preferences do not excuse a menu that may fail the older callers who use it.

tips: Eliminate: C raises a rights issue the facts never suggest, and D excuses a possible failure by assuming callers' preferences.
Final two: A beats B because synthetic voices can be made in any number, so count is not the problem; whether they sound like real callers aged over 80 is.
Exam cue: synthetic test data shows how a model handles the generator's idea of a group. Ask for real cases before trusting results for that group.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Equal error rates in a farm-credit model
questions.question: A Brazilian development agency's farm-credit model shows equal error rates for women and men farmers. Credit officers decide, and they overturn its approvals more often for women. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retest the model's error rates by sex on recent applications
options.B: Remove the officers' power to overturn the model's approvals
options.C: Test final decisions by sex, including the officers' overrides
options.D: Train officers on the model's validated equal error rates

questions.key_concept: Fairness testing must cover final human-plus-AI decisions; overrides can create a gap the model alone does not show.
questions.pre_read: Ask where in the process the women's applications are actually decided.
questions.correct_explanation: Farmers live with the final decision, not the model's suggestion, and here the officers' overrides could create the gap the model avoids. Testing final outcomes by sex, overrides included, shows whether the whole decision process is fair and where any gap arises. Retesting the model again measures only the part already shown to be even.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fairness tests usually target the model. But the model already shows equal errors; the possible gap arises after officers act.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it stops biased overrides. But it removes human oversight, including overrides that correct real model errors.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it builds confidence in the model. But it nudges officers to defer, and does not test whether their overrides are fair.

tips: Eliminate: B removes oversight to fix it, and D pushes officers toward deference without testing their decisions.
Final two: C beats A because farmers live with final decisions, and the overrides may create the gap; retesting the model measures a part already shown even.
Exam cue: test fairness where the decision is made. If people can change AI outputs, the human-plus-AI outcome is what needs testing.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Reasons shown to underwriters
questions.question: A South African life insurer's underwriters see the top three reasons an explanation tool gives for each risk score; validation tested the scores but not the reasons. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Show underwriters the top ten reasons for each score instead
options.B: Test whether changing a cited factor moves the score as claimed
options.C: Ask underwriters whether the reasons match their own judgment
options.D: Add a notice that the reasons shown are estimates, not exact causes

questions.key_concept: Explanations need validating for faithfulness: a cited reason should move the score when it changes, not merely look plausible.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option would prove about the reasons underwriters see.
questions.correct_explanation: An explanation tool approximates the model, and its reasons can look sensible while not reflecting what actually drives a score. Testing whether a cited factor really moves the score checks that the reasons are faithful. Underwriters' sense that reasons look right tests plausibility, and plausible but wrong reasons are exactly what could mislead their decisions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more detail seems more transparent. But ten untested reasons are no more reliable than three.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because experts know underwriting. But reasons that match expectations can still misstate what drives the model; plausible is not faithful.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is honest about limits. But it leaves underwriters relying on reasons nobody has tested.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more untested reasons, and D labels the reasons without testing them.
Final two: B beats C because only changing a cited factor shows whether it really drives the score; underwriters' agreement tests plausibility, not faithfulness.
Exam cue: explanations are outputs too. Validate that they reflect the model's behavior, not just that people find them convincing.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Red-teaming a paying agent
questions.question: A Colombian insurer plans to red-team its AI claims agent, which can approve and pay claims, by attacking the live agent through real customers' accounts. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Cap each claim payment during the test at a small fixed amount
options.B: Skip red teaming, as the vendor red-teamed the model
options.C: Red-team the model alone, with its payment tools detached
options.D: Red-team an identical copy wired only to test systems

questions.key_concept: Red-teaming an AI agent that can act should use an identical copy whose tools touch only test systems.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a successful attack would actually do during the test.
questions.correct_explanation: Attacks that succeed against the live agent cause real payments and touch real customers' claims. An identical copy wired only to test systems lets testers push the agent, with the same model, prompts and tools, as hard as needed without real harm. Testing the model with its tools detached is safe, but it misses the attacks that matter most: tricking the agent into paying.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it limits losses. But successful attacks still move real money and change real customers' claims during the test.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors test their models. But the vendor tested the model alone, not this agent with its payment tools.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes the risk of real payments. But without its tools the agent cannot be tricked into paying, so the riskiest attacks go untested.

tips: Eliminate: A still lets successful attacks move real money, and B relies on the vendor's tests of the bare model.
Final two: D beats C because an identical copy keeps the payment tools attacks target without touching real accounts; detaching the tools makes testing safe but misses the main risk.
Exam cue: agents act in the real world. Red-team them in an identically configured copy with tools pointed at test systems.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Varied attempts until a payment passed
questions.question: A Nigerian card issuer's fraud model refused thousands of slightly varied attempts at the same large purchase across many cards. Then variants began to pass. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Detect and throttle repeated declined attempts across cards
options.B: Retrain the fraud model every week on the latest fraud cases
options.C: Lower the decline threshold so more payments are refused
options.D: Cancel and reissue every card used in the attempts

questions.key_concept: Attackers can probe a model with many varied inputs to learn what passes; detecting and limiting repeated attempts blocks that feedback.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each failed attempt taught the attacker.
questions.correct_explanation: Thousands of slightly varied attempts at one purchase look like probing: fraudsters use the model's declines as feedback to learn what passes, then send the variants that fit. Detecting and throttling repeated declined attempts, across cards as well as within each, cuts off that feedback. Weekly retraining on new fraud helps, but attackers can probe each new version the same way, so the gap reopens after every release.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fresh fraud data improves models. But probing works against any version; without limits, attackers relearn what passes after each retrain.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it blocks more fraud. But it refuses more genuine payments, and probing simply finds the new cutoff.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the cards were used for fraud. But the attackers learned what the model passes, not just card numbers; they can reuse that lesson with other cards.

tips: Eliminate: C moves a cutoff that probing will find again, and D cancels cards while the attackers keep what they learned about the model.
Final two: A beats B because throttling repeated declines across cards denies attackers the feedback they learn from; retraining helps, but each new version can be probed the same way.
Exam cue: many slightly varied queries before an attack suggest probing. Limit and watch query patterns, not just the model.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A classifier kept secret
questions.question: A Czech bank's IT team says its phishing-email classifier is safe from evasion because its design is secret and no outsider can query it. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Insiders may leak the classifier's design to attackers
options.B: The classifier may slow email delivery at peak times
options.C: Emails crafted against similar public models often fool it too
options.D: Classifier updates may bypass the bank's change management

questions.key_concept: Attacks crafted on similar models often transfer, so keeping a model's design secret does not protect it from evasion.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether an attacker really needs to see this model to fool it.
questions.correct_explanation: Evasion does not need the design or direct access: attackers can craft emails against similar public models, and such adversarial examples often transfer to other models trained for the same task. Secrecy therefore gives weak protection, and the bank should test robustness itself. An insider leak would help attackers, but the defense fails even if the design never leaks.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because leaks defeat secrecy. But attackers do not need the design; emails crafted against similar models often work anyway.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because filters add delay. But speed is an operations matter, unrelated to the claim that secrecy prevents evasion.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI updates are changes. But nothing suggests updates bypass change control; the claim in question is about evasion.

tips: Eliminate: B is an operations issue, and D raises a change-control gap the facts never suggest.
Final two: C beats A because crafted emails often transfer from similar models, so the defense fails without any leak; an insider leak only adds another route.
Exam cue: secrecy is not robustness. Expect attackers to practice on similar models, and test the real one for evasion.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A gradual conversation
questions.question: A Spanish chemical distributor's product assistant refused every harmful single prompt its testers tried, but staff later got dangerous mixing instructions over a long, gradual conversation. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add the staff's prompts to the assistant's blocked-prompt list
options.B: Rerun the single-prompt tests after each assistant update
options.C: Limit each conversation with the assistant to ten turns
options.D: Test and screen whole conversations, not single prompts alone

questions.key_concept: Multi-turn jailbreaks spread a harmful request across harmless-looking steps, so tests and filters must assess whole conversations.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the testers' single prompts could never reveal.
questions.correct_explanation: Multi-turn jailbreaks build a harmful request step by step, so each message looks safe on its own, and single-prompt tests and filters pass them. Testing and screening whole conversations catches the pattern the attack depends on. Blocking the prompts staff used stops that exact path, but the same gradual approach can be reworded endlessly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it blocks the known attack. But gradual attacks can be reworded endlessly; a list of past prompts misses the next one.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because regression tests are useful. But these tests never caught the attack, so rerunning them proves nothing about it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because shorter chats limit build-up. But attacks can work in a few turns, and genuine long product questions get cut off.

tips: Eliminate: B reruns the tests that already missed the attack, and C caps turns that a gradual attack can fit within.
Final two: D beats A because the attack lives in the conversation's build-up, which only whole-conversation testing sees; a blocked list stops one wording of it.
Exam cue: if harmful output came from a sequence of harmless-looking steps, test and monitor the sequence, not each step.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An instruction saved to memory
questions.question: A Jersey trust company's staff assistant saves lasting 'memories' from chats. A tester's pasted document planted a memory telling it to copy future drafts to an outside address. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Wipe every user's saved memories at the end of each week
options.B: Block memory writes from documents and let users review memories
options.C: Tell the assistant in its prompt to ignore instructions in documents
options.D: Scan pasted documents for malware before the assistant reads them

questions.key_concept: Assistant memory can turn a one-time prompt injection into a lasting instruction; control writes to memory and let users review it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes this injection different from one inside a single chat.
questions.correct_explanation: Memory turns a one-time injection into a lasting instruction that steers every later session, so the risk sits in what may be written to memory. Blocking writes that come from document content, and letting users see and remove entries, stops planted instructions and exposes any that slip in. A weekly wipe still lets a planted memory act for days and erases useful ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it limits how long memories last. But a planted instruction still acts until the wipe, and the next document can plant it again.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it states the rule clearly. But injected text can override prompt instructions; a prompt rule is not a control.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because scanning catches harmful files. But the planted instruction is plain text, which a malware scan passes.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a prompt instruction that injection can override, and D scans for malware when the attack is plain text.
Final two: B beats A because controlling what reaches memory stops planted instructions persisting; a weekly wipe lets them act for days and returns with the next document.
Exam cue: an assistant's memory is a stored input. Control what can write to it, as you would any data that steers outputs.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Steps added after approval
questions.question: A Ghanaian data-center operator's AI operations agent asks an engineer to approve its plan, then carries out every step, including steps it adds after approval. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the tool layer block actions outside the approved plan
options.B: Have the agent explain each added step in its final report
options.C: Tell the agent in its prompt to keep strictly to approved plans
options.D: Have the engineer review each plan in more detail before approving

questions.key_concept: Approving an agent's plan does not control steps it adds later; the tool layer must block actions outside what was approved.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the engineer actually approved, and what the agent can do beyond it.
questions.correct_explanation: Approval of a plan means little if the agent can add steps afterward; added steps run with no one having seen them. Having the tool layer block actions outside the approved plan, and seek fresh approval for them, enforces the boundary whatever the agent decides. A more careful review of the plan improves the approval but cannot cover steps the agent invents later.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it records what happened. But the report comes after the added steps ran, and it is the agent's own account.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it states the rule. But a prompt instruction can be ignored, misread or overridden; it does not enforce limits.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because better review catches bad plans. But it cannot cover steps the agent adds after approval.

tips: Eliminate: B reports added steps only after they run, and C relies on a prompt rule the agent may not follow.
Final two: A beats D because blocking unapproved actions enforces the plan's limits; a closer review of the plan cannot see steps added after it.
Exam cue: approving an agent's plan is not approving its actions. Enforce the approved scope where the tools are called.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An agent that makes its own accounts
questions.question: A Finnish software firm's AI deployment agent acts on tickets any employee can file. It runs under an account that can create service accounts and access keys. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: New accounts may break the firm's naming standard for accounts
options.B: Ticket text could steer it into creating unreviewed access
options.C: Access keys the agent creates may lack an expiry date
options.D: Ticketed deployments may take longer while new accounts are created

questions.key_concept: An agent acting on text others write can be steered into creating access; identity creation should stay outside its reach.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can influence what the agent does.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent that acts on text anyone can write can be steered by that text, so a crafted ticket could make it create accounts and keys for an attacker, outside the approval and review applied to people. That steerable power to grant access is the greatest concern. Keys that never expire make the problem last longer, but the gap is that the access was never approved at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because standards aid reviews. But naming is cosmetic next to an agent that can be steered into creating access.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because old keys are a known risk. But expiry limits how long access lasts; the larger gap is that anyone filing a ticket can steer its creation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because speed matters in deployment. But delay is an efficiency issue, not a risk to the firm's systems.

tips: Eliminate: A is a naming standard and D is a speed issue; neither touches who can steer the agent into granting access.
Final two: B beats C because a crafted ticket can steer the agent into creating any access, unreviewed; key expiry only limits how long that access lasts.
Exam cue: an AI agent that reads text others write can be steered by it. Keep powers such as creating accounts out of its reach.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Deposits set out of sight
questions.question: A Romanian utility's model sets new households' security deposits. Customers are not told a model is involved. The utility's AI incident process starts only from complaints. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Complaint handlers may route AI-related complaints to the wrong team
options.B: The deposit model may breach the utility's pricing policy
options.C: The model may set higher deposits for some groups of households
options.D: Households unaware of the model may never report a wrong deposit

questions.key_concept: When people cannot tell AI made a decision, few report its errors, so incident detection cannot rely on complaints alone.
questions.pre_read: Check each concern against what the stem states, not what it might imply.
questions.correct_explanation: When people do not know a model set their deposit, they have little reason to suspect a systematic error, and many will simply pay. The incident process waits for complaints, so the deciding gap is detection: harm of any kind, unequal deposits included, can go unnoticed. Detection needs monitoring of the decisions themselves, not only a complaint channel.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because misrouting delays response. But it affects only complaints that arrive; the bigger gap is harm no one reports.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because pricing rules matter. But nothing suggests a breach; the issue is how errors would ever be noticed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deposit models can treat groups unequally. But nothing suggests that here, and a process that waits for complaints would miss such harm too.

tips: Eliminate: A matters only for complaints that arrive, and B assumes a pricing breach nothing suggests.
Final two: D beats C because a complaint-only process misses any harm customers cannot see, unequal deposits included; C guesses at one harm the facts never show.
Exam cue: complaints detect AI harm only when people can see it. Opaque AI needs monitoring of its decisions, not just a complaint channel.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A cloned voice passes verification
questions.question: A Kenyan mobile-money operator's voice-verification model accepted a cloned voice that emptied a customer's wallet; the fraud team refunded the customer and closed the case. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retrain the model on cloned voices before reopening the case
options.B: Add a second factor for that customer's future transactions
options.C: Treat it as a model attack and review other recent voice matches
options.D: Keep the case closed, since the customer was fully refunded

questions.key_concept: A cloned voice passing verification is an attack on the model, so the incident covers every account the model protects.
questions.pre_read: Ask what exactly the attacker defeated.
questions.correct_explanation: A cloned voice passing verification is an attack on the model itself, and the same technique can be used on any account it protects. Handling it as an AI incident and reviewing other recent voice matches finds other victims and shows whether the model can be fooled at scale. A second factor protects one customer while the weakness stays open for everyone else.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model needs to resist clones. But retraining before the attack is understood may not fix it, and it delays finding other victims.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it stops a repeat for this customer. But the model can be fooled for every account, not just this one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the customer is made whole. But a refund closes the loss, not the weakness that every account faces.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains before the attack is understood, and D treats a refund as closing a weakness every account shares.
Final two: C beats B because the cloned voice defeated the model, which guards every account; a second factor protects one customer while others stay exposed.
Exam cue: when an attack fools the model, the incident is the model's weakness, not one victim's loss. Triage it across everyone the model protects.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A library overwritten each night
questions.question: A Dutch tax-advice firm disengaged its client assistant after harmful advice and saved the chat logs; the tax-guidance library the assistant retrieves from is overwritten every night. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Move the saved chat logs to restricted, locked storage
options.B: Preserve the guidance library and its earlier versions now
options.C: Rerun the clients' questions to recreate the harmful advice
options.D: Correct the faulty guidance in the library before tonight

questions.key_concept: Retrieval content is evidence: the library an assistant read from can be overwritten, so preserve it before it changes.
questions.pre_read: List every input that shaped the advice, and when each could change.
questions.correct_explanation: The advice came from what the assistant retrieved, and the nightly overwrite will replace the guidance it read, leaving root cause work with logs but no source. Preserving the library, with any earlier versions still held, comes first. Moving the saved logs to restricted storage is good custody, but they are already kept, while the library changes tonight.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs need protection. But the logs are already saved; the library is the evidence about to be lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to rebuild events. But answers vary run to run, and the library will have changed, so reruns cannot show what clients were told.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because faulty guidance should be fixed. But correcting it now changes the evidence before anyone knows what the assistant read.

tips: Eliminate: C reruns a model whose answers vary, against a library that has changed, and D edits the evidence before it is preserved.
Final two: B beats A because the library is overwritten tonight while the logs are already kept; secure first what is about to disappear.
Exam cue: for retrieval-based AI, the documents it read are evidence. Preserve the index or library version before it refreshes.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A switch only the vendor holds
questions.question: During an AI incident, a Bulgarian ministry found that only its procurement-software vendor could turn off the AI supplier ratings. Doing so took four days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Secure a tested way for the ministry to switch the ratings off
options.B: Agree with the vendor a four-hour response time for AI incidents
options.C: Ask the vendor to roll the ratings back to last month's model
options.D: Give the IS auditor authority to stop the ministry's AI ratings

questions.key_concept: Owners need a tested way to disengage AI features in bought software themselves, without waiting for the vendor.
questions.pre_read: Ask what containment depended on in this setup.
questions.correct_explanation: Disengaging AI quickly is the first containment step, and here it depended entirely on the vendor's speed. A tested way for the ministry itself to switch the ratings off puts that step in the owner's hands. A four-hour response time shortens the wait but still leaves containment depending on the vendor answering, possibly at night or under its own pressures.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it cuts the delay. But containment still waits on the vendor, and four hours of harmful ratings may still be too long.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rollback is a standard AI containment step. But the rollback still waits on the vendor, the same dependence that took four days.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because someone must hold the authority. But stopping systems is the owner's call; the IS auditor assesses whether that ability exists.

tips: Eliminate: C still waits on the vendor to act, and D gives the IS auditor an operating power that belongs to the owner.
Final two: A beats B because the ministry's own tested switch lets the owner disengage at once; a faster vendor response still makes containment wait on another party.
Exam cue: for AI inside bought software, check the owner can disengage it without waiting for the vendor.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A flaw in a shared template
questions.question: A Greek museum group traced its chatbot's wrong prices to a prompt template shared with four assistants on other models. The problem record covers the chatbot alone. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Fix the template, retest the chatbot, then close the problem record
options.B: Have each assistant tell visitors to check prices on the website
options.C: Retrain the chatbot's model on the correct ticket prices
options.D: Extend the problem record to every assistant using the template

questions.key_concept: When an AI root cause sits in a shared component, the problem record must cover every system that uses it.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with the root cause the trace found.
questions.correct_explanation: The cause sits in a shared template, so the same flaw may already be giving wrong prices in four other assistants, and because a prompt behaves differently on each model, a fix proven on the chatbot proves nothing for them. Extending the problem record to every assistant using the template makes the fix, retesting and closure cover all of them. Retesting only the chatbot leaves four unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the fix reaches the shared template. But a prompt acts differently on each model, so the four other assistants stay unproven after the change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns visitors. But a notice leaves wrong prices in place across five assistants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model gave wrong prices. But the cause is the template, and retraining changes the wrong component.

tips: Eliminate: B warns visitors instead of fixing the cause, and C retrains a model when the cause is in the template.
Final two: D beats A because a prompt acts differently on each model, so a fix proven on the chatbot says nothing about the other four; the problem record must cover all five.
Exam cue: when an AI root cause is a shared component, such as a template, base model or index, widen the problem to every system using it and retest each.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Closed as staff error
questions.question: An Egyptian elevator-safety agency closed a problem record as staff error. Shown the model's 'low risk' rating, an inspector passed a faulty elevator using a checklist judged sound. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Show inspectors the model's confidence score beside each rating
options.B: Retrain the model on the faulty elevator's inspection records
options.C: Test if the model's ratings change how closely inspectors look
options.D: Accept the closure, as the checklist was judged sound

questions.key_concept: People anchor on AI ratings and check less, so 'staff error' is not a root cause until the review is tested beside the rating.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether another inspector, in the same seat, would have done the same.
questions.correct_explanation: A checklist that is sound on paper can still fail once a model's rating sits beside it: people predictably anchor on AI output and check less. One inspector's miss may be a symptom of that design. Testing whether ratings change how closely inspectors look, across all inspectors, finds a cause that would trip anyone. Accepting the closure because the checklist is sound never tests how it is used beside the rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it gives inspectors more to judge by. But it is a fix chosen before the cause is known, and a confident wrong rating may be trusted even more.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the model was wrong. But one record changes little, and it leaves the review that missed the error unexamined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the checklist passed review. But a sound checklist can be applied less carefully once a model's rating is shown; the closure never tests that.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a confidence score before the cause is known, and B tweaks the model with one record.
Final two: C beats D because AI ratings predictably change how closely people check; a checklist judged sound says nothing about how it is used beside a rating.
Exam cue: 'staff error' is rarely a full root cause for AI failures. Ask what in the human-AI design made the error likely.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Pooling clients' data for one model
questions.question: A Luxembourg payroll-software firm plans to train one salary-benchmarking model on every client company's payroll data; client contracts allow processing only to run each client's own payroll. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Train by federated learning so no client's data leaves its system
options.B: Have management obtain clients' agreement to shared model training
options.C: Proceed, since the firm already holds every client's data
options.D: Pilot the model on one client's data to measure accuracy

questions.key_concept: Holding data for one purpose does not grant the right to train a shared model on it; settle rights before any technical safeguard.
questions.pre_read: Note every limit the stem states before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The contracts allow each client's data to be processed only to run that client's payroll. A pooled model learns from every client's records and then serves all of them, a new purpose the contracts do not cover, so clients' agreement comes first. Federated training keeps each client's records in place, but the shared model still learns from all of them, so the use is still one the contracts do not cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because client data never leaves each client's system. But every client's data still trains a model that serves all clients, a purpose the contracts never allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the firm lawfully holds the data. But holding it to run payroll does not permit using it to train a shared model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it tests value early. But testing on a client's data is itself a use the contracts may not allow; rights come first.

tips: Eliminate: C treats holding data as permission for any use, and D tests on data before the right to use it is settled.
Final two: B beats A because a shared model is a new purpose wherever it trains; federated learning keeps data in place but still uses it for that purpose.
Exam cue: when data will train a model it was not collected for, rights to use come before any technical safeguard or test.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Retrieval rights that lag the source
questions.question: A Qatari sovereign wealth fund's research assistant indexes deal files with access rights. The index refreshes weekly, so a deal restricted on Monday stays retrievable fund-wide until Sunday. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Instruct the assistant not to quote restricted deals
options.B: Refresh the index's copy of access rights every night
options.C: Remove restricted deals from the index each quarter
options.D: Check each user's current rights at the moment of retrieval

questions.key_concept: A retrieval index holds copies of documents and their permissions; checking rights at query time keeps answers in step with the source.
questions.pre_read: Trace when the index learns that a deal was restricted.
questions.correct_explanation: The index holds its own copy of each file's access rights, so for up to a week after a deal is restricted, anyone at the fund can retrieve it through the assistant. Checking the user's current rights at the source each time the assistant retrieves closes that gap. Nightly refreshes shrink the window to a day, but a restricted deal can still reach the wrong staff within that day.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets the restricted deals. But a prompt instruction is not an access control, and rephrased questions can still draw them out.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it shortens the gap from a week to a day. But a restricted deal can still reach the wrong staff within that day.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes restricted files. But quarterly removal leaves them retrievable for months after a restriction.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt instruction, which is not access control, and C leaves restricted deals retrievable for months.
Final two: D beats B because rights checked at retrieval are always current; a nightly copy still lags the source by up to a day.
Exam cue: in retrieval systems, the index is a copy. Ask whether its access rights can fall out of step with the source.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A sawmill's grading data
questions.question: A Uruguayan sawmill cleaned its log-grading model's training data once, at build time. Live readings from its 12 scanners now feed daily grades and weekly retraining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Check live readings against ranges and patterns seen in training
options.B: Have the vendor recalibrate the 12 scanners once a year
options.C: Repeat the original cleaning checks before each weekly retraining
options.D: Rely on the model to discount readings that look faulty

questions.key_concept: Cleaning data once at build does not protect live use; inputs need checks wherever they reach the model, including for predictions.
questions.pre_read: Trace each path the data takes into the model.
questions.correct_explanation: A model gives confident grades even on faulty readings; it raises no error. Here the live readings feed both today's grades and each week's retraining, so checking them as they arrive, against what the model saw in training, protects both paths. Repeating the cleaning checks before retraining protects the next model but leaves every grade until then resting on unchecked readings.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scanners drift. But yearly calibration leaves faults between visits unchecked, and readings still reach the model untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it restores the build-time checks. But it covers only retraining; faulty readings still drive the grades issued every day in between.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because models seem to learn what normal looks like. But a model scores whatever it receives and rarely signals that an input is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: D expects the model to spot bad inputs, which models rarely do, and B fixes scanners yearly while readings go unchecked between visits.
Final two: A beats C because the readings drive daily grades as well as retraining; checking only before retraining leaves every grade exposed.
Exam cue: data checked once at build is not checked in production. Look for every path by which live data reaches the model.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Labelers who agree
questions.question: A Nigerian music-streaming app's comment filter learns from toxicity labels by six overseas contractors, who agree on 96% of comments. A third of the comments are in Nigerian Pidgin. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Sending users' comments to overseas contractors may breach privacy rules
options.B: Agreement below 100% shows the labels cannot be trusted
options.C: The contractors' agreement may reflect a shared misreading of Pidgin
options.D: Users may dodge the filter by writing abuse in Pidgin slang

questions.key_concept: High labeler agreement shows consistency, not accuracy; labelers who share a gap, such as a language, agree on the same wrong labels.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced the labels and what they were able to judge.
questions.correct_explanation: Agreement shows labelers are consistent, not that they are right. Six contractors outside Nigeria may all misread Pidgin slang or banter the same way, so 96% agreement can hide systematic errors on a third of the comments, and the filter would learn to treat Pidgin speakers' posts as toxic. Sending comments abroad raises a privacy question to manage, but it does not corrupt what the model learns.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because comments carry personal data. But that is a privacy question to manage; it does not corrupt the labels the filter learns from.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because labels should be reliable. But no labeling reaches full agreement; 96% is high, and the issue is what the agreement measures.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because evasion through slang is real. But nothing here points to it; the stated facts concern how the labels were made.

tips: Eliminate: B demands perfect agreement, which no labeling reaches, and D raises evasion, which nothing in the facts points to.
Final two: C beats A because shared misreadings corrupt the labels for a third of comments and bias the filter against Pidgin speakers; data access is a separate, manageable risk.
Exam cue: agreement among labelers is not accuracy. Ask whether the labelers could judge every kind of data they labeled.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Near-identical questions on both sides
questions.question: A Bruneian courier fine-tuned its delivery assistant on 6,000 emails. It used 600 others from the same months as unseen test questions. Customers often send near-identical questions. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add 600 more test emails drawn from those same months, then retest
options.B: Remove test emails that closely reword a tuning email, then retest
options.C: Remove test emails that exactly match a tuning email, then retest
options.D: Accept the score, as no test email was used in tuning

questions.key_concept: Separate test data must also differ in substance; reworded copies of training questions let a tuned model score from memory.
questions.pre_read: Consider how alike the training and test records are.
questions.correct_explanation: Customers often send near-identical questions, so many test emails are likely rewordings of tuning emails whose answers the model already learned. Its score then partly measures recall, not how it handles new questions. Screening out close rewordings leaves a test the model has not effectively seen. Removing exact matches catches copies but misses the rewordings, which a tuned model can often answer from what it learned.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a bigger test seems stronger. But emails drawn the same way carry the same overlap, so the score stays inflated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets duplicates directly. But customers rarely repeat a question word for word, so exact matching leaves most rewordings in the test.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the test emails are separate records. But near-identical questions let the model answer from what it learned in tuning.

tips: Eliminate: A enlarges a test drawn the same way, keeping its overlap, and D treats separate records as unseen ones.
Final two: B beats C because a tuned model can answer a reworded question from what it learned; exact matching misses most near-duplicates.
Exam cue: for language models, leakage includes paraphrases. Ask whether test items are new in substance, not just new in wording.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Photos removed from both sets
questions.question: A Latvian teledermatology clinic removed blurry and poorly lit photos from both training and test sets for its mole-checking model; patients will upload home phone photos. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test on photos left unfiltered, like those patients will send
options.B: Add blurry and dim photos to the training set, then retrain
options.C: Test separately on moles photographed on darker skin
options.D: Remove faces and backgrounds from patients' uploaded photos

questions.key_concept: Cleaning training data can be sound; filtering the test set the same way hides how the model handles the inputs it will really get.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each cleaning step changes about the results.
questions.correct_explanation: Removing blurry and dim photos from the test set means its results describe clean images only, yet patients' home photos will often be blurry or dim. Testing on an unfiltered set like the photos patients send shows how the model really performs on them. Adding such photos to training may help the model, but without an unfiltered test no one knows whether it does.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the model never learned from poor photos. But retraining is the owner's choice, and without an unfiltered test no one can tell whether it helped.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because skin-tone gaps are a known risk. But nothing here points to it; the stated fact is what the filtering removed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because home photos are sensitive. But that is a privacy step; it says nothing about how the model handles poor photos.

tips: Eliminate: C tests a risk the facts never raise, and D is a privacy step that leaves performance unknown.
Final two: A beats B because only a test that looks like real uploads shows how the model performs; retraining without one is a fix nobody can check.
Exam cue: cleaning training data can be fine; cleaning the test set hides the cases the model will meet. Test on inputs like those in use.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. An impact trigger tied to data type
questions.question: A Norwegian county's AI lifecycle requires an impact assessment only for models using personal data. Its snowplow routing model uses only road sensors, so it skipped the assessment. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a privacy review of the sensor data the routing model reads
options.B: Accept the exemption, since no personal data means low risk
options.C: Assess the model's impacts after its first full winter
options.D: Base the impact-assessment trigger on effects on people

questions.key_concept: AI can harm people without using their data; impact assessment follows who the decisions affect, not what data the model reads.
questions.pre_read: Read what the lifecycle rule measures and what the model does.
questions.correct_explanation: Plowing routes decide which roads are cleared first, so they can affect ambulance access, school travel and remote households, whatever data the model reads. A trigger tied to personal data misses AI that harms people through its decisions. Setting the trigger on effects on people brings this model, and others like it, into assessment. A privacy review of sensor data examines a risk the model barely has.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data reviews are familiar. But road sensors hold little personal data; the risk lies in which roads, and so which people, wait.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because privacy risk is low. But low privacy risk is not low impact; routing decides who gets cleared roads first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because real use shows effects. But assessing after a winter lets any harm to residents happen before anyone looks.

tips: Eliminate: B equates no personal data with low risk, and C assesses impacts only after a winter of use.
Final two: D beats A because the model affects people through its routes, not its data; a privacy review studies the wrong risk.
Exam cue: AI impact follows decisions, not data type. A model reading only sensors can still decide who waits and who gets served.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Teams choosing their own risk tier
questions.question: A Montenegrin health insurance fund's lifecycle lets each project team set its model's risk tier. The tier decides whether independent validation is needed. Most teams choose 'low'. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Let teams keep choosing, as they know their models best
options.B: Require independent validation for every model, whatever its tier
options.C: Have the AI governance committee confirm each model's risk tier
options.D: Have internal audit approve each project team's chosen tier

questions.key_concept: Risk tiers set how deep the lifecycle gates go, so someone outside the build team must confirm them; validating every model alike wastes scarce effort.
questions.pre_read: Follow how a tier choice changes the work a model must pass.
questions.correct_explanation: Teams that pick their own tier can avoid independent validation by choosing 'low', which most do. Having the AI governance committee confirm each tier keeps the decision with a body that approves high-impact uses and has no stake in an easy gate. Validating every model, whatever its tier, removes the incentive but spends scarce validation effort on low-impact models instead of the risky ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because teams know their models. But they also gain from a lighter gate, so their tier choice needs confirming.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it closes the loophole. But it treats a low-impact model like a high-impact one and spreads validators thin.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit is independent. But approving tiers is a management decision; internal audit would then assess its own decision.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves tiering with those who gain from a low tier, and D has internal audit take a management decision it must later assess.
Final two: C beats B because confirmed tiers send validation where risk is; validating everything treats low-impact models like high-impact ones.
Exam cue: when a tier decides how deep the gates go, check who sets it. Builders choosing their own tier is the gap.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. An open model for a chess app
questions.question: An Armenian chess-coaching app's engineers chose an open-weight model for its game-review helper, since the model's code repository carries an Apache 2.0 license. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have counsel check the weights' own license against the planned use
options.B: Confirm the Apache 2.0 license covers the planned commercial use
options.C: Test the model's reviews on real players' games
options.D: Proceed, since an open license permits any commercial use

questions.key_concept: Open-weight models' weights often carry their own license, separate from the code's, that may restrict uses or users; check it before building.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the team assumes from what is written down.
questions.correct_explanation: Open weights mean the model files can be downloaded, not that any use is allowed. The code that runs a model and its weights are often licensed separately, and many weight licenses restrict some uses, require separate terms above a number of users or set an acceptable-use policy. Checking the weights' license against the planned use comes first, because testing effort is wasted if the app may not use the model this way.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Apache 2.0 allows commercial use. But that license covers the repository's code; the weights often carry separate terms that can limit uses or users.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fitness must be shown. But it comes second: tests are wasted if the weights' license bars this use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because 'open' sounds unrestricted. But open-weight licenses can limit uses and users; only the terms say what is allowed.

tips: Eliminate: D reads 'open' as unrestricted, and C tests the model before anyone knows the app may use it.
Final two: A beats B because the Apache 2.0 license covers the repository's code, not necessarily the weights; only the weights' own terms say what use is allowed.
Exam cue: open weights are not open permission. Before building on a downloaded model, check what the weights' own license allows.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A model card's assumed review
questions.question: A Cambodian eye clinic's retinal-scan model has a vendor model card saying results assume an ophthalmologist reviews every scan. The clinic now clears scans rated normal without one. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model's accuracy may drift as cameras and patient groups change
options.B: The vendor's evidence no longer covers how the model is used
options.C: The model card may be too technical for clinicians to use
options.D: The vendor becomes accountable for every scan cleared

questions.key_concept: A model card's conditions of use are part of its evidence; using the model outside them leaves its results unsupported.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed after the model was bought.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor's results assume an ophthalmologist reviews every scan, so misses the model makes were expected to be caught. Clearing 'normal' scans without that review removes the safety net the results depend on, and patients with missed eye disease get no follow-up. Drift is a real risk for any model, but nothing here points to it; the stated change in use does.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because drift affects every model. But nothing here points to it; the stated fact is that the assumed review was removed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because documentation must be usable. But readability is minor beside using the model outside its stated conditions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the model. But the clinic that clears scans stays accountable for that decision.

tips: Eliminate: C is a documentation style issue, and D wrongly moves accountability for the clinic's decisions to the vendor.
Final two: B beats A because the stated change removes the review the card's results depend on; drift is a real risk the facts never raise.
Exam cue: model cards state conditions as well as scores. Using a model outside its stated conditions leaves its evidence behind.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Offline copies that outlive the server
questions.question: Bolivia's health ministry retired its faulty child-malnutrition screening model and shut its server, yet health workers screen children daily with offline copies on tablets the ministry manages remotely. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Take down the download link so no further tablets receive the model
options.B: Mark the model and its offline copies retired in the AI inventory
options.C: Retrain the model to fix the errors, then reissue it
options.D: Disable the model on every device that already holds it

questions.key_concept: A model retired on the server still acts wherever copies run; retirement must disable every copy, including offline ones on devices.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option changes for the next child screened.
questions.correct_explanation: Shutting the server stopped one copy, but the offline copies on tablets keep screening children with the faulty model, so wrong results still reach families. Because the ministry manages the tablets remotely, it can disable the model on every one now. Removing the download link prevents new copies but leaves every tablet that already has the model screening children with it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it stops the model spreading. But every tablet that already holds it keeps screening children with the faulty version.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the inventory should show every copy as retired. But a record changes nothing on the tablets still using the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the errors need fixing. But a retrained model is a new model needing validation, and the faulty copies keep running meanwhile.

tips: Eliminate: B updates a record while copies keep running, and C builds a new model that needs validation while the faulty copies stay in use.
Final two: D beats A because existing copies keep screening children; blocking new downloads protects only tablets that never had the model.
Exam cue: retiring a model means stopping every copy, including offline and on-device ones, not just the server.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Promises an agent left behind
questions.question: A Taiwanese logistics firm retired its customer chat agent. In chats, it promised 180 customers refunds, some after being coaxed past its rules. No refund system records them. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Restore the agent so it can complete the refunds it promised
options.B: Have the IS auditor decide which promises the firm honors
options.C: Have a service manager review each promise the agent made
options.D: Honor the promises the agent logged as within its rules

questions.key_concept: Agents make commitments in conversations that systems may not record; retirement includes finding and settling them under a named owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the agent left unfinished when it was switched off.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent's promises in chats can bind or mislead customers even when no system recorded them, and retiring the agent leaves nobody tracking them. A service manager reviewing each promise against the firm's refund rules decides which to honor, correct or explain, so every commitment has a named person accountable. Honoring the promises the agent logged as within its rules, option D, trusts the agent's own judgment, which the coaxing manipulated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the agent made the promises. But a retired agent settling its own promises decides again with no person accountable, including on promises it was coaxed into.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the auditor is independent of the agent. But deciding which promises to honor is management's call; the auditor assesses and recommends, never settles them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the agent's logs look like system evidence. But coaxing that got the agent past its rules can skew its own record too, so the log cannot sort them.

tips: Eliminate: A brings back a retired agent to settle its own promises, and B puts the auditor in management's seat, deciding which promises the firm honors.
Final two: C beats D because coaxing that got the agent past its rules can skew its own log too; only a person's review sorts the promises on their merits.
Exam cue: when an agent retires, look for what it left open: promises, bookings and tasks in progress. Each needs a named owner to settle it.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A change board that reads only code
questions.question: An Ethiopian telecom's change board approves each retrained airtime-loan model by reviewing its code differences, usually none, and the builders' accuracy summary. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Base approval on independent tests of how each version decides
options.B: Have the IS auditor sign off each retrained release
options.C: Ask the builders to explain each release's code changes in more detail
options.D: Fast-track retrained releases that show no code changes

questions.key_concept: Retraining changes a model's behavior with no code change, so change approval must rest on independent tests of how each version decides.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually changes when a model is retrained.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrain changes the model's weights through new data, usually with no code change, so a board reading code differences sees almost nothing, and the builders' own summary is not independent evidence. Basing approval on independent tests of how the new version decides shows what actually changed. More detail on code changes still describes the code, not the decisions the retrained model makes.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because auditors are independent. But approving releases is a management decision; the IS auditor would later audit their own sign-off.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it deepens the board's existing review. But a retrain changes weights, not code, so more code detail still shows nothing about how the model now decides.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because nothing in the code changed. But a retrain changes the model's weights, so a release with no code change can still decide very differently.

tips: Eliminate: B has the IS auditor take a release decision that belongs to management, and D waves retrains through because their code is unchanged.
Final two: A beats C because a retrained model changes through its data, not its code; more code detail cannot show how it now decides.
Exam cue: if a change process only sees code, retraining slips past it. Ask who approves a retrained model, and on what evidence.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. An emergency prompt fix
questions.question: A Kuwaiti cinema chain's assistant quoted outdated fees on cancellations and exchanges. Spot checks on fees alone show an emergency system-prompt line, 'never discuss refunds', stopped those quotes. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST next?

options.A: Check that users cannot prompt the assistant past the new line
options.B: Confirm with a sample of fee questions that quoting has stopped
options.C: Retrain the model so the new prompt line can be removed
options.D: Regression-test answers on every topic the assistant covers

questions.key_concept: A system prompt shapes every answer, so a one-line fix can change unrelated behavior; test across topics, not just the target.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else a change could affect besides what it was meant to fix.
questions.correct_explanation: A system prompt shapes every answer, and 'never discuss refunds' can also stop the assistant explaining the cancellations and exchanges it handles, yet the spot checks covered fees only. Regression tests across every topic show what else the emergency change altered. Checking that users cannot argue past the line tests resistance to attack, but the line was added for accuracy, and its effect on every customer's ordinary answers is the untested risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because prompt rules can be argued around. But the line was added for accuracy, not security; its untested effect on every customer's other answers is the larger risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it confirms the fix worked. But the spot checks already show that; the new line can change answers on other topics too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems a lasting fix. But retraining is a bigger change needing its own tests, and it leaves this edit untested.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats the spot checks already done, and C answers an untested change with a bigger one.
Final two: D beats A because a prompt line acts on every answer; bypass testing probes attackers, not what the line changed for every customer.
Exam cue: emergency AI changes still need testing afterward, and for prompts that means the whole range of answers, not just the target.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A baseline for a hosted assistant
questions.question: A Bahraini insurer's configuration baseline for its hosted claims assistant covers network, identity and encryption settings, which a monthly scan checks. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run the baseline scan weekly instead of monthly
options.B: Add the settings that shape answers, such as prompt and filters
options.C: Rely on the hosting vendor to keep the assistant's settings stable
options.D: Encrypt the assistant's chat logs at rest as well

questions.key_concept: For AI services, the prompt, model version, filters and retrieval sources are configuration items and belong in the baseline.
questions.pre_read: Think about what makes this system different from an ordinary server.
questions.correct_explanation: An assistant's answers depend on its system prompt, model version, safety filters and retrieval sources. None of these are in a baseline built for servers, so they can change without detection while every scan passes. Adding them lets the baseline catch changes that alter claims answers. Scanning weekly checks the same infrastructure settings more often and still misses every change to the assistant's behavior.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more frequent checks catch drift sooner. But the scan still covers only infrastructure, so changes to prompts or filters stay invisible.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor hosts it. But the insurer sets its own prompt and filters, and vendors change settings too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs hold personal data. But encryption protects stored chats; it does not track the settings that shape answers.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the insurer's own settings to the vendor, and D adds a security control that tracks no configuration.
Final two: B beats A because the gap is what the baseline covers; scanning infrastructure more often still misses prompt and filter changes.
Exam cue: an AI baseline lists what shapes outputs: model version, prompt, settings, filters and retrieval sources.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Cached answers after a rollback
questions.question: A Zambian agro-dealer chain rolled its farmer assistant back after wrong pesticide-mixing answers, but its response cache keeps serving stored answers to repeated questions for 30 days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Shorten the cache's expiry from 30 days to one day
options.B: Retest the restored version on pesticide-mixing questions
options.C: Stop serving answers cached under the withdrawn version
options.D: Add a notice that cached answers may be out of date

questions.key_concept: A rollback is complete only when nothing produced by the withdrawn version keeps reaching users, including cached generated answers.
questions.pre_read: Trace every path by which an answer reaches a customer.
questions.correct_explanation: The rollback restored the model, but the cache still hands farmers answers the faulty version wrote, so wrong mixing instructions keep going out for up to 30 days. Stopping those cached answers, while keeping a copy for the investigation, completes the rollback. A one-day expiry shortens future exposure but still serves today's wrong answers until they expire.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because shorter caching limits staleness. But wrong mixing answers already stored keep going out until they expire.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a rollback should be confirmed. But retesting the restored model checks fresh answers; the cache keeps serving the withdrawn version's answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns farmers. But wrong mixing instructions still reach them, and a notice does not withdraw them.

tips: Eliminate: D warns instead of withdrawing wrong answers, and B retests the restored model while the cache keeps serving old answers.
Final two: C beats A because answers already cached keep going out until purged; a shorter expiry limits future exposure, not today's.
Exam cue: after an AI rollback, look for what the bad version left in service: caches, stored outputs and downstream copies.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A feature the vendor switched on
questions.question: An Austrian notary office's hosted staff assistant gained a 'memory' feature in a vendor update. The feature keeps client details across chats and is on by default. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept it, since vendor updates fall under the vendor's testing
options.B: Pin the model version so that new vendor updates cannot apply
options.C: Review a sample of stored memories each quarter
options.D: Turn it off office-wide until assessed and approved as a change

questions.key_concept: Vendor updates can add capabilities, such as memory or tools, that change data flows and risks; treat them as changes before use.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of change the update made to the service.
questions.correct_explanation: A memory that keeps client details across chats changes what the assistant stores, who may see it later and how long it lasts, so it is a change for the office to assess and approve, with the feature off office-wide until then. Pinning the model version only stops future model changes; it does not switch off a feature already running.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor tests its releases. But vendor testing covers the vendor's product, not this office's client data or duties.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because pinning is a standard control for vendor model updates. But it stops future model changes; the memory feature has already arrived and stays on.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it looks at what is stored. But quarterly review finds client details only after they have been kept and reused.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on the vendor's testing for the office's own risks, and C reviews stored client details months after the fact.
Final two: D beats B because the memory is a service feature already running; pinning the model version stops future model changes but leaves it on and unassessed.
Exam cue: vendor updates can add features as well as change models. A new capability is a change for the deployer to assess.
