questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A same-day cutover
questions.question: An Ivorian cashew board plans a same-day cutover to its new nut-grading model, after both models graded last season's stored lots alike for a month. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Keep the old model runnable until the new one's live grades hold
options.B: Proceed with the cutover, since a month of parallel grading matched
options.C: Delete the old model's files and logs, now superseded
options.D: Retrain the old model on new data to serve as a backup

questions.key_concept: Until a replacement proves itself on live inputs, the old model stays runnable as the fallback; past-data comparisons cannot show live performance.
questions.pre_read: Picture the week after go-live before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Both models were compared only on last season's stored lots, and this harvest's live lots can differ, so the new model may grade badly in its first weeks. Keeping the old model runnable until live grades hold gives a quick way back. A month of matching parallel grading is sound changeover evidence, but it came from past lots, not the live inputs the new model now faces.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a completed parallel run is classic changeover evidence. But it used last season's stored lots, and this harvest's live lots can differ.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the new model takes over. But the old model's files and logs are evidence for past grades and should be kept under retention rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a backup sounds prudent. But a retrained old model is a new, untested model, not the proven fallback.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes records that past grades depend on, and D builds a new untested model instead of keeping the proven one.
Final two: A beats B because the parallel run used last season's stored lots; only live grades show the new model copes with this harvest.
Exam cue: retire the old model only after the new one proves itself on live inputs; until then the old one is the fallback.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A withdrawn version still listed as approved
questions.question: A Turkish bank withdrew a model version for age bias, but its registry still showed it approved. The card unit deployed it, as it tested most accurate. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the version on card data to correct the age bias
options.B: Have the card unit's manager approve each model it deploys
options.C: Have each withdrawal block the version in the registry
options.D: Delete the withdrawn version and its records from the registry

questions.key_concept: Withdrawing a model must change its status where teams pick models; accuracy tests will not reveal why it was withdrawn.
questions.pre_read: Trace how the card unit chose the version it deployed.
questions.correct_explanation: The card unit relied on the registry, which still showed the version approved, and its accuracy test could not reveal the age bias behind the withdrawal. Having withdrawal block the version in the registry stops any team reusing it. A manager's approval adds a check, but the manager sees the same 'approved' status and accuracy result, so the withdrawn version would pass again.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it fixes the bias for card use. But a retrained model is a new model needing validation, and the registry gap remains.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because approval adds a person. But the manager would see the same 'approved' status and accuracy result, so the version would pass again.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes the risk. But the version's records are evidence for decisions it made and must be kept, marked withdrawn.

tips: Eliminate: D destroys records of decisions the version made, and A treats a retrain as a quick fix while the registry gap stays.
Final two: C beats B because a manager would see the same 'approved' status and accuracy result; only the registry status can stop reuse.
Exam cue: a withdrawn model is still a deployable file. Make its status follow the decision, and keep its records.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. An app release that compresses photos
questions.question: An Egyptian car insurer's app team approved a release compressing claim photos more, unaware the damage-estimate model reads them. Data science heard of it by chance. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the release, since the model itself did not change
options.B: Map each model's input sources so any change to them triggers review
options.C: Have data science retest the model on compressed photos first
options.D: Monitor estimate patterns after each app release for unusual shifts

questions.key_concept: A model depends on every system that feeds it; recording those inputs lets their changes trigger an AI impact review.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the change came to light.
questions.correct_explanation: The app team did not know the model reads its photos, so nothing linked the release to the model; data science learned of it only by chance. Recording each model's input sources lets any change to them trigger an AI impact review. Retesting on compressed photos is right for this release, but the next upstream change would again depend on luck.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing in the model changed. But its inputs did, and a model trained on sharper photos can misjudge damage in blurrier ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it tests this release's effect directly. But it fixes one change found by chance; without a record of model inputs, the next one goes unseen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because monitoring catches silent shifts. But it detects harm only after claims are mispriced, and still leaves change owners unaware of the model.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an unchanged model as unaffected by new inputs, and D finds mispriced claims only after they happen.
Final two: B beats C because retesting fixes one change found by chance; recording each model's input sources makes every upstream change trigger review.
Exam cue: a model depends on every system that feeds it. Make those systems' changes visible to the model's owner.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Routing questions to a cheaper model
questions.question: A German online pharmacy's assistant now sends questions it rates as simple to a cheaper model. That model was approved after passing tests on simple questions. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Track complaints about routed answers after the switch
options.B: Accept it, since both models come from the same vendor
options.C: Retest the cheaper model on more questions the assistant rates simple
options.D: Test how the assistant rates medicine questions before routing

questions.key_concept: When an assistant routes questions between models, its routing judgment is part of the change and needs its own testing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the approval tests actually covered.
questions.correct_explanation: The cheaper model was tested only on questions already known to be simple, but the assistant itself decides which questions count as simple. If it rates a question about medicine interactions as simple, the cheaper model answers it untested. Testing how the assistant rates questions covers that. A larger simple-question test sharpens the evidence on the cheaper model, but still never tests the rating step.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because complaints show real effects. But they arrive after customers have acted on answers no one tested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because one vendor seems one system. But a cheaper model answers differently, whoever makes it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a bigger sample is stronger evidence. But every added question is one the assistant already rated simple, so a misrated medicine question stays untested.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes models from one vendor answer alike, and A learns of wrong answers only after customers act on them.
Final two: D beats C because more simple questions still skip the rating step; a medicine question rated simple reaches the cheaper model untested.
Exam cue: when AI routes work between models, the routing judgment is itself an AI output to test.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Three mills running 'v4'
questions.question: A Ghanaian palm-oil group's three mills each run a fruit-ripeness model. Change records show all three as approved 'v4', yet the mills grade the same test images differently. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the differences, since fruit varies from mill to mill
options.B: Check each mill's deployment log names the approved v4 release
options.C: Identify each deployed model by a hash of its files
options.D: Let each mill keep whichever version grades its fruit best

questions.key_concept: A version label is a name anyone can reuse; a hash of the model files shows which trained model is actually running.
questions.pre_read: Note what is the same and what differs across the three mills.
questions.correct_explanation: The same test images graded differently means something in what each mill runs differs, whatever the records say; a label is a name that retrained or edited copies can keep. A hash of each model's files identifies exactly which trained model runs where. Deployment logs are standard evidence, but like the change records they name the label, not the files.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fruit does vary. But the test images were identical, so the difference lies in what each mill runs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deployment logs show what was installed. But they record the label 'v4', which a retrained or edited copy keeps; only the files show what runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it suits each mill. But untracked local versions break the approved baseline and leave grades no one can trace.

tips: Eliminate: A blames fruit although the test images were identical, and D lets each mill drift from the approved baseline.
Final two: C beats B because deployment logs name the label, which retrained or edited copies keep; only a hash of the model files proves which model runs.
Exam cue: in AI version control, a model's identity is its exact files, not its name.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A rollback target the vendor retires
questions.question: A Danish container line's rollback plan for its hosted customs-filing assistant names the vendor's previous model version, which the vendor retires 60 days after each new release. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep a tested fallback that does not need the retired version
options.B: Accept the vendor's release notes as the rollback evidence
options.C: Rehearse rolling back to the previous version each quarter
options.D: Pin the current version so the vendor cannot retire it

questions.key_concept: Hosted model versions disappear on the vendor's schedule, so a rollback plan that names one is only good until it is retired.
questions.pre_read: Test each part of the plan against the stem's timeline.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan's only rollback target disappears 60 days after each new release, so a fault found later, for example when customs queries arrive, leaves nothing to roll back to. A tested fallback that does not depend on the retired version, such as a manual filing procedure, keeps filings going. Quarterly rehearsals prove the rollback works only while the previous version still exists.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because release notes describe changes. But notes are vendor claims and give the line nothing to roll back to.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rehearsal proves rollback works. But it can only rehearse a target that still exists; after 60 days there is none.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pinning controls versions. But a pin holds only until the vendor retires the version.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes pinning stops a vendor retiring a version, and B treats release notes as a way back.
Final two: A beats C because rehearsal only proves a rollback to a version that still exists; after 60 days the plan needs a fallback of its own.
Exam cue: for hosted AI, check how long the rollback target lasts. A plan that names a vendor version can expire.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Settings left at vendor defaults
questions.question: An Australian law firm's deposition-summary tool calls a pinned vendor model version but leaves output length and temperature at defaults; since a platform update, summaries stop mid-sentence. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the temperature so summaries vary less between runs
options.B: Add scheduled regression tests that check summaries are complete
options.C: Unpin the version so newer models handle longer text
options.D: Set every generation setting and keep it in the baseline

questions.key_concept: Settings left at vendor defaults change when the vendor changes them; a pinned model version does not pin its defaults.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed, given the model version did not.
questions.correct_explanation: Pinning fixed the model version, but settings left at default follow whatever the vendor sets; a platform update that shortened the default output length would cut summaries mid-sentence. Setting each generation setting explicitly and baselining it removes that dependency. Scheduled regression tests would catch the next such failure, but only after summaries break; values the firm can set itself should not be left to the vendor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because temperature affects variation. But a higher temperature makes answers vary more, not less, and length is the setting at issue.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scheduled regression tests catch vendor-side changes the firm cannot control. But these values are the firm's to set; tests would only flag the next change after summaries break.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because newer models handle longer text. But unpinning invites more unannounced change and does not fix unset defaults.

tips: Eliminate: C trades a pinned version for more unannounced change, and A misreads temperature, which raises variation as it goes up.
Final two: D beats B because the firm can set these values itself and remove the cause; scheduled regression tests would flag the failure only after summaries break.
Exam cue: a pinned model version does not pin its settings. Set and baseline every value you control, and keep regression testing to catch what only the vendor can change.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. An urgent vendor fix and a test window
questions.question: A Singapore payroll bureau gives vendor model updates a three-week test window; its chatbot vendor now offers an urgent update closing a jailbreak that exposes workers' payslips. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a system-prompt rule forbidding any talk of other workers' payslips
options.B: Apply it as an emergency change after a targeted retest, rollback ready
options.C: Hold it for the window, filtering payslip data from replies meanwhile
options.D: Apply it at once untested, since the vendor tested the update

questions.key_concept: An urgent AI fix still changes behavior; an emergency change with a targeted retest, then full regression testing, weighs exposure now against an untested change.
questions.pre_read: Read both the policy and the threat before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Every day the update waits, workers' payslips stay exposed through a known jailbreak, yet the update also changes the model's behavior. Applying it as an emergency change, after a targeted retest, with owner approval, a ready rollback and full regression testing to follow, closes the exposure without applying it blind. An output filter while waiting sounds like a compensating control, but a jailbroken model can be told to encode figures past it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets the leak. But a prompt instruction is not a control; the jailbreak exists to get past such rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an output filter looks like a compensating control. But a jailbroken model can be told to spell out or encode figures past it, so payslips stay exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the fix is urgent. But a vendor's own testing does not cover this bureau's use, and the update can break other answers.

tips: Eliminate: D trusts vendor testing that never covered the bureau's use, and A treats a prompt rule as a control against a jailbreak.
Final two: B beats C because a jailbroken model can be told to encode payslip figures past an output filter; an emergency change with a targeted retest, then full regression testing, closes the hole.
Exam cue: urgent AI fixes still get tested, but the test scales to the risk of waiting. Expedited is not untested.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. A city's approval step for AI outputs
questions.question: A Finnish city has one officer approve every AI output, from meeting summaries to notices ordering families to repay housing aid; most approvals take under ten seconds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Require officers to record a reason for each approval
options.B: Drop the approval step once outputs prove accurate for a month
options.C: Match each use's oversight to the impact of its outputs
options.D: Have a second officer also approve every AI output

questions.key_concept: Oversight should be proportionate to impact; reviewing every low-impact output breeds rubber-stamping that weakens review where it matters.
questions.pre_read: Read every number in the stem, then ask what it shows about how the review works.
questions.correct_explanation: One design for every use spends the same officer time on meeting summaries as on repayment notices that can hurt families, and approvals taking seconds show rubber-stamping. Matching oversight to impact cuts the volume of low-stakes approvals and focuses real review on high-impact notices. Requiring a reason for each approval adds evidence, but under the same volume reasons become boilerplate and automation bias persists.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recorded reasons evidence real review. But officers approving every output face the same volume, so reasons turn to boilerplate; the design drives the rubber-stamping.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy seems to earn trust. But a month of good outputs does not justify removing review of high-impact decisions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because two reviewers seem stronger than one. But it doubles the volume that breeds rubber-stamping, both may defer to the AI, and review is still not matched to impact.

tips: Eliminate: B removes review after a short run of good outputs, and D doubles an approval volume that already breeds rubber-stamping.
Final two: C beats A because recorded reasons leave the volume that breeds rubber-stamping; oversight matched to impact gives officers time for the notices that can harm families.
Exam cue: oversight is proportionate. Human-in-the-loop for high-impact decisions; lighter oversight where errors cost little.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Overrides limited to three slots
questions.question: A Portuguese hospital's surgical-waiting-list model proposes three operating slots per patient; surgeons may override only by choosing another of those three. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Let surgeons set any slot, with a recorded reason
options.B: Have surgeons rate the proposed slots to retrain the model
options.C: Have managers review a monthly sample of surgeons' overrides
options.D: Remove overrides so the schedule stays efficient

questions.key_concept: An override limited to the model's own options is not real oversight; people must be able to decide outside what the model offers.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the override actually lets surgeons change.
questions.correct_explanation: If all three proposed slots are wrong for a patient, for example too late for a worsening condition, surgeons cannot act on their judgment, so the model still decides. Letting them set any slot, with a recorded reason, makes the override real and gives the model owner data on errors. Reviewing a sample of overrides is sound monitoring, but every override it sees is still one of the model's own three slots.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because feedback improves models. But rating slots does not let surgeons fix a patient's slot today.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reviewing overrides is a sound detective control. But every override it sees is one of the model's three slots, so a case none of them suits stays unfixable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because overrides slow scheduling. But removing them leaves surgical timing entirely to the model, with no human check.

tips: Eliminate: D removes the human check, and B turns oversight into feedback that fixes no patient's slot today.
Final two: A beats C because a review sees only choices among the model's three slots; real override lets surgeons decide outside them.
Exam cue: an override that only picks among the AI's own options is not oversight. People must be able to decide differently.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Fairness after launch
questions.question: A US state's food-assistance fraud model passed fairness tests by age and race at launch; production records lack race, so monitoring tracks only overall fraud-flag rates. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rerun the launch fairness tests yearly on the launch test set
options.B: Review group results regularly, surveying samples if needed
options.C: Rely on overall flag rates, since launch tests found no gap
options.D: Remove age from the model so no group is treated differently

questions.key_concept: Fairness can drift after launch as people and patterns change; group results need monitoring in production, not only a launch test.
questions.pre_read: Ask which population each fairness check describes.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness shown at launch can drift as applicants and fraud patterns change, and overall flag rates can stay steady while one group's rate climbs. So group results need regular review in production, using surveyed or consented samples where records lack the data. Rerunning the launch tests yearly checks the same old records, so it cannot show how today's applicants are treated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it repeats a recognized test. But the launch test set is frozen in time and cannot show how today's applicants fare.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because launch tests passed. But overall rates can stay steady while one group's flags rise.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as fairness by removing inputs. But other inputs can stand in for age, and only measured outcomes show unequal treatment.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts an overall rate that can mask one group's rise, and D assumes dropping an input removes bias.
Final two: B beats A because a frozen launch test set cannot show how today's applicants are treated; production group results can.
Exam cue: fairness is monitored like accuracy. A launch test is a snapshot; drift can reopen gaps between groups.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Monthly checks of a helpdesk assistant
questions.question: An Indian IT-services firm's generative helpdesk assistant, built for IT help, answers any question. It passes a fixed 200-question IT test monthly. Logs hold every staff conversation. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Track staff ratings on each logged conversation
options.B: Check sampled logged IT answers against the IT knowledge base
options.C: Track the assistant's uptime and response times monthly
options.D: Sample logged conversations to see what staff use it for

questions.key_concept: People use generative assistants for tasks no one planned; monitoring must look at real use, not only a fixed test set.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the monthly check can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: The monthly checks test only the 200 IT questions someone planned. Because the assistant answers any typed question, staff can take it into HR, legal or security matters no check covers. Sampling real conversations finds the uses the checks miss, so those new uses and their risks can be assessed. Checking sampled answers against the IT knowledge base tests real answers, but only on the IT use already foreseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because users notice errors. But staff often cannot tell a confident wrong answer, and ratings show nothing about off-topic use.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it checks real answers. But it judges only IT answers; any other use staff make of the assistant is never looked for.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because availability is routine IT monitoring. But uptime and speed say nothing about whether answers are right or what staff use the assistant for.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on ratings from staff who may not spot wrong answers, and C watches the service, not its answers or how staff use it.
Final two: D beats B because checking answers against the IT knowledge base covers only the planned IT use; sampling conversations finds the unplanned uses the checks miss.
Exam cue: monitor generative AI for how it is used, not only how it scores. Real use drifts beyond intended purpose.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Logs for a retrieval assistant
questions.question: A New Zealand council's building-consent assistant logs each question, answer and model version; its guidance index changes weekly, and applicants dispute advice months later. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Log which passages, by version, each answer drew on
options.B: Rerun disputed questions today to recreate each answer
options.C: Shorten log retention to protect applicants' privacy
options.D: Log the system prompt version alongside each answer's model version

questions.key_concept: A retrieval assistant's answer depends on the passages it retrieved; logging their versions lets a disputed answer be traced to its sources.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the log would let staff explain months later.
questions.correct_explanation: Each answer depends on the guidance passages the assistant retrieved, and the index changes weekly, so months later no one can tell which guidance it relied on. Logging the passages and their versions with each answer lets staff trace a disputed answer to its sources. The prompt version also shapes answers and is worth logging, but it cannot show which guidance an answer relied on.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rerunning seems direct. But the index has changed since, and generated answers vary, so a rerun shows today's answer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as privacy. But disputes arrive months later, and shorter logs leave less evidence, not better evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because prompts shape answers. But the prompt cannot show which guidance an answer relied on; the retrieved passages can.

tips: Eliminate: B reruns against a changed index and varying output, and C cuts the evidence disputes depend on.
Final two: A beats D because the retrieved passages, not the prompt, show which guidance an answer relied on.
Exam cue: for retrieval-based AI, the decision log needs what was retrieved, by version, as well as the model and prompt.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeals and the next nightly run
questions.question: A Brazilian freelance platform's account-fraud model rescores every freelancer nightly. When reviewers lift a payout freeze on appeal, the next night's run often freezes the payout again. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model on upheld appeals, used as corrected labels
options.B: Rescore freelancers weekly so reviewers have time to act
options.C: Stop later runs reversing an upheld appeal without new evidence
options.D: Ask affected freelancers to appeal again whenever it recurs

questions.key_concept: A decision reversed on appeal must survive the model's later runs; otherwise automation quietly overrules the human reviewer.
questions.pre_read: Follow one appealed case through the days after the appeal.
questions.correct_explanation: Reviewers lift freezes on appeal, but the nightly run rescores the same freelancers on much the same data and freezes many again, so the model, not the reviewer, has the last word. An upheld appeal should hold unless new evidence arrives. Retraining on upheld appeals as corrected labels improves the model over time, but until it does, and even after, the next score can undo a reviewer's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because upheld appeals make valuable labels. But retraining comes later and may still score this freelancer as fraud; the reviewer's decision must hold now.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it slows the cycle. But a weekly run still overturns the reviewer's decision, only a few days later.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because freelancers can still seek review. But repeated appeals leave them frozen between rounds while the model keeps overruling reviewers.

tips: Eliminate: B only slows the run that overturns reviewers, and D puts the burden on freelancers while the model keeps overruling the appeal.
Final two: C beats A because retraining on appeal outcomes helps later, but only a rule that later runs cannot undo an upheld appeal makes the reviewer's decision final now.
Exam cue: a human reversal must outrank the model's next run. If automation can quietly reimpose a decision, oversight exists in name only.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Acceptance by comparison with the live model
questions.question: An Argentine aircraft-maintenance firm accepts each new engine-crack detection model if it misses fewer cracks than the live one, whose misses have drifted above management's tolerance. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the tolerance to match what the live model achieves
options.B: Require new models' misses to fall within the tolerance
options.C: Keep the rule, since any improvement lowers the risk
options.D: Require fewer misses than the live one on every crack type

questions.key_concept: Acceptance criteria come from risk tolerance; beating the current model is not enough when the current model falls short.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the acceptance rule compares a new model with.
questions.correct_explanation: Each new model only has to beat a live model whose misses have drifted above management's tolerance, so a model still outside tolerance can be accepted, and the bar sinks as the live model degrades. Acceptance should require misses within the tolerance. Comparing crack type by crack type is sounder than one overall figure, but beating a failing model on every type can still leave it short of the safety limit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it makes the live model compliant. But moving the limit to fit results hides the risk instead of meeting the criterion.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fewer misses is better. But better than an unacceptable model is not the same as acceptable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one overall figure can hide weak spots. But beating a model that already misses too many cracks, even on every type, can still leave misses above tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: C treats any improvement as enough, and A moves the limit to fit the results.
Final two: B beats D because beating a failing model on every crack type is still only relative; acceptance needs misses within management's tolerance.
Exam cue: acceptance criteria are absolute limits set from risk tolerance. 'Better than before' is not a pass mark.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A simulated portal that never fails
questions.question: An Italian freight forwarder's AI agent books truck slots through ports' booking portals; its acceptance tests used a simulated portal that always answered successfully. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before go-live?

options.A: Test the portal connector's error codes for failures and timeouts
options.B: Rely on the portals' own checks to reject bad bookings
options.C: Test how the agent acts when a portal fails or times out
options.D: Raise the pass mark on the successful simulated runs

questions.key_concept: Agents may retry, guess or report success when a tool fails; acceptance tests must include tool errors, not only perfect responses.
questions.pre_read: Compare the test environment with the live one.
questions.correct_explanation: A simulator that always succeeds never shows what the agent does when a portal errors, times out or returns partial data, and agents can retry repeatedly, book twice or report a booking that never happened. Testing those failures before go-live shows whether it handles them safely. Testing the connector's error codes shows the error reaches the agent, not what the agent then chooses to do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because error handling is classic interface testing. But a correct error code only reaches the agent; whether it then retries, double-books or claims success stays untested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because portals validate input. But they cannot stop the agent booking twice or reporting a booking that failed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a higher bar sounds stricter. But the runs never included a failure, so any pass mark measures the wrong thing.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the agent's choices to outside systems, and D raises a bar on tests that never included a failure.
Final two: C beats A because a correct error code only reaches the agent; only failure tests of the agent show whether it retries, double-books or reports false success.
Exam cue: test AI agents under tool failure. Perfect simulated tools hide how an agent improvises when things go wrong.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Fairness tests of a typing-rhythm check
questions.question: A British building society's sign-in model checks members' typing rhythm. Its fairness tests compared false rejections by age and sex, the only groups in the society's records. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the tests, since no member group showed a gap
options.B: Add a disability field to the model's inputs
options.C: Break the results down further, by combined age and sex groups
options.D: Test it with members who have motor or vision impairments

questions.key_concept: Fairness tests cover only the groups tested; behavioral models need testing with groups, such as people with disabilities, that records may not hold.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the sign-in model actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Typing rhythm depends on how people use a keyboard, so members with tremors, limited dexterity or screen readers may be rejected far more often. The records hold no disability data, so the tests could not see them. Testing with members who have these impairments fills that gap. Combining age and sex is a sound intersectional step, but it still looks only at recorded groups.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tests passed. But they covered only the groups on record, not people whose typing differs most.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it records disability. But adding an input does not test outcomes, and the society should not need it to verify identity.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because combined groups reveal hidden gaps. But they are still built from age and sex; groups the records lack stay invisible.

tips: Eliminate: A treats tests of recorded groups as complete, and B adds an input instead of testing outcomes.
Final two: D beats C because finer splits of age and sex still miss groups the records never hold, such as people whose disability changes how they type.
Exam cue: ask who the model's input could disadvantage, then test those groups, even when records do not hold them.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Equal error rates against past ratings
questions.question: A Dutch warehouse operator tested its promotion-readiness model against supervisors' past ratings, which a staff survey says favor men. The model's error rates for women and men match. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Equal error rates cannot show fairness against disputed ratings
options.B: A staff survey is opinion and cannot outweigh measured test results
options.C: Removing sex from the inputs would settle the concern
options.D: Equal error rates on past ratings show it treats both sexes fairly

questions.key_concept: A fairness test is only as sound as its labels; matching biased ratings equally well reproduces their bias.
questions.pre_read: Examine every part of the test, not only its result.
questions.correct_explanation: Error rates show how often the model disagrees with its labels, here supervisors' past ratings. If those ratings favor men, a model that matches them equally well for both sexes has learned the same bias, so equal error rates prove little. A survey is weaker evidence than a measurement, but it questions the labels themselves, which the test assumes are right.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because measured results usually beat opinions. But the measurement assumes the ratings are fair; the survey questions exactly that assumption.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as fairness by removing inputs. But the bias sits in the ratings the model learned, and other inputs can stand in for sex.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because equal error rates are a common fairness test. But equal agreement with biased ratings reproduces the bias.

tips: Eliminate: D reads equal error rates as proof of fairness, and C assumes removing an input removes bias held in the labels.
Final two: A beats B because the test measures agreement with ratings the survey calls biased; a measurement cannot outweigh doubt about its own yardstick.
Exam cue: before trusting a fairness metric, check the labels it is measured against. Biased labels make biased models look fair.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A public jailbreak library
questions.question: A Swiss private bank's client chatbot passed red-team testing that used only a public jailbreak library, which its model vendor also uses in safety training. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the results, since the library holds the best-known attacks
options.B: Add attacks written fresh for the chatbot and its uses
options.C: Rerun the public library on the chatbot after each vendor update
options.D: Ask the vendor to share its own safety-training test results

questions.key_concept: A model trained against a public attack library can pass it from memory; red teaming needs fresh attacks the model has not seen.
questions.pre_read: Check the source of any test before trusting its result.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor trains its model on the same public library, so the chatbot may refuse those exact prompts from memory while failing new or reworded attacks; a pass shows little. Fresh attacks written for this chatbot and its uses test what the library cannot. Rerunning the library after each vendor update keeps testing regular, but it repeats prompts the model was trained to refuse.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the library covers well-known attacks. But the model was trained on those prompts, so passing them shows memory, not resistance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retesting after updates is sound practice. But it repeats prompts the model was trained to refuse, so it keeps passing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor ran safety training. But its results are vendor claims about the same library, not tests of this bank's chatbot.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a pass on well-known prompts as resistance, and D relies on the vendor's own results about the same library.
Final two: B beats C because rerunning a library the model was trained on keeps passing; only attacks it has never seen show real resistance.
Exam cue: a test the model may have trained on is not a test. Red teams need fresh attacks, not only public lists.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A fees assistant's robustness tests
questions.question: A Chilean language school's student-fees assistant passed robustness tests in which each of 300 fee questions was asked five times, always in the questions' standard wording. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Ask each question twenty times to measure variation better
options.B: Require students to choose questions from a fixed menu
options.C: Accept the results, since five runs already show stable answers
options.D: Retest with reworded, misspelled and informal versions

questions.key_concept: Repeating one wording tests run-to-run variation; robustness also needs varied wordings, because small changes in phrasing can change answers.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of variation the tests covered.
questions.correct_explanation: Asking each question five times in its standard wording tests whether the assistant answers consistently, not whether it copes with how students really write: rewording, typos and slang can change a generated answer. Retesting with varied versions of each question checks that. Twenty runs per question measures the same run-to-run variation more precisely, but still never changes the wording.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more runs sharpen the estimate. But they measure the same variation; the wording students use still goes untested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it limits inputs. But it defeats the assistant's purpose and does not test the assistant itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because consistent answers are reassuring. But consistency on one wording says nothing about reworded questions.

tips: Eliminate: C treats consistency on one wording as robustness, and B narrows inputs instead of testing them.
Final two: D beats A because more runs measure the same variation; only varied wordings test how students really ask.
Exam cue: generative AI has two kinds of variation to test: the same input run many times, and the same meaning phrased many ways.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Precise scores from a face-entry API
questions.question: An Emirati gym chain fine-tuned a face model on members' photos; partner apps submitting any image get a precise match score per member. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Firewall gaps letting partners reach the member database
options.B: Partners keeping score logs past the agreed retention period
options.C: Rebuilding members' likenesses by tuning images against scores
options.D: Partner apps slowing door entry through heavy API use

questions.key_concept: Precise per-person scores let attackers rebuild likenesses of people a model learned, so the scores themselves expose biometric data.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each threat by likelihood and who it would harm.
questions.correct_explanation: Precise per-member scores for any submitted image let an attacker adjust an image step by step until one member's score peaks, rebuilding a likeness of that member's face, which harms members and cannot be recalled. Partners keeping score logs too long is a data-handling gap, but the exposure comes from the live scores themselves, whoever keeps them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as classic network risk. But the stem gives no firewall gap, while the score design is an AI-specific exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retention breaches are classic data risk. But the scores leak faces as they are served, so deleting logs on time would not stop a likeness being rebuilt.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because API load is real. But slower entry is an inconvenience, not exposure of members' biometric data.

tips: Eliminate: D is a capacity issue, and A assumes a network gap the stem never gives.
Final two: C beats B because the scores leak faces as they are served; deleting logs on time cannot stop a likeness being rebuilt.
Exam cue: precise per-person scores enable model inversion. Treat a model's scores as exposing the people it learned.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Model files on a shared drive
questions.question: A Maltese online casino's collusion-detection model files sit on a read-only shared drive open to 300 staff and contractors. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Cheaters testing evasions offline on a leaked model copy
options.B: Attackers flooding the model with queries to slow detection
options.C: Staff altering the model files to hide their own collusion
options.D: A rival casino reusing a leaked copy to save development costs

questions.key_concept: A leaked model lets attackers test evasions offline, unseen and unlimited; for a detection model that outweighs the loss of its design.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each party could do with a copy of the files.
questions.correct_explanation: With a copy of the model files, colluding players or their helpers can try endless variations offline until play goes undetected, with no queries the casino could notice. That defeats the model's purpose and harms honest players. A rival reusing the model is a real intellectual-property loss, but the casino keeps detecting collusion; leaked detection logic is the greater harm.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as denial of service. But flooding needs access to the live service; copies of files on a drive do not enable it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because insiders can tamper. But the drive is read-only, so staff can copy the files but not alter them there.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model has commercial value. But a rival's reuse leaves detection working, while cheaters with a copy can learn to beat it.

tips: Eliminate: C needs write access the read-only drive does not give, and B attacks the live service rather than the stored files.
Final two: A beats D because a leaked detection model lets cheaters test evasions unseen, defeating its purpose; reuse by a rival is a business loss only.
Exam cue: model files are sensitive assets. For detection models, leaked weights mean attackers can rehearse evasion offline.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. One agent reading for another
questions.question: A South Korean trading house's research agent summarizes supplier websites for its purchasing agent, which can issue orders; only the research agent reads web content. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run both agents under one account to simplify monitoring
options.B: Require human approval for orders that rely on web summaries
options.C: Trust the summaries, since the purchasing agent does not read the web
options.D: Filter web pages for known injection phrases before reading

questions.key_concept: Text from one agent that read untrusted content can carry injected instructions to the next; limit what downstream agents can do.
questions.pre_read: Follow the web content from where it enters to where it acts.
questions.correct_explanation: A supplier page can hide instructions that the research agent passes on inside its summary, so the purchasing agent receives web content after all, just secondhand. Requiring human approval for orders that rely on those summaries stops planted text from turning into purchases. Filtering for known phrases helps, but injection wording varies endlessly, so some will reach the summaries.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting for simpler monitoring. But one account gives the web-reading agent purchasing rights, widening what an injection can do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the purchasing agent is isolated from the web. But the summaries carry web content to it secondhand.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because filtering blocks known attacks. But new wording slips past, and nothing then stops a planted instruction from becoming an order.

tips: Eliminate: C treats summaries as clean although they carry web text, and A hands purchasing rights to the agent that reads the web.
Final two: B beats D because filters miss new wording; approval stops planted text from becoming an order whatever wording gets through.
Exam cue: in multi-agent systems, an agent's output is only as trusted as what it read. Limit actions downstream of untrusted content.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An assistant with no tools
questions.question: An Irish price-comparison site's shopping assistant, which has no tools or account access, summarizes retailers' product pages for shoppers. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Its summaries using more tokens than the site budgeted
options.B: Retailers copying its summaries onto their own websites
options.C: Shoppers coaxing it into rude replies that embarrass the whole site
options.D: Planted page text steering shoppers to a fraudulent payment link

questions.key_concept: Injection needs no tools to cause harm: planted text can make an assistant mislead the people who read its answers.
questions.pre_read: Note who writes the content the assistant summarizes.
questions.correct_explanation: Retailers' pages are written by outsiders, so a page can carry hidden instructions that make the assistant tell shoppers to pay through a fraudulent link. No tools are needed; the shoppers act on the answer. Coaxed rude replies are a real jailbreak risk, but they mainly embarrass the site, while planted fraud takes shoppers' money.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model costs are real. But overspending is a budget issue; injected text that misleads shoppers harms people.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as an intellectual-property concern. But reuse of summaries harms no shopper and is not an injection risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because jailbreaks are common. But rude replies mainly embarrass the site, while planted fraud costs shoppers money.

tips: Eliminate: B is a content-reuse issue, not an injection harm, and A is a budget issue rather than a threat to shoppers.
Final two: D beats C because planted fraud takes shoppers' money, while a coaxed rude reply mainly embarrasses the site.
Exam cue: an assistant with no tools can still be steered. If people act on its answers, injected text can harm them.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An agent that opens every link
questions.question: A Belgian drug maker's literature-review agent opens every web link found in the papers it reads, from a server inside the company network. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Instruct the agent not to open links to internal network pages
options.B: Check each link against a list of known malicious sites
options.C: Limit the agent's network access to approved outside sites
options.D: Give the agent an administrator account so no link fails

questions.key_concept: An agent that follows links from untrusted content can be steered to internal systems; restrict where it can connect, outside the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chooses the links the agent opens.
questions.correct_explanation: Papers come from outsiders, so a planted link can point the agent at internal addresses, such as administration pages or data services, reachable from its server. Limiting its network access to approved outside sites stops that at the network. Checking links against a malicious-site list catches known bad sites, but internal addresses appear on no such list.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it states the rule. But a prompt instruction is not a control, and planted text can override it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reputation lists are a standard web control. But internal addresses appear on no such list, so the agent can still reach them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a fix for failed links. But it hands the agent broad rights, so any manipulation does far more damage.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt instruction as a control, and D grants broad rights to make the agent useful.
Final two: C beats B because known-bad lists never include internal addresses; limiting where the agent can connect blocks them.
Exam cue: bound an agent's reach by network and access controls, not by instructions or blocklists.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. What payment approvers see
questions.question: A Colombian builder's finance agent prepares supplier payments. Before the payment tool sends each one, approvers see only the agent's own one-line summary of it. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Show approvers the payee and amount the payment tool will send
options.B: Require a second approver for payments to new or changed payees
options.C: Let the agent approve payments under a set amount
options.D: Have the agent describe each payment tool request in fuller detail

questions.key_concept: Approvers must see what the tool will actually execute; an agent's own description of an action can be wrong or manipulated.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the approver actually sees.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent writes the summary approvers see, so an error or an injected instruction could make it describe one payment while the tool sends another. Showing approvers the payee and amount taken from the payment tool lets them check what will really happen. A second approver adds a person, but both would read the same agent-written summary.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because dual approval is a classic control. But both approvers would read the same agent-written summary, not the real payment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small payments seem low risk. But it removes the human check and invites splitting payments under the limit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more detail seems clearer. But fuller text from the agent is still the agent's account, not what the tool will send.

tips: Eliminate: D still relies on the agent's own account, and C removes the human check from part of the flow.
Final two: A beats B because a second approver reading the same agent summary adds no new evidence; the tool's own payee and amount do.
Exam cue: approval of agent actions must show the exact action from the tool layer, not the agent's description of it.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. An email agent's unapproved send
questions.question: A Mexican event planner's email agent sent a client's unapproved budget to a venue; policy defines incidents as access breaches, so IT logged none. What is the GREATEST gap for the IS auditor to report?

options.A: Nobody reviews a sample of the agent's sent emails
options.B: The policy misses harm an AI does within its permissions
options.C: The agent's credentials follow no rotation policy
options.D: The client's budget went to a venue without approval

questions.key_concept: An AI incident is harm or near harm from AI behavior, even when the system stayed within its permissions.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the agent was allowed to do from what happened.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent stayed within its permissions, so a policy that defines incidents as access breaches let real harm go unlogged and untriaged. Until the definition covers harm from AI behavior, this and similar sends will never reach incident handling or root cause work. A review of sent emails could spot such sends, but under this policy what it found still would not be handled as an incident.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a detective review is a sound control. But under a breach-only policy, what the review finds still would not be logged and triaged.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because credential hygiene matters. But nothing suggests compromised credentials; the agent misbehaved under its own permissions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it names what went wrong. But it describes this one event, not the gap that kept it out of incident handling.

tips: Eliminate: C treats AI misbehavior as a credential problem, and D restates this one event instead of the gap behind it.
Final two: B beats A because a review could spot harmful sends, but a breach-only policy would still keep them out of incident handling.
Exam cue: harmful AI behavior is an AI incident even inside its permissions. Check that the incident policy says so.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Invoices in a new layout
questions.question: A fuel supplier changed its invoice layout. A Ugandan flower farm's invoice-coding model then misposted 40 invoices. Finance logged an AI incident and corrected them. What should the IS auditor expect triage to establish FIRST?

options.A: Whether the 40 corrected entries now match their invoices
options.B: Which clerk approved the misposted entries for posting
options.C: Whether the supplier will keep using the new layout
options.D: Which other invoices have arrived in changed layouts

questions.key_concept: An input change can make a model fail silently on every input like it; triage first finds how many decisions are affected.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the corrections did and did not cover.
questions.correct_explanation: The model misread the new layout without any alert, so the same silent failure may be hitting other suppliers' invoices whose layouts changed. Triage should first establish how many postings are affected, which sets the incident's impact and the cleanup. Checking the 40 corrections is sound verification, but those are the errors already found; unknown misposts keep reaching the books.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because verifying corrections is careful work. But these are the errors already found; the risk lies in misposts nobody has spotted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because approvals are a control. But the model's misreading caused the errors, and who approved them does not size the incident.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the layout triggered the errors. But suppliers change layouts freely, and the model's exposure to other changes matters more.

tips: Eliminate: B asks who approved the postings, which does not size the incident, and C focuses on one supplier's choices instead of the model's exposure.
Final two: D beats A because the 40 corrections are known errors, while other changed layouts may be misposting unnoticed; scope comes first in triage.
Exam cue: AI fails silently on inputs like the one that broke it. Triage asks how many decisions are affected before fixing the known ones.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A hosted chatbot before a vendor update
questions.question: A South African vehicle-tracking firm disengaged its hosted billing chatbot over wrong late-payment penalties; its portal keeps text-only transcripts, and the vendor's update replaces the model on Friday. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retrain the chatbot on the correct penalty rules
options.B: Export the chat transcripts that the firm's own portal keeps
options.C: Ask the vendor to keep the version and settings now in use
options.D: Have the vendor restart it with a disclaimer on penalties

questions.key_concept: For hosted AI, the model version and settings sit with the vendor; ask for them to be kept before an update replaces them.
questions.pre_read: Ask where each record of the incident lives.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm's portal keeps text-only transcripts, which show what customers were told but not which model version and settings produced the wrong penalties. Once the vendor's update replaces the model on Friday, that version may be gone. Asking the vendor to keep the version and settings now in use preserves what root cause work needs. The firm's own transcripts stay under its control and can be exported later.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it fixes the error. But retraining before preserving evidence risks losing what root cause analysis needs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because transcripts are strong evidence. But text-only records show what was said, not which version or settings said it, and Friday's update replaces that version.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it restores service. But a disclaimer does not fix wrong penalties, and Friday's update still replaces the version behind them.

tips: Eliminate: A fixes before preserving evidence, and D restores service with a disclaimer that fixes nothing.
Final two: C beats B because the firm's transcripts show the wrong answers but not the version or settings behind them; only the vendor holds those, and Friday's update replaces them.
Exam cue: for hosted AI incidents, the version in use is evidence the vendor holds. Ask for it to be kept before a vendor update replaces it.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Choosing a rollback version after planted reports
questions.question: A Norwegian classifieds site's scam-listing filter, retrained weekly on user reports, began passing scams; bot accounts have filed false 'not a scam' reports for six weeks. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Roll back to a version trained before the false reports began
options.B: Roll back to last week's version, the latest approved one
options.C: Retrain the filter at once on this week's reports
options.D: Delete the false reports and wait for next week's retrain

questions.key_concept: Poisoned data persists in every version trained after it entered; choose a rollback target from data lineage, not recency.
questions.pre_read: Line up the stem's timeline before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: The filter retrains weekly, so every version from the last six weeks learned from the planted reports. Rolling back to last week's version, the usual target, restores a poisoned model. The target must be the last version trained before the false reports began, which lineage records identify. Retraining or deleting reports and waiting both leave scams passing in the meantime.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the previous version is the usual rollback target. But it was trained on five weeks of planted reports.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fresh data helps. But this week's reports include the bots' planted ones, so retraining relearns the poison.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes the bad data. But scams keep passing until the retrain, and deleting reports destroys evidence of the attack.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains on data that still holds the planted reports, and D leaves scams passing for a week and destroys evidence.
Final two: A beats B because last week's version also learned from the planted reports; only a version trained before they began is clean.
Exam cue: after poisoning, roll back by data lineage, not by date. Every version trained after the poison entered carries it.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Three months of misrouted parcels
questions.question: A Hungarian postal service's address-reading model misrouted parcels for three months at high confidence; its closed problem record cites a changed scanner feed, since fixed. What is the GREATEST gap the IS auditor should report?

options.A: It closed before the model was retrained on fixed data
options.B: Nothing explains why monitoring did not flag the errors
options.C: Nothing shows the feed fix went through change control
options.D: It names a feed instead of the person responsible

questions.key_concept: AI often fails silently; a root cause analysis should ask why detection took so long, not only what broke.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the closed record covers from what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: The feed fix removed this cause, but the model misrouted parcels for three months with high confidence scores, so monitoring missed it. AI errors are often silent, and without knowing why monitoring did not flag them, the next fault of any kind could run as long. Whether the feed fix went through change control matters, but it does not stop the next silent failure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining often follows errors. But the model was fed bad input; once the feed is fixed, retraining is not the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an unrecorded fix is a change-control gap. But it concerns how this one fix was made; the bigger gap is that a silent failure ran three months unflagged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because accountability matters. But a root cause analysis names causes and control gaps, not people to blame.

tips: Eliminate: D wants a person blamed rather than a cause found, and A assumes a retrain is needed after an input fix.
Final two: B beats C because change control governs this one fix; the detection gap lets the next silent failure run just as long.
Exam cue: AI fails silently. A root cause analysis should ask why detection took so long, not only what broke.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Rerunning a failed batch
questions.question: A Bangladeshi ceramic-tile maker's glaze-defect model passed a flawed batch last month. To find out why, engineers rerun the batch's images through today's model, retrained twice since. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain again with the flawed batch labeled as defective
options.B: Have inspectors first confirm the flaws shown in the batch's images
options.C: Close it if today's model now flags the batch's images
options.D: Analyze the version and settings in use when the batch passed

questions.key_concept: Root cause work on an AI failure uses the exact version, inputs and settings at the time; a retrained model is a different model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what has changed since the failure.
questions.correct_explanation: Today's model has been retrained twice, so it is a different model from the one that passed the batch; whatever it does now cannot show why the earlier version failed. The analysis needs the version, settings and inputs in use at the time. Inspectors confirming the flaws is useful evidence that the batch was bad, but it still says nothing about why that version missed them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it teaches the missed case. But it treats the symptom before the cause is known.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confirming the flaw is sound evidence. But it shows the batch was bad, not why the earlier version passed it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the current model may now catch it. But that says nothing about why last month's version failed.

tips: Eliminate: C judges a past failure by today's model, and A retrains before the cause is known.
Final two: D beats B because confirming the flaws shows the batch was bad; only the version in use at the time can show why it passed.
Exam cue: investigate the AI that failed, not its successor. Root cause needs the exact version, inputs and settings at the time.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Police reports behind a fraud model
questions.question: A Namibian accident fund trained its claim-fraud model on police crash reports shared only for fraud detection; managers now want its scores to rank claimants for rehabilitation funding. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Validate the model's scores for ranking rehabilitation needs
options.B: Proceed, since the model holds scores, not police reports
options.C: Have the data owner confirm the agreement allows this new use
options.D: Remove claimant names from the scores before ranking

questions.key_concept: Use limits on data can carry over to models trained on it, so a new use of the model needs the data's rights confirmed first.
questions.pre_read: Read each option for what it would settle and what it would leave open.
questions.correct_explanation: The crash reports were shared only for fraud detection, and a model trained on them can carry that limit, so using its scores to rank claimants for funding is a new use the agreement may not allow. The data owner must confirm it before anything else. Validating the scores for the new ranking is a necessary later gate, but it is wasted effort if the use is not permitted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a new use needs validation. But validation shows fitness, not permission; the shared data may not be usable for funding decisions at all.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a model stores weights, not reports. But it was built from data shared for one purpose, and that limit can follow the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a privacy step. But removing names does not change what the shared data may be used for.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a trained model as free of its data's limits, and D removes names without settling whether the use is allowed.
Final two: C beats A because validating a new use matters only once the data's terms allow it.
Exam cue: When a model takes on a new use, confirm the rights to its training data before testing its fitness.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Purchased standards behind a public assistant
questions.question: A Greek fire-safety authority's public assistant quotes retrieved passages from fire standards licensed for internal use; engineers see no license issue, since no model was trained on them. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Its answers share protected text with people not entitled to it
options.B: Answers may merge passages from different standards wrongly
options.C: Its quotes may come from standards since revised or withdrawn
options.D: Its answers cannot show which standard each passage came from

questions.key_concept: Retrieval quotes stored documents to whoever asks, so a source's license must cover the people the assistant serves.
questions.pre_read: Match each option to a fact stated in the question.
questions.correct_explanation: Retrieval quotes stored passages straight to whoever asks, so the public assistant republishes the standards to people an internal-use license does not cover, whether or not the model was trained on them. That is a stated fact and the greatest concern. Outdated quotes are a real retrieval risk, but nothing in the question says any standard was revised.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retrieval can stitch passages together badly. But nothing points to wrong advice; the stated license excludes the public the assistant serves.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retrieval indexes go stale. But the question gives no revision; it does give a license that excludes the public.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting if retrieval seems opaque. But retrieval tools can, and usually do, record which document each passage came from.

tips: Eliminate: B raises merged passages the facts never suggest, and D forgets that retrieval keeps track of each passage's source.
Final two: A beats C because the license limits who may see the text and retrieval shows it to the public; no revised standard is mentioned.
Exam cue: Retrieval publishes what it finds to whoever asks; check that each source may be shown to that audience.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Inspectors' grades as labels
questions.question: A Chilean salmon processor will train a fillet-defect camera model on line inspectors' past grades; inspectors earn a bonus whenever their line's reject rate stays under 3%. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Grades may vary widely between inspectors working different shifts and lines
options.B: The model may reject far more fillets than inspectors did
options.C: Inspectors may grade more strictly once the model checks them
options.D: The model may learn to pass fillets inspectors should have rejected

questions.key_concept: Labels made by people with an incentive carry that incentive; a model trained on them learns the same bias and repeats it at scale.
questions.pre_read: Trace each option back to a fact in the question that supports it.
questions.correct_explanation: Inspectors were paid to keep rejects under 3%, so some defective fillets were likely graded as passes. A model trained on those grades learns that leniency as the standard and applies it to every fillet. Grades varying between shifts would add noise, but nothing in the question suggests it, and the stated bonus pushes every inspector's grades the same way.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because label consistency matters. But the question gives no shift differences; it gives a bonus that pushes all grades one way.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting if a model seems stricter than people. But it learns from the grades it is given, so it copies their leniency.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because watched staff may change. But the model trains on past grades, which no future strictness can change.

tips: Eliminate: B expects a model to be stricter than its labels, and C looks at future grading when training uses past grades.
Final two: D beats A because the stated bonus skews every inspector's grades the same way; shift differences are never mentioned.
Exam cue: Ask who made the labels and what they were rewarded for; a model learns the incentive along with the labels.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Berth-fee declarations as training data
questions.question: A Croatian port authority trains an anomaly model to detect fraud. It uses two years of shipping agents' berth-fee declarations, minus every one its old rules engine flagged. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model needs labeled fraud cases before it can flag any
options.B: Underdeclarations the old rules missed may be learned as normal
options.C: Two years of declarations may be too short a history
options.D: Genuine declarations the old rules wrongly flagged may now look unusual

questions.key_concept: An anomaly model learns its training data as normal; if an older system filtered that data, the misses it left in become normal too.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against what the question says, not what is usual.
questions.correct_explanation: An anomaly model learns its training data as normal. Removing only what the old rules flagged leaves in every underdeclaration they missed, so the model learns those patterns as normal and inherits the old engine's blind spots. Genuine declarations wrongly flagged and removed, option D, may add false alerts, but those show up where people can check them, while missed underdeclarations stay silent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting if every model needs labels. But anomaly models learn normal patterns and flag departures, without confirmed fraud cases.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models need enough history. But two years covers each season twice; what matters is what the data holds, not its length.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removing genuine declarations skews the data. But that shows up as false alerts people can check; missed underdeclarations learned as normal stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes anomaly detection needs labeled fraud, and C blames the length of history when two years covers every season twice.
Final two: B beats D because the model learns whatever remains as normal, so the old rules' misses become invisible; wrongly removed genuine declarations only add false alerts, which show up.
Exam cue: When an older system filtered the training data, ask what it missed; an anomaly model learns those misses as normal.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A hail-damage model's test set
questions.question: An Indian crop insurer's hail-damage model team keeps its held-back test set in the team's shared folder, which members open freely while tuning the model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Make the test set read-only so members cannot alter it
options.B: Enlarge the test set so a few looks cannot bias it
options.C: Have someone other than the builders hold and score the test set
options.D: Draw a fresh test set from training data before every new release

questions.key_concept: A test set stays unseen only if the builders cannot look at it; holding it apart, with outside scoring, keeps it unseen.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the risk the facts describe.
questions.correct_explanation: Builders who can open the test set while tuning can steer the model toward it, even without meaning to, so its score stops showing performance on unseen data. Holding the set outside the team, with others scoring each release, keeps it unseen. Making it read-only is a sound integrity control, but the leak comes from looking, which read-only access still allows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it protects the test set from tampering. But the leak comes from looking, not editing; read-only members can still tune toward it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because bigger samples resist noise. But repeated looks bias tuning whatever the size, so a larger set stays exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fresh data sounds clean. But records drawn from training data are not unseen, so the test would measure memory.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts size to undo repeated looks, and D draws test records from data the model already trained on.
Final two: C beats A because the leak comes from builders seeing the test set while tuning, and read-only access still lets them look.
Exam cue: A test set must be unseen by the people tuning the model; protecting it from edits is not enough.
