questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. An ended data-sharing agreement
questions.question: A Rwandan feed maker trained its demand model on a cooperative's herd records; their ended agreement requires deleting the records and 'derived data', which it never defines. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Obtain proof that every copy of the herd records was deleted
options.B: Have counsel confirm whether the model must also be deleted
options.C: Keep using the model, since it stores none of the herd records
options.D: Retrain the model on public data, then delete the herd records

questions.key_concept: A model is built from its training data and may retain parts of it, so losing rights to the data can reach the model.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would settle and what it would leave open.
questions.correct_explanation: The agreement requires deleting derived data without defining it, and a model trained on the records is built from them and may retain parts of them. Whether the model counts is a question of rights, so counsel should settle it first. Proof that every copy of the records was deleted is careful evidence work, but it leaves the model, the likeliest derived item, unexamined.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deletion must be shown. But record copies may be only part of what the agreement covers; the model built from them is still in use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a model stores weights, not rows. But it is built from the records and can retain parts of them, so it may count as derived.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to end the dependence. But it acts before anyone has settled whether the current model may be kept or used.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a model as separate from the data it learned from, and D acts before the right to keep the model is settled.
Final two: B beats A because deleting record copies leaves the model in use, and the agreement may reach it too.
Exam cue: When rights to training data end, ask what happens to the models built from it, not just to the data.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A weather vendor's station data
questions.question: An Azerbaijani hazelnut grower's frost-damage model trains on a weather vendor's data; the vendor fills gaps, common on icy nights, with unmarked estimates from its own model. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The vendor's estimates make the data personal and need consent
options.B: Unmarked estimates may breach the vendor's own license terms
options.C: Station readings may not match frost conditions in the orchards
options.D: Frost readings it learns from may be the vendor's guesses

questions.key_concept: Data a supplier fills with its own model's estimates mixes guesses with measurements; a model trained on them learns the supplier model's errors.
questions.pre_read: Trace each option back to a fact stated in the question.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor fills gaps with its own model's estimates without marking them, and gaps are common on icy nights, exactly the conditions a frost model must learn. So much of what it learns about frost may be another model's guesses, carrying that model's errors. Station readings differing from orchard conditions is a real data-fitness risk, but nothing in the question points to it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because consent rules apply to some training data. But weather readings are not personal data, so consent is not the issue.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because licenses set terms of use. But nothing suggests the license requires marking; the risk is what the model learns.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because station location matters for frost. But the question gives no distance; it gives unmarked estimates filling icy-night gaps.

tips: Eliminate: A treats weather readings as personal data, and B turns a data-quality problem into a license question the facts never raise.
Final two: D beats C because unmarked estimates fill the very nights the model must learn, while station distance is never mentioned.
Exam cue: Ask whether bought data holds measurements or another model's estimates; unmarked estimates pass that model's errors on.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Choosing patients for a care program
questions.question: An Indonesian health insurer predicts treatment costs to pick patients for a chronic-care program; daily-wage workers use fewer services, as a clinic visit costs a day's pay. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Treatment costs may rise faster than the program's budget
options.B: Workers in real need may rank low for spending less
options.C: Last year's costs may not reflect patients' current health
options.D: Daily-wage workers' records may be too few to train on

questions.key_concept: A proxy target, such as spending standing in for need, carries whatever shapes the proxy, so groups with poor access look healthier than they are.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learns to predict costs, but the program is meant for patients in need. Daily-wage workers spend less because a visit costs them a day's pay, not because they are healthier, so the model may rank them low and leave them out. Costs lagging behind current health is a real limit of yearly data, but the question gives a stated reason why one group's spending understates its need.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a budget worry. But the concern here is who the model leaves out, not how much the program costs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because yearly data lags. But the question states why one group spends less; that cost barrier skews the target itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because small groups train poorly. But the stated cause is lost wages, which skews costs, not the record count.

tips: Eliminate: D blames the record count when the stated cause is lost wages, and A weighs the budget rather than who the model picks.
Final two: B beats C because spending stands in for need, and the question says daily-wage workers spend less for reasons other than health.
Exam cue: Check what a model's target really measures; a proxy carries every barrier that shapes it.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Copies of rare track videos
questions.question: A Japanese rail operator copied each of its nine track-obstruction videos 400 times, after setting test data aside, so its detection model has enough examples. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Copies may push the model to raise more false alarms
options.B: Copying may lower the accuracy of the videos' labels
options.C: Copies add no new kinds of obstruction to learn from
options.D: Storing 3,600 copied videos may strain the team's storage

questions.key_concept: Copying rare examples (oversampling) raises their count but adds no variety, so a model may learn only those few cases.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: Copying nine videos 400 times gives 3,600 files but still only nine situations, so the model may learn those exact scenes and miss other objects, light or track positions. More copies are not more evidence. Oversampling can also make a model flag obstructions more often, but that is tuned with the alert threshold; no threshold adds the scenes it never saw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because oversampling shifts how often a model flags the rare class. But that is tuned with the alert threshold; no threshold adds scenes the model never saw.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data handling can corrupt labels. But each copy keeps its video's label, so label accuracy is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a practical cost. But storage is easy to add; the risk is a model that has seen only nine scenes.

tips: Eliminate: B expects copying to change labels, which copies keep, and D weighs storage cost rather than what the model learns.
Final two: C beats A because extra false alarms can be tuned with the threshold, while nine copied scenes cannot teach obstructions the model never saw.
Exam cue: More copies of the same rare case are not more evidence; ask how many different cases the model really saw.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A leaf-disease model's 99%
questions.question: A Ugandan cassava-research institute's leaf-disease model scored 99% on a random test split; most diseased-leaf photos carry a date stamp that only the lab's camera adds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the 99%, since a stamp does not change the leaf
options.B: Test it on photos from this year's growing season
options.C: Add more diseased-leaf photos to the training set
options.D: Test it on photos with any date stamps cropped out

questions.key_concept: A model can learn a shortcut, such as a mark on one class's images; a test drawn from the same pool cannot reveal it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the reported score could and could not show.
questions.correct_explanation: If the lab's camera stamps most diseased-leaf photos, the model can score 99% by spotting the stamp instead of the disease. A random split keeps stamped photos in the test set, so it cannot reveal the shortcut; photos with the stamps cropped out can. Photos from a new season test change over time, but if taken with the same camera they keep the same clue.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a stamp says nothing about disease. But a model learns any pattern that tracks the label, so it may be reading the stamp.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because out-of-time tests catch drift. But if the new photos come from the same lab camera, they carry the stamp too, so the shortcut can survive.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more examples help. But more stamped lab photos strengthen the very clue the model may be relying on.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a model learns only the disease, and C adds more of the stamped photos behind the shortcut.
Final two: D beats B because only removing the stamps takes the clue away; newer photos from the same camera may keep it.
Exam cue: When a mark or setting tracks one class, test on data where it is gone before trusting the score.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Weekly re-splits of freight data
questions.question: A Bulgarian rail freight operator retrains its wagon-demand model weekly, starting from last week's model, and each week randomly re-splits all data into training and test sets. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Weekly scores cannot be compared on a common test set
options.B: An earlier version it builds on may have trained on test records
options.C: Re-splitting weekly means the test set holds no recent weeks
options.D: Starting from last week's model will stop it from learning new patterns

questions.key_concept: A model retrained from earlier weights keeps what those versions learned, so a fresh random test split may hold records it already trained on.
questions.pre_read: Picture the weekly process step by step before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Each week starts from last week's model, so what earlier versions learned carries forward. Because the data is re-split at random every week, records in this week's test set were often training records in an earlier week, so the score partly measures memory. Scores lacking a common test set is a real comparability problem, but it does not inflate any single week's result.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because comparisons need a fixed yardstick. But that limits trend reading; the inherited exposure inflates every weekly score.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting if random splits seem to skip recent data. But a random split draws test records from every period, recent weeks included.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting if earlier weights seem to lock a model in. But training from them still learns from each week's new data.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes earlier weights stop new learning, and C misreads a random split as excluding recent data.
Final two: B beats A because the inherited training inflates each week's score, while comparability is a lesser reporting problem.
Exam cue: When a model builds on earlier versions, ask what those versions saw; a test set must be unseen by the whole chain.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A rate model run from a notebook
questions.question: A Moroccan car-rental firm's model sets each day's rental rates. It runs nightly from an analyst's notebook and has never entered the firm's AI lifecycle. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Take the model through the data and validation stage gates
options.B: Compare its nightly rates with rates staff set by hand
options.C: Rewrite the notebook as production code with the same logic
options.D: Switch the model off until the analyst documents how it works

questions.key_concept: A model found outside the lifecycle needs its data and validation gates; matching manual results today does not show its data or limits are sound.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not cover.
questions.correct_explanation: The model sets each day's rates but has never passed the lifecycle's gates, so nobody knows whether its data is fit or its rates are sound. The data and validation gates test exactly that. Comparing its rates with rates staff set by hand is a careful check, but agreement on today's cases does not show that its data is fit or where its limits lie.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because matching manual rates looks like proof. But agreement on today's cases does not show its data is fit or where it fails.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because production code is sturdier. But rewriting keeps the same untested logic, so its pricing is no better known.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a cautious stop. But documentation alone does not show the rates are sound, and switching the model off halts the firm's daily pricing.

tips: Eliminate: C rewrites untested logic without testing it, and D waits on documentation that would still not validate the model.
Final two: A beats B because matching today's manual rates shows plausible outputs, not fit data or known limits; the gates test those.
Exam cue: A model found outside the lifecycle needs its gates; plausible outputs today are not validation.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A revalidation rule tied to changes
questions.question: A Zambian copper smelter's lifecycle requires revalidation only after a model or its code changes; its furnace-wear model, unchanged since validation in 2021, still schedules relining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model each year so that it stays current
options.B: Confirm from the change records that nothing has changed since 2021
options.C: Retest models on a schedule and when monitoring shows a shift
options.D: Replace it with a newer model, since 2021 is too old

questions.key_concept: A model can lose accuracy with no change to it, as the world it predicts moves; revalidation tied only to changes misses that.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not establish.
questions.correct_explanation: Models can degrade while nothing about them changes, because the conditions they predict move, such as ore blends and furnace age. A rule that revalidates only after changes never retests this model. Retesting on a schedule and when monitoring shows a shift closes that gap. Confirming from change records that nothing changed is careful evidence work, but it only proves the rule was followed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fresh data helps. But a retrain is itself a change needing validation; it does not replace testing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it checks the 'unchanged' claim. But an unchanged model is exactly what the rule never retests, though its world has moved.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model is old. But age alone does not show it fails; testing against criteria does.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps testing for a retrain that would itself need validation, and D judges the model by age instead of by testing.
Final two: C beats B because models degrade without changes, so proving nothing changed says nothing about current accuracy; time and monitored shifts must trigger retests too.
Exam cue: Software stays the same until changed; a model's accuracy can slip while nothing about it changes.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Comparing two captioning options
questions.question: A Finnish university needs year-round captions for deaf students. It compared a hosted API with an in-house open-weight model, on today's accuracy and cost. The API's provider updates it silently. Which added criterion matters MOST to the IS auditor?

options.A: Whether each option's vendor publishes its training code
options.B: Which option's model has more trained parameters
options.C: Who controls when each option's model is changed
options.D: Each option's exit terms if the university switches

questions.key_concept: A hosted model can change without notice, so today's accuracy comparison can go stale unless the buyer controls when its model changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the comparison already covers and what it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: The accuracy scores compare two models as they are today, but the captions must stay accurate all year. The hosted API's provider can update its model without notice, while an in-house open-weight model changes only when the university decides, so the comparison holds only while someone controls changes. Exit terms matter when leaving a supplier, but they do not protect caption quality while the service is in use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because openness sounds like assurance. But published code does not show how either model behaves on lectures.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because bigger models often score higher. But the accuracy comparison already measures performance; size adds nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because exit planning is part of sourcing. But it matters at the end; silent model changes could degrade captions any week before then.

tips: Eliminate: B uses model size in place of the accuracy already measured, and A treats published code as evidence of behavior.
Final two: C beats D because a hosted model can change silently, undoing today's accuracy comparison, while exit terms matter only when leaving.
Exam cue: In build-or-buy choices, ask who decides when the model changes; that decides how long test results stay true.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A one-line limitations section
questions.question: An Omani port plans to buy a vendor's container-damage photo model whose model card lists one limitation: 'outputs may be inaccurate.' What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Ask for the vendor's accuracy results on a public benchmark
options.B: Accept the card, since every model can be inaccurate
options.C: Have the vendor add an accuracy disclaimer to every output
options.D: Ask for the conditions where the vendor's tests found it fails

questions.key_concept: A limitation that applies to every model tells the buyer nothing; useful documentation names the conditions where this model fails, from testing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option would tell the port that it does not know now.
questions.correct_explanation: 'Outputs may be inaccurate' is true of every model, so it documents nothing. The port needs to know where this model fails, such as in poor light, rain or on certain container types, which the vendor's own testing should show. A public benchmark score is a useful figure, but one average says nothing about which conditions at a port cause the misses.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because benchmarks are independent. But one average score does not say which conditions cause errors at a port.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the statement holds. But it holds for every model, so it tells the port nothing about this one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it warns users. But a disclaimer adds no knowledge of where the model fails.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a limit true of every model, and C adds a warning instead of knowledge of where it fails.
Final two: D beats A because the port needs the conditions behind errors, and a benchmark average hides them.
Exam cue: Useful model documentation says when and where the model fails; a generic warning is not a limit.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. An index left after retirement
questions.question: An Icelandic ombudsman retired its complaints assistant but will keep its vector index of complaint letters indefinitely for a successor; complainants may challenge answers for six years. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the index, since a successor may reuse its embeddings
options.B: Apply the complaint letters' retention rules to the index
options.C: Re-embed the complaint letters with a newer model before archiving
options.D: Delete the index at once, since the assistant is retired

questions.key_concept: Embeddings can often be inverted to recover much of their source text, so an index of embedded letters falls under the letters' retention rules.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would do with the stored data.
questions.correct_explanation: Embeddings are numbers, but inversion methods can often recover much of the text behind them, so the index still holds the substance of complainants' letters. It follows the letters' retention rules: kept while complainants may challenge past answers, then disposed of on schedule, not kept for possible reuse. Deleting it at once looks like data minimization, but it can destroy records needed for six years of challenges.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a successor might reuse the index. But inversion can often recover much of the letters' text, so keeping it indefinitely keeps their content beyond its retention.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as an upgrade before archiving. But it makes fresh copies of the letters' content before anyone settles how long it may be kept.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as data minimization. But complainants may challenge past answers for six years; the letters' retention rules, not the retirement, set when the index goes.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps a copy of the letters' content indefinitely for possible reuse, and C makes new copies before anyone settles how long the content may be kept.
Final two: B beats D because the index holds the letters' content, so their rules decide how long it stays; deleting it now may lose records needed for six years of challenges.
Exam cue: At retirement, follow every copy of the data, embeddings and indexes included, to its retention rule.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Saved memories and a new assistant
questions.question: A New Zealand campervan-rental firm is replacing its booking assistant; the vendor offers to copy 18 months of customers' saved 'memories' into the new one. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Test that the new assistant reads the copied memories correctly
options.B: Delete every memory along with the old assistant at switch-off
options.C: Copy every memory so customers keep a seamless service
options.D: Review what the memories hold before any are copied over

questions.key_concept: Saved memories act as standing facts and instructions for an assistant, so migrating them can carry stale details or planted instructions into its successor.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would settle and what it would leave open.
questions.correct_explanation: An assistant treats its saved memories as standing facts and instructions, so copying them passes on whatever they hold: outdated preferences, personal details kept too long or instructions someone planted. The assistant's owner must first decide what may move. Testing that the new assistant reads the copied memories is sound migration practice, but it checks that the copy works, not whether the contents should move.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because migrations need testing. But a working copy proves only that memories transfer, not that their contents are fit to keep.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as data minimization. But deleting before review may destroy records the firm must keep or customers expect.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting for continuity. But copying everything moves stale details and any planted instructions into the new assistant unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: C moves every memory unexamined, and B deletes before anyone checks what must be kept.
Final two: D beats A because memories steer the assistant, so their contents need review before a copy is tested.
Exam cue: Retiring an assistant means deciding what its memories, logs and indexes hold before anything moves or goes.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A new banner on the review screen
questions.question: A Mexican online bank's release replaced the money-mule score on account reviewers' screens with a red 'Likely mule' banner, approved as a routine interface change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the routine approval, since the model itself is unchanged
options.B: Retest the mule model's accuracy on recent accounts
options.C: Test how the banner shifts decisions on flagged accounts
options.D: Add the banner's wording to the model's documentation

questions.key_concept: How AI output is shown shapes how people act on it, so a display change alters the human-AI system even when the model is unchanged.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not establish.
questions.correct_explanation: A red 'Likely mule' banner invites reviewers to agree without checking, a form of automation bias, so the release may shift reviewers' decisions on flagged accounts, even though the model is unchanged. That makes it a change to the AI system, needing tests of the decisions people make with it. Retesting the model's accuracy is sound practice after changes, but the model did not change; what changed is how people use its output.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because only the screen changed. But the screen shapes how people act on the score, so decisions can shift.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retesting follows change. But the model did not change; the risk is in how reviewers act on the banner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because documentation should match use. But recording the wording does not show its effect on decisions.

tips: Eliminate: A limits an AI change to the model itself, and D records the banner without testing its effect.
Final two: C beats B because the model is unchanged, while the banner can push reviewers to agree with flags unchecked.
Exam cue: Changes to how AI output is shown, routed or reviewed are AI changes too; test the decisions people make with it.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Reweighting for an age gap
questions.question: A Greek lender's data scientists approved and released a loan model retrained with reweighting; their tests showed it closed an over-60s approval gap but raised default-prediction errors. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retest the model's error rates for every group on recent loans
options.B: Accept the release, since a bias fix reduces risk
options.C: Reweight again to bring the default errors back down
options.D: Have the model owner decide the trade-off within tolerance

questions.key_concept: Bias fixes often trade one error for another; choosing that balance within tolerance is the model owner's decision, not the builders'.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not settle.
questions.correct_explanation: Reweighting closed one gap but raised default-prediction errors, so the release trades one harm against another, and the builders approved it themselves. Choosing that balance, within the tolerance senior management set, is the model owner's decision, not the builders'. Retesting every group's error rates on recent loans is careful evidence work, but the builders' tests already show the trade-off; what is missing is the owner's decision on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because group results matter. But the builders' tests already show the trade-off; more testing informs a decision that belongs to the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the aim was to reduce harm. But this fix also raised default-prediction errors, so it is a trade-off someone with authority must decide.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a quick correction. But another reweighting is a further builder decision on a trade-off the owner must make.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a fix as risk-free though it raised errors, and C has builders reweight again on their own judgment.
Final two: D beats A because the trade-off is already known; the model owner decides fairness and accuracy trade-offs within tolerance, not the builders.
Exam cue: A bias fix that shifts other errors is a trade-off; look for the owner deciding it within tolerance, not the builders.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Retraining in each environment
questions.question: A Spanish canned-tuna plant's pipeline retrains its can-seal defect model separately in the test and production environments, from the same versioned code and data. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain in production and skip the test environment
options.B: Promote the exact tested model file, checking its hash
options.C: Compare both models' scores on one test set before release
options.D: Accept the setup, since the same code and data give one model

questions.key_concept: Training the same code on the same data can produce a different model, so only the exact tested file shows what runs in production.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not establish.
questions.correct_explanation: Training is not exactly repeatable: random starting points and hardware differences mean the same code and data can yield a different model. So the production model is not the one that was tested. Promoting the tested file, verified by its hash, closes that gap. Comparing the two models' scores is careful, but similar scores can hide different decisions on individual cans.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a simplification. But it removes testing entirely, leaving the production model untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because matching scores look like proof. But two models can score alike yet decide individual cans differently.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because software built from the same source matches. But training can yield a different model from identical inputs.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes training repeats like a software build, and A drops testing instead of fixing what is promoted.
Final two: B beats C because only the tested file is known to behave as tested; similar scores can hide different decisions.
Exam cue: Promote the tested model artifact itself; retraining, even from the same inputs, makes a new model.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Rolling back a weather-risk model
questions.question: An Argentine grain broker rolled its weather-risk model back to last month's version; its price model, retrained last week on the newer version's scores, kept running. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retest the price model on the restored model's outputs
options.B: Confirm the price model's file matches the registry's hash
options.C: Retrain the weather-risk model to correct the newer version
options.D: Log the rollback as an emergency change for later approval

questions.key_concept: A model trained on another model's scores learns that version's score patterns, so rolling back the upstream model changes the downstream model's inputs.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not establish.
questions.correct_explanation: The price model learned from the newer weather-risk version's scores, so the rollback quietly changed its input even if its own file did not. It should be retested on the restored version's outputs before its prices are relied on. Confirming the price model's file against the registry's hash is sound practice, but it proves only that the file is unchanged, not how the model behaves on the restored scores.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hashes prove which version runs. But a matching hash shows only that the price model's file is unchanged; the scores it now receives have changed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the newer version needs fixing. But a retrain is a new change needing its own tests, and it leaves the price model's input unexamined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rollbacks are changes that need recording. But logging it does not test what it changed for the price model.

tips: Eliminate: C makes a further change before the first one's effects are known, and D records the rollback without testing its effect downstream.
Final two: A beats B because a matching hash shows only that the price model's file is unchanged, while the scores it learned from have been replaced.
Exam cue: When a model is rolled back, ask which models use its outputs; their inputs changed too.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Patch bundles for an inspection appliance
questions.question: A Slovak glassworks runs an on-premises bottle-inspection appliance. Each month the vendor sends patch bundles that include new inspection-model weights. IT installs them as routine patches. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Treat bundles that change the model as AI changes, tested first
options.B: Stop patching so the inspection model stays as approved
options.C: Install bundles once the vendor's release notes are reviewed
options.D: Have the vendor certify each bundle's security before install

questions.key_concept: A patch can replace an AI model's weights, changing its decisions; such patches need testing on the organization's own cases, not routine handling.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would reveal about how inspections might change.
questions.correct_explanation: New model weights change what the appliance passes or rejects, so these bundles alter inspection decisions, not just software. Each needs testing on the glassworks' own bottles before use. Reviewing release notes first is careful practice, but notes describe what the vendor intended and may not show how the new weights grade this factory's bottles.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting for stability. But skipping patches leaves security and other fixes uninstalled.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because release notes flag changes. But notes cannot show how new weights grade this factory's bottles; only testing can.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a supplier check. But security certification says nothing about how the new model grades bottles.

tips: Eliminate: B trades the model's stability for missing fixes, and D checks security when the change is to inspection decisions.
Final two: A beats C because release notes describe intent, while testing shows how new weights behave on the firm's own bottles.
Exam cue: Ask whether a vendor patch carries model weights; if it does, it is an AI change, whatever it is called.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A pinned version near its end
questions.question: A Bahamian card issuer's dispute assistant is pinned to a vendor model version that no longer gets safety updates and retires in June. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Let the vendor move it to its newest version automatically
options.B: Add an outside filter for jailbreaks found since updates ended
options.C: Have the owner test a supported version and plan the move
options.D: Keep the pinned version, as pinning prevents unplanned changes

questions.key_concept: Pinning stops unplanned changes, but a pinned version loses safety fixes when support ends and vanishes at retirement; test and plan the move first.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option leaves in place by June.
questions.correct_explanation: Pinning protected the assistant from unplanned changes, but the version no longer gets safety fixes and will be retired in June, forcing a move anyway. The assistant's owner should test a supported version now and plan the switch. An outside filter for new jailbreaks is a sensible stopgap, but it covers only known attacks and does nothing about the June retirement.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting for keeping current. But an automatic switch skips the testing every model change needs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a compensating control. But it covers only known jailbreaks and leaves the June retirement unplanned.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pinning blocks surprises. But the version gets no safety fixes and disappears in June regardless.

tips: Eliminate: D treats pinning as permanent though the version retires, and A accepts a model change with no testing.
Final two: C beats B because a filter patches known attacks, while a tested move answers both lost safety fixes and the coming retirement.
Exam cue: Pinning is a hold, not a home; plan and test the move before the pinned version loses support.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. One controller and 30 haul trucks
questions.question: At a Swedish iron mine, one remote controller oversees 30 autonomous haul trucks and must take over within ten seconds whenever a truck halts unexpectedly. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the controller approve each truck's moves in advance
options.B: Rely on the trucks halting safely when they are unsure
options.C: Log each takeover for the mine manager's monthly review
options.D: Set trucks per controller from tested takeover times

questions.key_concept: On-the-loop oversight works only if the overseer can respond in time, so set how many systems each person watches from tested response times.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: A controller watching 30 trucks may face several halts at once, so the ten-second takeover may be impossible exactly when it matters. The number of trucks per controller should be set from tested takeover times. Logging takeovers for monthly review is good oversight evidence, but it looks back at events and does nothing to make a timely takeover possible.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approval sounds safest. But approving every move of 30 trucks is unworkable, so it would become a rubber stamp.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because halting is a safe default. But halted trucks still need a takeover, which is the gap in question.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because takeover records support oversight. But reviewing them monthly cannot make a ten-second response possible across 30 trucks.

tips: Eliminate: A puts a person in the loop for every move of 30 trucks, and B relies on halting, which still needs a takeover.
Final two: D beats C because oversight must work in real time, and a monthly review cannot speed up a takeover.
Exam cue: Oversight on the loop needs people who can act in time; check how many systems each overseer must watch.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Acceptance staff hired after launch
questions.question: A Qatari cargo airline's acceptance staff, all hired since its AI model launched, were trained only to confirm or reject the model's dangerous-goods flags. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Teach staff to check shipments unaided, then test them
options.B: Have senior staff recheck a sample of new staff's decisions
options.C: Let the model clear shipments directly, as staff add little
options.D: Show staff the model's confidence beside each flag

questions.key_concept: Reviewers who never learned to judge cases alone cannot spot a model's errors; real oversight needs the skill to decide without the AI.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change about the checks.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff trained only to confirm or reject flags have never checked a shipment for dangerous goods themselves, so they cannot tell when the model is wrong and will tend to defer to it. They need the skill to judge shipments unaided. Rechecking a sample of their decisions is sound quality control, but it finds errors after shipments fly and leaves the skill gap in place.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as quality control. But rechecks find errors after the fact; staff still cannot judge shipments themselves.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting if review looks weak. But removing people from acceptance removes oversight instead of fixing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confidence seems to help judgment. But confidence is the model's own estimate and may be high when it is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on the model's own confidence, and C removes oversight rather than strengthening it.
Final two: A beats B because rechecks catch errors late, while unaided skill lets staff catch them at the time.
Exam cue: Oversight needs people who could decide the case alone; if they can only agree or disagree, expect deference.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Yarn-strength forecasts after an upgrade
questions.question: For six weeks since a lab-system upgrade, one reading fed to a Pakistani textile mill's yarn-strength model has stayed at the same in-range value; forecasts look normal. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Monitor forecasts for shifts outside their usual ranges
options.B: Retrain monthly so the model adapts to the lab feed
options.C: Compare each input's spread with its training data
options.D: Add range checks that reject impossible lab readings

questions.key_concept: A feed stuck at a plausible value passes range checks and can leave outputs looking normal; comparing input distributions with training data catches it.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: For six weeks the model has used one unchanging reading, yet its forecasts look normal, so monitoring outputs alone would not raise an alarm. Comparing each input's spread with its training data shows a reading that no longer varies. Watching forecasts for unusual shifts is a sound monitor, but the question says the forecasts look normal.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because output shifts often signal trouble. But these forecasts look normal, so a stuck reading would pass unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining adapts models. But training on a stuck reading teaches the model to disregard a real input.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because input validation is a standard control. But the stuck value is in range, so range checks pass it.

tips: Eliminate: B trains on the stuck reading instead of catching it, and D's range checks pass a value that is in range.
Final two: C beats A because forecasts look normal, so only comparing each input's spread with training data reveals a reading that never varies.
Exam cue: Models fail quietly on bad inputs; monitor each input's distribution as well as the outputs.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Arrears after field visits
questions.question: A Jamaican electricity distributor's model picks overdue accounts for field visits, and arrears fell 25% after launch. What should the IS auditor recommend to BEST show whether the model's picks drove the fall?

options.A: Measure the model's accuracy on recent overdue accounts
options.B: Visit a random sample of overdue accounts for comparison
options.C: Survey field staff on which visits worked best
options.D: Compare arrears with the same months a year before launch

questions.key_concept: Outcomes after a model goes live mix its effect with everything else; a random comparison group shows what the model's choices add.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option could and could not show.
questions.correct_explanation: Arrears could fall because visits help, because of the economy or because of seasonal pay patterns, whichever accounts are chosen. Visiting a random sample of overdue accounts as well, and comparing, isolates what the model's choices add. The model's current accuracy is careful evidence of how well it predicts, but accurate picks may be accounts that would have paid anyway.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recent accuracy beats launch figures. But predicting arrears well does not show that visiting those accounts is what cut arrears.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because staff see results firsthand. But opinions cannot separate the model's effect from the visits'.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it controls for season. But it cannot separate the model's picks from the visits and other changes since launch.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on opinions that cannot separate causes, and D mixes the model's picks with the visits and every change since launch.
Final two: B beats A because a model can predict arrears accurately yet pick accounts that would have paid anyway; only a random comparison shows what its picks add.
Exam cue: To show what a model adds, compare its choices with a random choice under the same treatment.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Weekly crew allocations
questions.question: A Brazilian city publishes its model's weekly allocations of street-cleaning crews among neighborhoods; residents can appeal littering fines, but nothing lets them challenge allocations. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Give neighborhoods a channel for concerns a named owner must review
options.B: Let residents challenge allocations through the fines appeal process
options.C: Add the factors behind each week's allocation to the published lists
options.D: Have the model move crews to neighborhoods whose complaints rise

questions.key_concept: Some AI decisions affect whole communities rather than individuals; they need a feedback route the owner must act on, not only individual appeals.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not change for residents.
questions.correct_explanation: Allocations affect whole neighborhoods, not individuals, so the fines appeal cannot address them, and a neighborhood left uncleaned has nowhere to go. A channel for community concerns, reviewed by the model's owner, gives affected groups a voice and the owner evidence. Routing challenges through the fines appeal reuses a working process, but it judges individual fines and has no authority over how crews are allocated.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a ready-made route. But the fines process judges individual fines; it has no authority over crew allocations.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because explanations support accountability. But residents can already see allocations; knowing the factors still gives them no way to have one reviewed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as fast feedback. But complaint volume favors vocal areas, and it leaves the decision to the model rather than a person.

tips: Eliminate: C explains allocations without giving residents a way to have one reviewed, and D leaves the response to the model instead of its owner.
Final two: A beats B because the fines appeal judges individual fines, while allocations affect whole neighborhoods and need a route the owner reviews.
Exam cue: When AI affects groups rather than individuals, look for a feedback route that a named owner must review.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeals decided by a rescore
questions.question: A Chilean municipality's model sets school-transport eligibility. On appeal, families correct their data and the model rescores. Staff may not grant transport against the new score. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Send families the model's main factors with each new score
options.B: Have staff check each corrected input against source records first
options.C: Retrain the model on each appeal's corrected data
options.D: Let appeal staff decide against the score, giving reasons

questions.key_concept: An appeal that only reruns the model with corrected data cannot fix errors in the model's judgment; someone must be able to decide against it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change about appeals.
questions.correct_explanation: Rescoring after a data fix only corrects input errors. If the model misjudges a family's situation, for example a dangerous walking route it does not weigh, the new score repeats the mistake, and staff cannot override it. Letting staff decide against the score, with reasons, makes the appeal real. Checking corrected inputs against source records is good practice, but it improves only the inputs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as transparency. But knowing the factors does not let anyone overturn a wrong result.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it guards against false corrections. But it still leaves the model as the final judge of every appeal.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because corrections improve data. But retraining on each appeal changes the model without fixing how appeals are decided.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the model instead of the appeal, and A explains a result nobody can overturn.
Final two: D beats B because better inputs still leave the model the final judge, while staff authority can correct its judgment.
Exam cue: A real appeal can reach a different answer than the model; rerunning the model is not an appeal.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A grading model as the pass mark
questions.question: A Saudi housing ministry tunes its complaint-reply assistant until a grading model rates its replies 4 out of 5; each tuning round made replies longer and marks higher. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Longer replies may be harder for complainants to read
options.B: The grading model may be updated between tuning rounds
options.C: Marks may be rising with reply length, not quality
options.D: A pass mark of 4 may be too low for complaint replies

questions.key_concept: Grading models can favor longer answers, so tuning an assistant against one can raise its marks by adding length rather than quality.
questions.pre_read: Rank each concern by its likely effect on the acceptance decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Grading models are known to favor longer answers, and here marks rose as replies grew, so the tuning may be teaching the assistant to write more rather than better. The marks would then overstate quality. Longer replies being harder to read is a real usability cost, but it is a smaller harm than accepting an assistant on marks that may not measure quality.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because long replies tire readers. But that is a usability cost; the larger risk is accepting the assistant on marks that may reward length.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hosted graders can change silently. But nothing in the question says the grader changed, while marks rose with length.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because complaints matter. But a higher mark from a grader that rewards length is no better evidence.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes a grader update the question never mentions, and D raises the bar on marks that may not measure quality.
Final two: C beats A because marks that rise with length may not measure quality at all, while readability is a lesser cost.
Exam cue: When AI grades AI, check what the grader rewards; tuning against it can chase its bias.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. An appointment assistant moves to the phone
questions.question: A Peruvian veterinary clinic chain's appointment assistant passed acceptance tests on typed questions; on its new phone line, it will receive callers' words through a speech recognizer. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test it on spoken questions passed through the recognizer
options.B: Add more typed questions with spelling mistakes to the tests
options.C: Test the recognizer's word accuracy on recorded calls
options.D: Accept the typed results, since the assistant is unchanged

questions.key_concept: Acceptance holds for the system as tested; adding a speech recognizer in front changes the inputs, so the whole chain needs testing.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not test.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant was accepted on clean typed text, but callers' words will arrive through a speech recognizer that can mishear names, places and dates. Only end-to-end tests with spoken questions show how the combined system answers. Testing the recognizer's word accuracy is a sound component check, but it cannot show whether the assistant asks again or confidently books the wrong pet, date or clinic when a word is misheard.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a stand-in for messy input. But typing errors differ from mishearings, so it still misses the real chain.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because each part should be tested. But word accuracy alone cannot show how the assistant answers misheard questions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the assistant itself is unchanged. But its inputs change, and acceptance covered only typed text.

tips: Eliminate: D carries acceptance over to new inputs, and B simulates speech errors with typing errors.
Final two: A beats C because a generative assistant may act confidently on a misheard word instead of asking; only end-to-end tests show how often it does.
Exam cue: When a new component feeds an accepted AI, test the chain as deployed, not each part alone.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A ranking model's launch fairness test
questions.question: An Austrian crowdfunding platform ranks projects with a model retrained weekly on backers' clicks. In its launch fairness test, the model ranked projects by women and men alike. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Ranking should stay fair, as sex is not one of its inputs
options.B: The launch result can stand until ranking accuracy falls
options.C: Backers' clicks are neutral, so retraining is unlikely to add bias
options.D: Feedback from its own rankings can open a gap later

questions.key_concept: A model retrained on behavior its own outputs shape, such as clicks on its rankings, can widen group gaps after launch, so fairness needs retesting.
questions.pre_read: Check each conclusion against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: Backers tend to click what a ranking shows first, and the model retrains weekly on those clicks, so any early dip for one group's projects can mean fewer clicks, lower ranks and fewer clicks again. Each weekly retrain replaces the model the launch test described. Waiting for accuracy to fall, option B, sounds careful, but accuracy measured on those same clicks can hold steady while a gap grows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting if sex is not an input. But other signals, including the clicks it learns from, can track creators' sex.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because falling accuracy often triggers a retest. But accuracy measured on clicks its own rankings shaped can stay steady while one group's projects sink.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because clicks look like plain behavior. But people tend to click what a ranking shows first, so retraining on clicks feeds its own rankings back into it.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a model without a sex input cannot treat creators differently, and C treats clicks as neutral, though people tend to click what a ranking shows first.
Final two: D beats B because the model learns from clicks its own rankings shape, so a gap can grow each week while accuracy measured on those clicks holds steady.
Exam cue: When a model retrains on behavior its own outputs shape, a one-time fairness test goes stale; expect retests after retraining.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Error size in compensation amounts
questions.question: A Danish workplace-injury insurer uses a model to set compensation amounts. The model shows the same average size of error for claimants with and without disabilities. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the result, since equal error shows equal treatment
options.B: Compare whether its errors underpay or overpay each group
options.C: Compare average error size on a larger, recent sample
options.D: Remove disability status from the model's inputs

questions.key_concept: Equal error size can hide a direction gap: if one group's errors are mostly underpayments, it is harmed even when average error matches.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would add to the evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Average error size counts an underpayment and an overpayment of the same amount alike, yet one leaves an injured claimant short. If claimants with disabilities are mostly underpaid while others are mostly overpaid, the averages match and the harm is hidden. Comparing direction by group shows it. A larger, recent sample makes the size estimate firmer but keeps the same blind spot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the numbers match. But equal sizes can hide one group being mostly underpaid.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because firmer estimates help. But a larger sample measures the same size-only figure, still blind to direction.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a fairness fix. But other inputs can carry disability, and removing it does not show who is underpaid.

tips: Eliminate: A reads equal error size as equal treatment, and D removes an input instead of testing outcomes.
Final two: B beats C because a size-only measure hides who is underpaid, however large the sample.
Exam cue: For amounts, check which way the errors fall for each group; equal error sizes can hide one-sided harm.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A credit validation unit's first chatbot
questions.question: A Jordanian bank's validation unit, experienced with credit-scoring models, plans to validate its first customer chatbot with its usual accuracy, stability and backtesting checks. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the chatbot vendor's safety report instead
options.B: Run its usual checks on a far larger sample of customer chats
options.C: Add tests by skilled staff for invented and harmful replies
options.D: Skip validation, as the chatbot makes no credit decisions

questions.key_concept: Chatbots fail in ways credit-model checks do not test, such as invented facts and harmful replies, so validation must fit the model type.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not test.
questions.correct_explanation: Accuracy, stability and backtesting suit scoring models with numeric outputs, but a chatbot fails differently: it can invent facts (confabulation) or give harmful replies in fluent text. Validation needs tests for those failures, run by people who know how to find them. A larger sample makes the usual checks firmer, but it still does not look for the failures that matter in a chatbot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors test safety. But the vendor's tests may not cover the bank's chatbot as configured.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more data firms up results. But the usual checks do not look for invented facts or harmful replies at any sample size.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no credit decisions are made. But wrong or harmful replies to customers still carry real risk.

tips: Eliminate: A substitutes the vendor's testing for the bank's, and D ties validation only to credit decisions.
Final two: C beats B because the usual checks miss generative failures, and a bigger sample does not change what they test.
Exam cue: Match validation methods and skills to the model type; generative AI needs tests for invented and harmful output.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A dam-break scenario
questions.question: A Mozambican disaster agency's flood-extent model, validated on every recorded flood since 1990, will guide evacuations for a dam-break scenario larger than any recorded flood. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test it on simulated floods beyond anything in its data
options.B: Rely on its validation, since it covered every recorded flood
options.C: Revalidate it on recorded floods, region by region
options.D: Retrain it on recent small floods to sharpen it

questions.key_concept: Validation shows how a model performs only within the range of its data; an event larger than any seen needs stress tests beyond it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not test.
questions.correct_explanation: Every recorded flood is smaller than the dam-break scenario, so the model has never seen water at that scale and may extrapolate badly, for example by stopping the flood's extent where real water would spread. Simulated larger floods, from hydraulic studies, test that range. Revalidating region by region on recorded floods adds detail, but every one of those floods is still smaller than the scenario.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because coverage looks complete. But complete coverage of smaller floods says nothing about a larger one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because regional results reveal weak spots. But every recorded flood is smaller than the scenario, so the key range stays untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because recent data is current. But small floods teach nothing about an event larger than any recorded.

tips: Eliminate: B mistakes complete history for coverage of a bigger event, and D adds small floods to model a large one.
Final two: A beats C because only simulated larger floods test the range the scenario needs.
Exam cue: Ask whether the planned use lies inside the range the model learned from; outside it, stress-test before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A shared model trained across banks
questions.question: Eight Swiss cantonal banks train a shared fraud model by federated learning; secure aggregation means no one, the coordinator included, sees any single bank's update. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: The shared model running too slowly for live payments
options.B: A bank inferring other banks' customers from the shared updates
options.C: Customer records exposed when each bank sends its data
options.D: One bank's crafted updates planting a hidden flaw in the shared model

questions.key_concept: Federated learning shares updates, not records; secure aggregation hides each update from others, which also hides a poisoned update from inspection.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each threat against the design the question describes.
questions.correct_explanation: Secure aggregation means no one can see any single bank's update, which greatly narrows the inference threat. But it also means nobody can inspect any update, so a member that crafts poisoned updates can plant a hidden flaw in the shared model unseen. Inference from updates is a real federated-learning risk, but the stated design is built to narrow exactly that.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a performance worry. But the training method says little about scoring speed, and nothing points to delay.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because updates can leak training details. But secure aggregation hides each bank's update, leaving only the combined result, which narrows this route.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting if records seem to be pooled. But federated learning keeps records at each bank and shares only updates.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes records leave each bank, and A raises speed, which the facts never question.
Final two: D beats B because secure aggregation narrows the inference route but also hides a poisoned update from inspection.
Exam cue: A privacy safeguard can hide manipulation; ask what each design choice stops others from seeing.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A list of photo addresses
questions.question: A Slovenian beekeepers' association trains its hive-disease model on a public list of image web addresses, fetched afresh at each retrain. Some listed domains have expired. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Expired domains shrinking the training set at each retrain
options.B: Photo owners objecting to the association's use of their images
options.C: Expired domains being bought to serve crafted photos
options.D: Rivals copying the model through the public address list

questions.key_concept: A training set built from web addresses fetched at each retrain trusts whoever controls each address now; expired domains can be bought and serve poison.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each threat against the data path the question describes.
questions.correct_explanation: The model fetches its photos from listed addresses at every retrain, so whoever controls each address decides what it learns. Anyone can buy an expired domain and serve crafted photos at the listed addresses, poisoning the next retrain. Dead links are a real data-quality loss, but they only remove photos, while a bought domain lets an attacker choose what the model learns.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because lost photos weaken training. But dead links only remove data, while a bought domain lets an attacker choose what the model learns.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because image rights matter. But an objection is a legal question, while a bought domain lets anyone feed the model chosen images.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the list is public. But it holds addresses of training photos, not the model, so it gives no route to copy it.

tips: Eliminate: B raises an image-rights question, not a threat to what the model learns, and D imagines copying the model from a list of photo addresses.
Final two: C beats A because a bought domain lets an attacker choose the training photos, while dead links only lose some.
Exam cue: When training data is fetched from addresses, ask who controls each address today, not who did when the list was made.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A browsing assistant's approved sites
questions.question: A Singaporean property agency's home-search assistant browses only 20 approved property websites, their tenant review pages included, when answering customers. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Customers coaxing it into quoting rents it cannot honor
options.B: Instructions hidden in public posts on approved sites
options.C: Approved sites tracking customers through its browsing
options.D: An approved site being hacked to carry hidden instructions

questions.key_concept: An allowlist limits which sites an assistant reads, not who writes on them; any page open to public posts can carry injected instructions.
questions.pre_read: Rank each threat by likelihood and impact in this setting.
questions.correct_explanation: Approving sites limits where the assistant reads, but review pages on those sites accept text from anyone, so an attacker needs only to post a review with hidden instructions. That makes indirect injection through reviews the likeliest route. A hacked approved site would do the same, but it requires breaching the site itself, which is far harder than posting a review.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because coaxed promises can cost a firm. But each customer coaxes only their own chat, while planted reviews can steer every customer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a privacy worry. But nothing in the question points to tracking, while review pages are a stated open input.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because trusted sites can be compromised. But that needs a breach, while anyone can post a review today.

tips: Eliminate: A weighs one customer's coaxing in their own chat over outside steering, and C raises tracking that nothing in the question points to.
Final two: B beats D because anyone can post a review, while hacking an approved site takes a breach.
Exam cue: Approving a site approves its owner, not its users; check which approved pages accept public content.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A reply filter for a pension agent
questions.question: A Uruguayan pension fund uses an agent that reads uploaded documents and can switch members' savings between investment funds. The only injection defense filters the agent's replies. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Planted instructions can trigger actions no reply filter sees
options.B: Attackers can reword replies so they slip past the filter's rules
options.C: Uploaded documents may carry malware into the fund's systems
options.D: The filter may block some genuine replies to members

questions.key_concept: An agent acts through tool calls before any reply is written, so filtering replies cannot stop injected actions.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against what the agent can do.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent can switch members' savings through its tools, and a document with hidden instructions can make it do so as it works, before any reply exists. A reply filter checks only the text the member sees, so the switch has already happened. Rewording to slip past the filter is a real weakness of filters, but it concerns what the agent says, not what it does.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because output filters can be evaded. But even a perfect reply filter leaves the switches, the real harm, unchecked.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because uploads can carry malware. But injected instructions are plain text a malware scan would not flag, and they can switch savings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because filters can misfire. But blocking some genuine replies is an annoyance next to unauthorized fund switches.

tips: Eliminate: D weighs blocked replies over moved savings, and C looks for malware when the risk is plain-text instructions.
Final two: A beats B because a switch happens through tools before any reply, so even a perfect filter is too late.
Exam cue: For agents, ask what injected text could make them do, not only say; reply filters cannot stop actions.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An intake agent's service account
questions.question: A Kenyan immigration consultancy's intake agent reads clients' uploaded documents and files visa forms under its own service account, whose rights pass every quarterly access review. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Alert on the service account's sign-ins from unusual locations
options.B: Tell the agent in its prompt to ignore instructions in uploads
options.C: Monitor the agent's actions for any that no task explains
options.D: Scan clients' uploads for malware before the agent reads them

questions.key_concept: Injected instructions can steer an agent into misusing rights it legitimately holds, so agent accounts need activity monitoring, not only access reviews.
questions.pre_read: Ask which risk each option addresses and which it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: Uploaded documents can carry hidden instructions that steer the agent into actions its rights allow, such as filing a visa form nobody asked for. An access review confirms which rights the account holds, not how they are used; monitoring the agent's actions against its tasks shows the misuse. Sign-in alerts, option A, catch a stolen account, but a steered agent signs in as usual.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because unusual sign-ins flag a stolen account. But a steered agent signs in as usual and misuses rights it legitimately holds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it targets injected text. But a prompt instruction is not a control, and injected text can talk the agent around it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because uploads are untrusted input. But injected instructions are ordinary text, not code, so a malware scan passes them to the agent.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on a prompt instruction, which injected text can override, and D scans for malware, which plain-text instructions do not contain.
Final two: C beats A because a steered agent signs in as usual; only comparing its actions with its tasks shows outside text steering it within its valid rights.
Exam cue: An agent's account is a user that outside text can steer; review what it may do, then watch what it does.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Supplier edits made for staff
questions.question: A Lithuanian paint manufacturer's procurement agent edits supplier records under its own ERP identity for whichever employee asks; the ERP audit trail does not show who asked. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have each employee confirm the edits made at their request
options.B: Run the agent under one shared administrator account
options.C: Keep the agent's own log of requesters beside the ERP trail
options.D: Record each edit's requesting employee in the ERP trail too

questions.key_concept: An agent acting for others should be traceable, in the system it changes, to itself and to the person it acted for.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not establish.
questions.correct_explanation: With only the agent's identity in the trail, nobody can tell which employee's request led to each supplier edit, so misuse or a crafted request cannot be traced to its source. Recording the requester in the ERP's own trail fixes that. Keeping the agent's own log of requesters helps, but it is the agent's account of itself, which crafted requests can skew.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as human oversight. But confirmations do not change what the audit trail records, so requesters stay untraceable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting for simpler setup. But a shared admin account hides even the agent's identity and widens its rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a separate log adds detail. But the agent writes it, and a coaxed or injected agent can record misleading entries.

tips: Eliminate: A adds confirmations that leave the trail without requesters, and B merges the agent into a shared account with wider rights.
Final two: D beats C because the ERP's own trail is the system of record, while the agent's log is its own account.
Exam cue: When an agent acts for people, the system it changes should record both the agent and the person it acted for.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A rise in approved top-ups
questions.question: A Thai ride-hailing app's wallet fraud model is hash-matched to the approved release. This month it approved 15% more top-ups, most from new accounts. Managers credit the rise to fewer false declines. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Adjust the decision threshold to bring top-up approvals down
options.B: Have the owner log a possible incident and check the extra top-ups
options.C: Have the model retested on its original holdout set
options.D: Report the rise as a model improvement to the board

questions.key_concept: A model's outputs can shift with no change to it when its inputs change, as under evasion; triage an unexplained shift as a possible incident.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would do now and what it would leave open.
questions.correct_explanation: The running model matches the approved release, yet it approves 15% more top-ups, most from new accounts. An unchanged model's outputs can shift when its inputs change: fraudsters may have learned what it passes, or an input may be broken. Fewer declines are not proof of fewer false declines. Having the owner log a possible incident and check the extra top-ups finds out now. A holdout retest would only repeat the release scores.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a quick correction. But changing the threshold before knowing the cause is an untested change.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a retest is evidence-based. But an unchanged model scores the same on its original holdout set, which holds none of this month's inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the result looks good. But an unexplained shift needs explaining before it is reported as a gain.

tips: Eliminate: A changes the threshold before the cause is known, and D reports an unexplained shift as success.
Final two: B beats C because an unchanged model's outputs can shift when its inputs change; its original holdout set holds none of this month's new-account top-ups.
Exam cue: An unexplained jump in an AI's outputs, even a welcome one, is a possible incident to triage now.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Three reports on one morning
questions.question: Three teams at a Mexican toy maker each run their own assistant on one hosted model. One morning, each team logged wrong toy-safety answers from its assistant as low severity, citing few users. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Harm from one shared fault may be rated too low
options.B: Three incidents in a morning may overload the incident team
options.C: Each team may record a different cause for one fault
options.D: Low-severity incidents may not reach the vendor's support desk

questions.key_concept: AI uses that share a model can fail together; incidents triaged team by team can understate the combined harm of one shared fault.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts the question states.
questions.correct_explanation: Three assistants on one hosted model giving wrong safety answers the same morning point to one shared fault, perhaps a model update. Each team judged severity by its own assistant's few users, so the combined reach of wrong safety advice from all three may be rated far too low, slowing the response. Mismatched causes are a problem-management issue that slows the fix later; the understated severity slows the response now.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a capacity worry. But three incidents is a small load; the issue is that they are not linked.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one fault needs one cause. But that matters for problem records later; how severe the safety fault is rated decides how fast the response comes now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors fix hosted models. But reporting to the vendor follows triage; the issue is how severe the fault is rated.

tips: Eliminate: D focuses on vendor reporting before triage, and B worries about volume instead of linkage.
Final two: A beats C because understated severity slows the response now, while mismatched causes matter later.
Exam cue: When AI incidents share a model, data feed or prompt, triage them together; split reports understate harm.
