questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Model files on a forum
questions.question: Copies of a Vietnamese online lender's application-fraud model files have appeared on a hacking forum. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the forum take the files down and watch for reposts
options.B: Rotate the API keys that applications use to call it
options.C: Add other fraud checks while a changed model is prepared
options.D: Keep using the model, as attackers cannot read its weights

questions.key_concept: A leaked model lets attackers test evasions offline until they pass; containment means reducing reliance on that model, since copies cannot be recalled.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not stop.
questions.correct_explanation: With the model files, fraudsters can test applications offline until they find ones it passes, then submit them for real. Any copies already downloaded cannot be recalled, so the lender should add other fraud checks now and prepare a changed model. Having the forum take the files down and watching for reposts are sensible steps, but they cannot reach any copies already taken.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because takedowns are standard. But any copies already downloaded stay usable for offline evasion testing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because leaks often involve credentials. But the files themselves, not API access, give attackers their advantage.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because weights are unreadable to people. But attackers need not read them; they can run the model to test evasions.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a model leak as a credential leak, and D assumes unreadable weights are harmless.
Final two: C beats A because downloaded copies cannot be recalled, so reliance on the exposed model must drop.
Exam cue: A leaked model is a test bench for attackers; contain by reducing reliance on it, not just by removing the post.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Restarting a hijacked agent
questions.question: A Belgian cold-storage firm suspended its hijacked operations agent. The attacker rewrote the agent's saved memories and tool settings. The team will restart it after rotating its keys. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Restart the agent with a stricter system prompt
options.B: Rotate the agent's own keys and its account password
options.C: Delete its altered memories, tool settings and logs
options.D: Restore its memories and tool settings from a clean copy

questions.key_concept: A hijacked agent's saved memories and tool settings are part of its configuration; if rewritten, new keys do not stop them steering it after restart.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not stop.
questions.correct_explanation: Rotating keys stops the attacker signing in as the agent, but the rewritten memories and tool settings would steer it again the moment it restarts. They must be restored from a copy made before the attack, with the altered versions kept as evidence. Rotating the agent's keys and password is good hygiene, but it leaves the attacker's changes inside the agent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a fix. But a prompt is not a control, and restarting with the attacker's memories and settings in place invites the same steering.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because credentials are rotated after compromise. But new keys leave the rewritten memories and tool settings in the agent.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as cleanup. But deleting the altered memories, settings and logs destroys the evidence needed to find what the attacker did.

tips: Eliminate: A restarts the agent with the attacker's changes still in it, and C destroys the evidence needed for root cause.
Final two: D beats B because new keys stop the attacker signing in, while rewritten memories and tool settings would steer the agent again on restart.
Exam cue: Containing an agent covers what it remembers and how its tools are set, not only its credentials.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A fixed flaw in a sold product
questions.question: A Hungarian firm sells a scholarship-ranking model to universities. A year-old flaw made it rank vocational-school applicants too low. The firm fixed the flaw, added regression tests and closed the problem record. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the record closed, since the fix is now live
options.B: Have the product owner tell customers the flaw and when it applied
options.C: Retrain the product on more vocational-school applicants
options.D: Monitor monthly whether the fixed flaw returns for vocational applicants

questions.key_concept: When a sold AI product's flaw is fixed, customers who relied on its past outputs need to know the flaw and when it applied.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not address.
questions.correct_explanation: Universities relying on the product's rankings over that year may already have passed over vocational-school applicants. The fix and regression tests change future rankings only. The product owner should tell customers the flaw and when it applied, so they can review affected decisions. Monthly monitoring of the rankings is sound practice, but it also looks forward, not at past scholarship decisions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the fix is live. But universities may still hold decisions made with the flawed rankings.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more data can help. But the flaw is fixed; retraining does nothing for decisions already made.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because monitoring catches a flaw's return. But like the new regression tests it looks forward; decisions universities made in the flawed year remain unaddressed.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains after the fix is already live, and A closes while universities may still rely on flawed past rankings.
Final two: B beats D because monitoring watches future rankings, while universities must learn of decisions already made with the flawed rankings.
Exam cue: After fixing a sold AI product, ask who relied on its past outputs and make sure the owner tells them.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A workaround after 14 months
questions.question: An Irish veterinary lab has an open problem. As a workaround, its technicians have checked each model-assigned test code for 14 months. Checks fell from a minute to five seconds. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The checks may have stopped catching wrong codes
options.B: Checking every code costs more than fixing the cause
options.C: Technicians may be checking codes that need no review
options.D: The problem has stayed unresolved for over a year

questions.key_concept: A human check used as a workaround, a compensating control, can decay as people grow used to the AI; rushed checks suggest it misses errors.
questions.pre_read: Rank each concern by its likely effect.
questions.correct_explanation: The workaround relies on technicians catching the model's wrong codes, but checks that fell from a minute to five seconds suggest they have become a glance: people who check an AI's work for months tend to stop looking closely. Wrong codes may send samples to the wrong tests, missing disease. A year-old open problem is a real problem-management finding, but the more immediate risk is that its only safeguard may have stopped working.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a cost point. But cost does not show harm, and nothing gives the cost of fixing the cause.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because checking every code seems wasteful. But the problem is still open, so every code still needs a real check.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because aged problems need escalation. But the more immediate harm is that the workaround protecting test orders may have stopped working.

tips: Eliminate: B weighs cost when a workaround is judged by whether it still stops wrong codes, and C questions checks the open problem still requires.
Final two: A beats D because a decayed check lets wrong codes through now, while an aged record is a slower risk.
Exam cue: A human-review workaround weakens over time; look for signs, such as rushed checks, that it has become a rubber stamp.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. An accounting assistant's documents
questions.question: A Slovak accounting-software vendor's assistant serves 300 client firms from one retrieval index filtered by client tags set at upload; one firm's answer quoted another's payroll file. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add an output filter that masks other firms' names in answers
options.B: Keep each firm's documents in a separate index
options.C: Test the tag filter quarterly with sample queries from each firm
options.D: Encrypt the shared index and its backups with managed keys

questions.key_concept: In one shared retrieval index, a single query-time filter keeps clients apart, so one filter fault can expose every firm; separate indexes contain it.
questions.pre_read: Restate the setup in your own words before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Retrieval returns the passages closest in meaning to a question from anywhere in the index, so one query-time tag filter is all that keeps 300 firms' files apart, and it has already failed once. Separate indexes mean each firm's questions can reach only its own documents. Quarterly test queries are sound practice but sample a moment; they cannot catch a filter fault or wrong tag arising the day after.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets what users see. But masking names leaves the rest of another firm's passages in the answer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing a control is careful practice. But quarterly sample queries cannot catch a filter fault or wrong tag arising between tests.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a data-protection control. But encryption protects stored copies; the assistant decrypts and retrieves passages for anyone the tag filter lets through.

tips: Eliminate: A masks names but still shows other firms' passages, and D protects stored copies, while retrieval decrypts and returns whatever the filter allows.
Final two: B beats C because separate indexes keep each firm's questions to its own documents whatever the filter does, while periodic tests only sample one shared filter.
Exam cue: When many clients share one retrieval index, look for separation, not one shared filter tested now and then.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A mid-year change of terms
questions.question: A Czech hiking app's terms permit model training only on trip reports uploaded from March onward; its trail-description model will be fine-tuned on all reports since 2016. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Strip usernames and contact details from older reports first
options.B: Proceed, since the app's terms now cover model training
options.C: Email users about the new terms, offering an opt-out
options.D: Train only on reports tagged as posted under the new terms

questions.key_concept: Rights to train follow each record's terms; a later change covers new uploads, and a tuned model cannot simply drop the rest.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not address.
questions.correct_explanation: The app's terms allow training only on reports uploaded since March; reports from 2016 to February were shared without that permission. Tagging each report with the terms it came under keeps tuning within rights, and it must come first, because content in a tuned model cannot be pulled out without retraining. An email with an opt-out is sound notice for the future, but it does not show earlier users agreed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as privacy care. But removing names does not give the app rights to train on reports users shared under the earlier terms.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training is now permitted. But the permission covers reports uploaded from March; earlier reports were shared on other terms.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because notice is good practice. But an opt-out email does not show users agreed for past reports, and opt-outs after tuning would need retraining.

tips: Eliminate: B reads the March terms as covering every report, and A treats removing names as if it granted rights to train on them.
Final two: D beats C because only reports posted under permitting terms are cleared now, while an opt-out email gives no agreement for older ones.
Exam cue: Training rights follow each record's terms; settle them per record before tuning, since a tuned model cannot drop records later.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Outage reports from residents
questions.question: A Ghanaian city sends repair crews where its model predicts streetlight outages; it learned from residents' app reports, which come mostly from districts with high smartphone use. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Survey a sample of lights in every district for outages
options.B: Weight reports from low-reporting districts more heavily in retraining
options.C: Remove district from the inputs the model uses to predict
options.D: Retrain on the districts that report the most outages

questions.key_concept: When labels come from reports, places that report less look problem-free; independent checks show where outages really occur.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how directly they address the stated facts.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learns outages only where residents report them, so districts with low smartphone use look as if their lights rarely fail, and crews are sent elsewhere. Surveying a sample of lights in every district gives an independent count of outages and lets the owner correct the labels. Weighting the few reports from those districts more heavily fixes a skewed mix of cases, not outages that were never reported.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reweighting can correct a skewed mix. But it multiplies the few reports and still treats unreported outages as working lights.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a fairness step. But the gap is in the labels, not the district input; the model still learns that quiet districts rarely fail.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because those reports seem most reliable. But training on high-reporting districts deepens the gap for districts that report little.

tips: Eliminate: C removes an input although the bias sits in the labels, and D trains on high-reporting districts, deepening the gap.
Final two: A beats B because a survey in every district finds outages never reported, while reweighting only multiplies the reports that exist.
Exam cue: When outcomes are recorded only where someone reports them, seek an independent source of truth before reweighting.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Three labels per complaint
questions.question: Three staff label each complaint for a Malaysian aviation regulator's complaint-classification model, keeping only the majority label; they split on 40% of complaints labeled 'unfair fees'. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the labels, since two of three staff agreed each time
options.B: Have a fourth labeler review each complaint to settle splits
options.C: Have the owner clarify the 'unfair fees' rule using split cases
options.D: Drop the split 'unfair fees' complaints from training

questions.key_concept: Wide labeler disagreement signals an unclear label rule; a majority vote hides it, and the model learns an arbitrary line as if it were certain.
questions.pre_read: Decide what problem the stated figures reveal before judging fixes.
questions.correct_explanation: When staff split on 40% of one label, the rule defining it is unclear, so each majority vote records how two people happened to lean, not a shared standard. The model learns that arbitrary line and presents contested complaints as clear-cut. The owner should clarify the rule using the split cases, then relabel. A fourth labeler adds votes but not a clearer rule, so splits are settled no more consistently.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a majority agreed on every complaint. But with splits on 40% of one label, agreement by vote hides an unclear rule.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more labelers seem more reliable. But extra votes on an unclear rule still settle splits arbitrarily; the definition needs fixing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because contested labels look noisy. But dropping them removes the hardest complaints, so the model is never trained on cases staff find difficult.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts majority votes despite a 40% split, and D removes the hardest complaints, so the model never learns them.
Final two: C beats B because the split shows an unclear rule; clarifying it fixes labels, while a fourth vote settles splits just as arbitrarily.
Exam cue: High labeler disagreement on one label points to its definition; fix the rule before adding labelers or votes.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Misread pages and the test set
questions.question: Before each release, a Swedish archive's team moves every test page its handwriting model misreads into training data. A new page replaces each one. Scores rise each release. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Retraining on misread pages may teach the model wrong readings
options.B: The test set keeps losing the pages the model finds hardest
options.C: New replacement pages may enter the test set with wrong labels
options.D: Pages moved into training leak test answers into the model

questions.key_concept: Removing every failed test case shifts the test set toward easy cases, so scores rise without real gains.
questions.pre_read: Follow the stated process step by step before weighing concerns.
questions.correct_explanation: Each release removes exactly the test pages the model gets wrong, while the pages it reads correctly stay and new pages join. Over releases the test set fills with pages earlier models found easy, so scores climb even if reading hardly improves. Wrong labels on new pages are a real quality risk, but nothing suggests them, and they would not explain a steady rise.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model got those pages wrong. But they keep their correct transcriptions, so training on them is how the model learns hard handwriting.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because new labels need checking. But nothing points to label errors, and they would not make scores rise release after release.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because moving test data sounds like leakage. But a moved page is no longer tested; the distortion comes from which pages stay.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about training on hard pages, which carry correct transcriptions, and D calls it leakage, though moved pages are no longer tested.
Final two: B beats C because removing only misread pages makes the test set easier each release, while label errors are unsupported and cannot explain steady gains.
Exam cue: When failed test cases leave the test set, rising scores may reflect an easier test, not a better model.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Acceptance documents shared with a vendor
questions.question: A Nigerian insurer sends its vendor the 2,000 labeled claim documents it uses to accept each new release of the vendor's document-extraction model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept each release the vendor reports as passing the documents
options.B: Have the vendor sign that it will not train on the documents
options.C: Send the vendor a larger test set with each release
options.D: Keep a separate test set that the vendor never receives

questions.key_concept: A test set the vendor holds can be tuned against, so acceptance needs a held-back set the vendor never sees.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not show.
questions.correct_explanation: Once the vendor holds the acceptance documents, each release can be tuned against them, by training, prompt changes or threshold choices, deliberately or not, so passing them no longer shows how the model handles unseen claims. A held-back set the vendor never receives keeps acceptance meaningful. A signed promise not to train covers only one route, and the insurer cannot verify it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the documents are the insurer's own. But a vendor-reported pass is a vendor claim on documents it can tune against.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because contracts can bar misuse. But prompt or threshold changes can fit a model to the documents without training on them, and the insurer cannot verify the promise.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a larger set gives more confidence. But sending more documents widens what the vendor can tune against; the set stays seen.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the vendor's own report of a pass, a vendor claim, and C sends a larger set, widening what the vendor can tune against.
Final two: D beats B because a set never shared cannot be tuned against, while a promise covers training only and cannot be verified.
Exam cue: An acceptance test stays unseen only if the party being tested never holds it; keep a private set.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. An applicant assistant's design
questions.question: A Paraguayan social-housing agency is designing a generative assistant that tells applicants their positions. The waiting list is pasted into its prompt. Validators will check 500 test replies. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have each position looked up from the list, not generated
options.B: Check every position in the 500 test replies against the list
options.C: Add a note that generated positions may be approximate
options.D: Launch it, then correct positions that applicants dispute

questions.key_concept: Generated figures can be wrong and vary run to run; exact facts people act on should be looked up from the record, a design choice.
questions.pre_read: Note the project's current stage before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A language model reading a long list can miscount or mix up similar names, and its reply can differ each time it is asked, so 500 correct test replies show only that those runs were right. Positions applicants act on should be looked up from the list, with the model only wording the reply; design is where that choice is made. Checking every test reply still leaves later answers unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because checking every test reply is thorough. But generated replies vary from run to run, so passing tests cannot make each later position exact.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it warns applicants. But a position is a fact people plan around; a note does not make a wrong one right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because real disputes show errors. But applicants may act on a wrong position without ever disputing it.

tips: Eliminate: C warns about errors instead of preventing them, and D waits for disputes applicants may never raise.
Final two: A beats B because only a lookup makes each position exact, while 500 correct test replies show only that those runs were right.
Exam cue: When an AI answer must be exact, design it to fetch the fact from the record; testing cannot make generated figures exact.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Summaries for gate approvers
questions.question: An Austrian life insurer's gate approvers read only a language model's summary of release tests; one pilot summary omitted a fairness test the release had not cleared. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Return to test write-ups the data team drafts by hand
options.B: Check a sample of past summaries against the test results
options.C: Show the test system's pass/fail list beside each summary
options.D: Ask the platform vendor to certify the summarizer's accuracy

questions.key_concept: A generated summary of test results can omit or misstate failures, so gate approvers need the system's own results beside it, not the summary alone.
questions.pre_read: Picture how approvers reach their decision today before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A language model's summary is generated text: it can drop a failed test, as the pilot showed, or misstate a figure, and approvers reading only the summary would not know. Showing the test system's own pass/fail list beside each summary puts every failure in front of approvers. Checking a sample of past summaries suits a fixed report, but each generated summary can differ, so a clean sample cannot clear the next one.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it removes the generated text. But hand-written summaries can omit failures too; the fix is putting the results beside the summary, not dropping a useful tool.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sampling is how report accuracy is usually tested. But each generated summary can differ; a clean sample says nothing about the next release's summary.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the tool. But a certificate of general accuracy is a vendor claim; it cannot show any one summary is right.

tips: Eliminate: A drops the tool though hand-written summaries can omit failures too, and D relies on a vendor's general claim, not checks of each summary.
Final two: C beats B because each generated summary can differ, so only the results beside every summary catch its omissions; a clean sample of past summaries cannot.
Exam cue: When AI writes the evidence summary for a decision, expect the decision-maker to see the source records beside it.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A prior-art assistant purchase
questions.question: A Swiss biotech firm will buy a vendor's generative prior-art assistant that answers from its training alone; its model card says training data ends in June 2025. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Ask the vendor for a full list of its training data
options.B: Require it to draw on a current patent search
options.C: Confirm the vendor's security certification covers the firm's queries
options.D: Test it on the firm's past prior-art searches first

questions.key_concept: A generative model knows only its training data; work that needs recent facts requires a current source, and tests on past cases cannot replace one.
questions.pre_read: Ask which risk each option reduces and which it leaves.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that answers from its training knows nothing published after June 2025, yet later prior art can block a patent, and the assistant may answer confidently without it. The firm should require answers drawn from a current patent search before buying. Testing on past searches looks careful, but much of that art may sit in the training data, and no score closes a gap the model card already shows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because documentation comes before reliance. But a fuller list of training sources still ends in June 2025; it adds no coverage of later patents.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because queries describe unpublished inventions. But a certification covers how queries are protected, not whether answers miss recent prior art.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing on the firm's own work is sound. But older art may sit in the training data, and no test closes the gap the model card shows.

tips: Eliminate: A lists training sources that still end in June 2025, and C secures the firm's queries without touching whether answers miss recent patents.
Final two: B beats D because the model card already shows the June 2025 gap; testing on past searches, often art the model may have trained on, cannot close it.
Exam cue: A model knows only its training data; where answers must be current, require a live source before relying on it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-06 (Due diligence before entering supplier relationships)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A bank-breach cutoff
questions.question: A Scottish canal trust's operations team set 0.35 as the bank-breach score that sends crews to inspect; the model card records the model's metrics, not this cutoff. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Set the cutoff at the point where overall accuracy is highest
options.B: Record precision and recall at every cutoff in the card
options.C: Let crews adjust the cutoff for each area as they see fit
options.D: Record the cutoff, who set it and the trade-off it accepts

questions.key_concept: The cutoff, not the model alone, decides what is acted on; record its value, its owner and the error trade-off it accepts.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option adds and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: The 0.35 cutoff decides which stretches of canal bank crews inspect, trading missed breaches against wasted visits, yet the model card omits it. Documenting its value, who set it and the trade-off accepted lets reviewers detect changes, judge it against tolerance and explain a missed breach. Precision and recall at every cutoff describe the model's behavior but still leave the cutoff in use, its owner and its reason unrecorded.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accuracy sounds neutral. But when breaches are rare, the most accurate cutoff can miss many; the cutoff should reflect what each error costs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because full metrics are good documentation. But they describe the model, not which cutoff is in use, who chose it or why.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because crews know local conditions. But untracked cutoff changes alter what gets inspected; a cutoff edit is a change needing control.

tips: Eliminate: A picks the cutoff by accuracy, not by what each kind of error costs, and C lets crews change a decision setting without control.
Final two: D beats B because recording the cutoff, its owner and its trade-off documents the decision in use, while full metrics describe only the model.
Exam cue: A model's cutoff is a business decision; expect its value, owner and reason recorded with the model's documentation.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A booking agent outside tolerance
questions.question: A Kenyan horticulture exporter's freight-booking agent has missed its accuracy tolerance for five months despite monthly retraining; the team plans to keep retraining it. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain it weekly until it meets the tolerance again
options.B: Raise the tolerance to match its recent accuracy
options.C: Have the owner set retirement criteria and apply them now
options.D: Report each month's breach to the AI governance committee

questions.key_concept: Retraining cannot always restore a model; the owner needs set criteria for when a failing model is retired, not endless retrains.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Five monthly retrains have not brought the agent back within tolerance, which suggests a change retraining cannot fix, yet the plan is simply more retraining with no point at which it stops. The owner should set retirement criteria, such as months outside tolerance, and apply them now. Reporting each breach keeps the committee informed, but reporting alone decides nothing, so the failing agent keeps booking freight.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining often restores performance. But five monthly retrains have not, and more frequent ones only postpone the retirement decision.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the agent would then pass. But moving a tolerance to fit a failing model hides the failure rather than deciding what to do.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because breaches should be reported. But reporting alone decides nothing; the agent keeps booking freight outside tolerance with no point at which it stops.

tips: Eliminate: A adds retrains though five have failed, and B moves the tolerance to fit a failing model.
Final two: C beats D because set retirement criteria force a decision, while monthly reports alone leave the failing agent running.
Exam cue: A model that retraining cannot bring back within tolerance needs retirement criteria, not another retrain.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Two models after a merger
questions.question: Merging Irish energy suppliers will keep one of their two models that pick homes for free insulation. One served mainly prepaid-meter homes. IT favors higher overall accuracy. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Compare both models' errors for prepaid-meter homes
options.B: Keep the more accurate model, as IT proposes
options.C: Run both models side by side another quarter on overall accuracy
options.D: Keep the model that mainly served prepaid-meter homes

questions.key_concept: Before retiring one of two models, compare errors for each group the survivor will serve; overall accuracy can hide a group it fails.
questions.pre_read: Read every option before ranking any of them.
questions.correct_explanation: Overall accuracy across both customer bases can be highest for a model that serves most homes well and prepaid-meter homes poorly, and after the merger those homes would depend on the model kept. Comparing each model's errors for prepaid-meter homes and others shows which serves both acceptably before one is retired. Another quarter side by side adds data but, judged on overall accuracy, would hide the same gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because higher accuracy sounds better. But an overall figure can hide poor results for prepaid-meter homes, which would then rely on that model alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more evidence helps. But another quarter judged on overall accuracy repeats the comparison that can hide a gap for prepaid-meter homes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to protect those homes. But choosing by origin is not evidence; the other model may serve them better.

tips: Eliminate: B judges on overall accuracy, which can mask poor results for one group, and D picks by a model's origin rather than evidence.
Final two: A beats C because group-level errors show which model fails prepaid-meter homes, while more time on the same overall measure hides it again.
Exam cue: When choosing which model to retire, compare errors for each group it will serve, not one overall score.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Running a model at lower precision
questions.question: An Australian fire agency will run its bushfire-spread model at reduced numeric precision; change testing found forecasts unchanged on 200 typical-weather days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Close change testing, since the 200 forecasts were unchanged
options.B: Compare old and new forecasts on extreme fire-weather cases
options.C: Compare old and new forecasts on 200 more random days
options.D: Retrain the model at reduced precision before it is used

questions.key_concept: Reduced numeric precision can leave typical outputs unchanged yet shift extreme ones; change tests must cover the conditions where errors matter most.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not show.
questions.correct_explanation: Reduced precision rounds the model's arithmetic; its effect can stay invisible on typical inputs and appear on extreme ones, beyond the ranges the change test covered. Extreme fire weather is also when spread forecasts matter most. Comparing old and new forecasts on such cases tests where harm would fall. Two hundred more random days would mostly repeat typical weather.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because every forecast matched. But typical days are where reduced precision is least likely to show; extreme cases went untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more cases add confidence. But random days are mostly typical weather, so the cases where rounding matters most stay rare.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the setup changed. But retraining makes a different model; the question is whether this one still forecasts the same in extreme conditions.

tips: Eliminate: A treats typical-day results as covering every condition, and D retrains, creating a new model instead of checking this one.
Final two: B beats C because extreme cases are where reduced precision and harm both concentrate, while more random days mostly repeat typical weather.
Exam cue: When how a model runs changes, retest the conditions where small numeric shifts would matter most, not just typical cases.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A monthly quota of inspections
questions.question: A Uruguayan environmental agency inspects factories that its model scores above 0.7. It will switch to inspecting each month's 200 top scorers, logged as a scheduling tweak. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the tweak, since the model and its scores are unchanged
options.B: Confirm inspectors can visit 200 factories each month
options.C: Retrain the model so its top 200 are more accurate
options.D: Assess which factories the new rule skips or adds, before use

questions.key_concept: The rule turning scores into action is part of the AI system; changing a cutoff to a fixed count changes which cases are selected.
questions.pre_read: Work out what the stated change does in practice before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A fixed count of 200 selects different factories than a 0.7 cutoff: in months with many high scores, some factories above 0.7 go uninspected, and in quiet months inspectors visit factories scoring below 0.7. The rule turning scores into inspections can change outcomes as much as a retrain, so it needs impact assessment and approval as an AI change. Matching 200 to capacity is sensible but says nothing about who is missed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model is untouched. But the rule turning scores into inspections decides which factories are visited, so changing it changes outcomes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a plan must be workable. But capacity shows inspectors can do 200, not which risky factories the new rule leaves out.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because better scores help. But retraining does not address the new rule, which can skip factories above the old cutoff in busy months.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the rule as separate from the AI system, and C retrains a model whose scores did not change.
Final two: D beats B because assessing the rule shows which factories it skips or adds, while a capacity check only shows 200 is workable.
Exam cue: Cutoffs, quotas and other rules that turn model scores into action are part of the AI system; changing them is a change.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A tag called 'latest'
questions.question: A Canadian ticket reseller's servers load whichever price model is tagged 'latest'. Nightly retraining moves that tag once tests pass. New servers start as traffic rises. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the last seven nightly models in storage for rollback
options.B: Add stricter automated tests before each nightly tag move
options.C: Have servers use an approved version by its fixed identifier
options.D: Limit new server starts to low-traffic hours to avoid surprises

questions.key_concept: A moving 'latest' tag lets servers started at different times run different models; production should load a fixed, approved version.
questions.pre_read: Trace what the stated setup does over several nights.
questions.correct_explanation: Because the tag moves nightly and servers load it whenever they start, servers launched before and after a retrain run different models side by side, and which model a customer gets depends on when a server happened to start. Using an approved version by its fixed identifier makes each deployment deliberate and traceable. Stricter tests improve each candidate but leave the mixing in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because kept versions allow rollback. But storage does not stop servers started at different times running different versions side by side.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because better tests catch weak models. But passing tests does not stop servers started at different times running different versions side by side.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fewer starts mean fewer surprises. But it gives up capacity at peak times, and servers started on different nights still run different models.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps old models but leaves servers mixing versions, and D gives up peak capacity while servers started on different nights still differ.
Final two: C beats B because a fixed approved version stops servers mixing versions, while stricter tests only improve each candidate.
Exam cue: Production should run a fixed, approved model version; with a moving tag, each restart can load a different model.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Reruns at temperature 0
questions.question: To confirm a Malaysian palm-oil trader's hosted research assistant matches its approved baseline, the IT team reran 50 recorded prompts at temperature 0; nine replies differed in wording. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Wording differences alone do not show the configuration changed
options.B: The wording changes show the assistant drifted from its baseline
options.C: Someone has edited the assistant's prompts without approval
options.D: The check is inconclusive until the 50 replies match exactly

questions.key_concept: Hosted generative models can vary even at temperature 0, so wording differences alone do not prove a change; check version and settings records.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each conclusion against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Hosted generative models are not perfectly repeatable, even at temperature 0, partly because of how providers batch and compute requests, so some wording differences are expected with no change at all. Nine reworded replies therefore do not show the baseline changed. The team should compare the recorded model version and settings, and check replies for required content. Concluding drift goes beyond what the evidence supports.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the replies changed. But wording can vary with no change at all, so differences alone cannot show drift; version and settings records can.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an edit would explain the differences. But nothing points to one; hosted models can reword replies at temperature 0 anyway.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because exact matches look like proof. But hosted models can reword replies with no change, so demanding identical text means the check could never pass.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes an unapproved edit the facts never show, and D demands identical replies, which hosted generative models do not guarantee.
Final two: A beats B because hosted models can reword replies even at temperature 0, so differences alone cannot show the baseline drifted.
Exam cue: Hosted AI is not perfectly repeatable; confirm a baseline from version and settings records, not identical reruns.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A shop assistant's model version
questions.question: A Greek musical-instrument shop's assistant uses a preview model its vendor may change or retire without notice; the general release scored lower but met the shop's targets. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the preview model, since it beat the general release in tests
options.B: Ask the vendor to give notice before changing the preview
options.C: Pin the assistant to the preview's current version
options.D: Run production on the general release at a fixed version

questions.key_concept: Preview models can change or be retired without notice; production AI runs a general release that meets its targets, held at a fixed version.
questions.pre_read: Read every option before ranking any of them.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor may change or retire the preview without notice, so the assistant could alter its answers or stop working without warning. The general release already meets the shop's targets, and holding it at a fixed version puts changes back under the shop's control. Pinning the preview does not help: it is not a stable release, and the vendor can still retire it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it scored higher. But the vendor may change or retire the preview without notice, and the general release already meets the shop's targets.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because notice allows testing. But the vendor may still change or retire a preview without notice; a request does not bind it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because pinning holds a hosted model steady. But a preview is not a stable release; pinned or not, the vendor can retire it without notice.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts a version the vendor may change without notice for a score gain, and B asks for notice the vendor is not bound to give.
Final two: D beats C because only a general release gives a stable version to hold, while a preview, pinned or not, can still be retired.
Exam cue: Preview or experimental AI versions do not belong in production when a supported version exists.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Notice of vendor updates
questions.question: A Belgian energy supplier gets six weeks' notice of each vendor update behind its email-reply assistant, but can use the new version only from the change date. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept each update, since six weeks' notice is given
options.B: Require access to each new version before it takes effect
options.C: Require three months' notice of each new version instead
options.D: Test each update on live emails during its first week

questions.key_concept: Notice of a hosted model update helps only if the new version can be tested before it applies; require pre-release access.
questions.pre_read: Read every option fully before ranking them.
questions.correct_explanation: Regression tests need the new version itself: with access only from the change date, six weeks' notice gives time to plan but nothing to test, so each update reaches customers' email replies untested. Requiring access to each version before it takes effect makes the notice usable. Three months' notice lengthens the wait but still leaves nothing to test until the update is live.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because notice is a contract right. But notice without access lets updates reach customers untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more time seems safer. But without access, a longer notice period still leaves nothing to test before the update applies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because live emails are realistic. But testing after the switch means customers already receive the new version's replies.

tips: Eliminate: A treats notice as control though nothing can be tested, and D tests only after customers already get the new replies.
Final two: B beats C because pre-release access lets the owner run regression tests, while a longer notice period still offers nothing to test.
Exam cue: For hosted AI, a test window means access to the new version before it applies, not just advance warning.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Moderators and drafted block notices
questions.question: A Danish job platform's model blocks ads it finds discriminatory, with no appeal. Moderators, who cannot lift blocks, edit the tone of notices that a language model drafts. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Employers may not trust a block notice drafted by AI
options.B: Notices may give reasons the blocking model did not use
options.C: Wrong blocks may stand with no person judging them
options.D: The language model may word notices differently each time

questions.key_concept: Human review of an AI-drafted message about a decision is not oversight of the decision; someone must be able to judge and reverse the decision.
questions.pre_read: Trace one blocked ad from the model to the employer before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Blocks have no appeal, and moderators, who cannot lift them, edit only the notices' tone, so no one tests whether the screening model was right. A lawful employer's ad, and the jobs in it, can stay blocked with no person judging the case. A notice may cite reasons the model did not use, a real generated-text risk, but even an accurate notice would announce a block no one judged.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because trust affects how notices land. But trust is a communication issue; the control gap is that no person judges the blocks.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generated text can misstate why a decision was made. But even an accurate notice announces a block no person judged; the decision itself goes unreviewed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generated wording varies run to run. But moderators edit every notice; unjudged blocks can stop lawful jobs being posted.

tips: Eliminate: A treats employers' trust in AI wording as the risk, a reception issue rather than a control gap, and D worries about varied wording, which generated text shows and moderators edit anyway.
Final two: C beats B because correcting a notice's reasons still leaves the block itself unjudged, and a wrong block stops a lawful employer's jobs.
Exam cue: check where the person sits in the chain; reviewing AI-written wording is not reviewing the AI's decision.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Building-inspection scores
questions.question: A Chilean fire service's inspection-ranking model fills in typical values where permit records are missing, as for many older buildings; inspectors see only each score. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Flag on screen each score that rests on filled-in values
options.B: Train inspectors on the model's inputs and design
options.C: Have supervisors review a sample of inspection choices
options.D: Stop filling in values and score complete records alone

questions.key_concept: A score built on filled-in values looks as sure as any other; overseers need each output's weak inputs shown when they decide.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option would change in inspectors' decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: A score built on filled-in typical values looks as solid as one built on real records, so inspectors may trust a low score for a building whose actual permits might show serious risk. Flagging those scores on screen tells inspectors, at the moment they decide, which ones to question or check in person. Training on the model's inputs is useful background, but it cannot tell an inspector which individual score rests on guesses.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because understanding a model aids oversight. But general training cannot show which individual score rests on filled-in values, since only some older buildings lack records.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because supervision catches poor choices. But a sample finds misplaced trust after inspections are missed, and supervisors see the same bare scores.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes guessed values. But buildings with missing records, often older ones, would then get no score and could drop out of the ranking unseen.

tips: Eliminate: C finds misplaced trust only after inspections are missed, and D leaves buildings with missing records unscored.
Final two: A beats B because a flag shows which score rests on guesses as each decision is made, while general training cannot.
Exam cue: Overseers need to know when an AI output rests on weak or filled-in inputs; show it beside the output, not only in training.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. An overnight jump in accuracy
questions.question: An Irish florist's order-cancellation model rescores orders hourly. Its live accuracy rose from 81% to 97% without retraining, the week a new courier feed began filling one input. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tighten the drift alert limits now that accuracy is higher
options.B: Report the gain to the AI governance committee as a success
options.C: Recheck accuracy on orders scored since the feed began
options.D: Check whether the feed records events after orders are canceled

questions.key_concept: An unexplained jump in live accuracy can mean an input now carries the outcome itself; check what the input records and when.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could explain the stated change before acting on it.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that has not been retrained rarely becomes far better overnight; a jump timed with a new feed suggests the input now holds information recorded after the outcome, such as a courier's 'order canceled' status. If so, the accuracy is illusory and predictions made before cancellation gain nothing. Rechecking accuracy on orders scored since the feed began would draw on the same input and show the same inflated figure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a better model seems to need less slack. But the jump itself is unexplained; tightening alerts builds on a figure that may be false.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because gains should be reported. But reporting an unexplained jump to the AI governance committee as success spreads a figure that may come from leakage.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperforming a measure is careful. But orders scored since the feed began carry the same input, so a leaked outcome would inflate the recheck too.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both act on an unexplained jump as if it were real, before anyone knows what caused it.
Final two: D beats C because only checking what the feed records reveals leakage, while a recheck on orders using the same feed repeats it.
Exam cue: Treat a sudden, unexplained rise in AI performance as an alert; look for an input carrying the answer.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. More false alerts after new fencing
questions.question: A Portuguese railway's trespass-alert model still catches about 90% of people on its tracks; since new fencing halved trespassing, controllers find a larger share of its alerts false. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The model is improving, since fewer people trespass now
options.B: Less trespassing alone can raise the share of false alerts
options.C: The larger false share shows the model has drifted
options.D: Controllers may be marking more genuine alerts as false

questions.key_concept: When the event a model detects grows rarer, a larger share of its alerts is false even with no drift: precision falls.
questions.pre_read: Read each conclusion against every fact in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The model still catches about 90% of trespassers, and nothing suggests it now raises more alerts on empty tracks, so false alerts stay roughly level while true ones halve with the trespassing. The share of alerts that are false therefore rises even if nothing in the model has drifted. Concluding drift, and retraining, goes beyond the facts; the owner may instead review the cutoff and alert handling.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because less trespassing sounds like success. But the catch rate is unchanged; the fencing, not the model, cut trespassing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because worse alerts suggest decay. But the catch rate holds; fewer real trespassers among the same false alarms raises the false share without drift.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because controllers judge which alerts are false. But nothing suggests they changed; the fall in trespassing alone explains the rise.

tips: Eliminate: A credits the model for a fall the fencing caused, and D blames controllers with no fact pointing to them.
Final two: B beats C because a steady catch rate with half the trespassing explains more false alerts, so drift is not shown.
Exam cue: When the event a model looks for becomes rarer, expect a larger share of false alarms even from an unchanged model.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Eligibility answers in chat
questions.question: Staff at a Philippine private hospital decide charity-care applications, and applicants can appeal. The hospital's chat assistant tells patients whether they qualify. Those told no rarely apply. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have staff review a monthly sample of its eligibility chats
options.B: Ground it on the hospital's current charity-care policy
options.C: Have it explain the criteria instead of giving a verdict
options.D: Add a notice that patients told no may still apply

questions.key_concept: An AI answer people treat as a refusal needs a recorded staff decision open to appeal, or should give no verdict.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option changes for the patients involved.
questions.correct_explanation: Patients treat the assistant's 'no' as a refusal and stop, yet no refusal exists: no staff decision, no recorded reasons and nothing to appeal, so a wrong 'no' reaches no one able to reverse it. Explaining the criteria instead leaves each decision to staff, through an application that is recorded and open to appeal. Grounding it on current policy improves answers, but each 'no' still leaves no decision anyone can challenge.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sampling is how outputs are checked. But it finds wrong answers after patients have given up applying, and those turned away still have nothing to appeal.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because current policy gives better answers. But a better-grounded 'no' still turns patients away without a staff decision, recorded reasons or anything to appeal.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it tells patients they may still apply. But a notice beside the assistant's 'no' may not change what they do, and that 'no' stays unappealable.

tips: Eliminate: A finds wrong answers only after patients have given up applying, and D keeps the verdict patients act on, so a wrong 'no' stays unappealable.
Final two: C beats B because without a chat verdict patients are left to apply, getting a recorded, appealable decision; a better-grounded 'no' still turns some away unchallenged.
Exam cue: When people treat an AI's answer as a decision, it needs a decision's record and appeal route, or it should not give the verdict.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. A grant agency's appeal letters
questions.question: A Polish student-grant agency retrains its refusal model monthly; appeals take up to four months, and outcomes are filed as letters in a separate case system. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Record each appeal outcome with the model version that refused it
options.B: Report each month's count of overturned refusals to the model owner
options.C: Scan each appeal letter into the student's grant file
options.D: Have appeal staff note the main reason in each letter

questions.key_concept: When a model is retrained often, appeal outcomes reveal a version's errors only if each is tied to the version that decided.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would let the owner learn.
questions.correct_explanation: Each monthly retrain makes a new model, and an appeal decided up to four months later may concern any of several versions. Unless each outcome is tied to the version that refused the student, the owner cannot see whether a retrain raised wrong refusals or feed confirmed errors back to the right model. A monthly count of overturned refusals shows a trend, but each count mixes refusals made by several versions.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a reversal trend is useful monitoring. But appeals lag by up to four months, so each count mixes refusals from several model versions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complete student files help later reviews. But scanned letters still say nothing about which model version made each refusal.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reasons show why refusals were overturned. But they cannot show which version's refusals were wrong, so a bad retrain stays hidden.

tips: Eliminate: C files letters more completely without tying them to the model, and D adds reasons that still cannot show which version erred.
Final two: A beats B because tying each outcome to its version shows whether a retrain made things worse, while lagging monthly counts mix several versions.
Exam cue: For a model retrained often, feedback such as appeal outcomes is evidence only when tied to the version that made each decision.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Correct refunds in acceptance
questions.question: A Slovenian retailer's returns agent, which can email customers, update stock and pay refunds, passed acceptance because each of 200 test returns ended with the correct refund. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add 200 more test returns to raise the statistical confidence
options.B: Run each test return several times and compare refunds
options.C: Accept the results, since emails and stock follow from the refund
options.D: Review every tool action it took in each test return

questions.key_concept: An agent can reach the right result through wrong actions; acceptance checks every action it takes, not just its final outcome.
questions.pre_read: Read each option for what it would add to the evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Checking only the final refund misses everything the agent did on the way: it may have emailed customers wrong promises, sent duplicates or changed stock levels wrongly while still ending with the right refund. Acceptance should review every tool action from the test runs. Repeating each test shows whether refunds vary between runs, which is useful, but it still looks only at the final refund.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more cases add confidence. But more returns judged only on the final refund still miss what the agent did along the way.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because agent results can vary between runs. But repeated runs judged only on refunds still miss wrong emails and stock changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the refund is the end result. But the agent chose each email and stock change itself, and none of them was checked.

tips: Eliminate: A adds cases to a test that checks only refunds, and C assumes the agent's other actions were right because its refunds were.
Final two: D beats B because reviewing each tool action catches wrong emails and stock changes, while repeated runs still look only at refunds.
Exam cue: For an AI agent, acceptance covers the path as well as the result: every tool action and message it produces.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Beating examiners on scans
questions.question: An Indian bank will accept its document-fraud model if it beats examiners' accuracy; for the comparison, examiners judged scanned copies instead of the originals they normally handle. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model may drift later as forgers change their methods
options.B: The comparison may understate how well examiners really perform
options.C: The comparison may hide the model losing on rare forgeries
options.D: Examiners may resent being measured against a model

questions.key_concept: A 'better than staff' criterion is only as fair as the staff baseline; people must be measured as they really work before comparing.
questions.pre_read: Rank each concern by how directly the stated facts support it.
questions.correct_explanation: Examiners normally see originals, where paper, ink and stamps can reveal forgeries that scans may hide, yet they were scored on scans. Their accuracy may be understated, so a model that 'beats' them could still catch fewer forgeries than current practice and be accepted anyway. Losing on rare forgery types is a real risk worth testing, but nothing in the facts points to it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because forgers adapt. But that is a monitoring concern after launch; the stated flaw is in the acceptance comparison itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because averages can hide weak spots. But nothing points to rare types, while the handicapped baseline undermines the whole comparison.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff reactions matter. But resentment does not affect whether the model is fit to accept; a skewed baseline does.

tips: Eliminate: A raises a later monitoring issue, not the acceptance decision, and D concerns staff feelings, not fitness.
Final two: B beats C because scoring examiners on scans can make a weaker model look better, while rare-type gaps are unsupported.
Exam cue: When AI must beat people to be accepted, check the people were measured under their normal working conditions.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Credit bands for solar customers
questions.question: A Nigerian pay-as-you-go solar company sets households' credit allowances by its model's score band; its fairness test found women- and men-headed households equally spread across bands. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the result, since both groups spread equally across bands
options.B: Compare error rates for both groups at the lowest band's cutoff
options.C: Compare actual repayment within each band for both groups
options.D: Remove inputs linked to the household head's sex, then retest

questions.key_concept: A score band should mean the same risk for every group; compare actual outcomes within each band, group by group.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each fairness check would and would not reveal.
questions.correct_explanation: Allowances follow the band, so fairness turns on whether a band means the same repayment risk for each group. If women-headed households repay more often than men-headed ones in the same band, they receive smaller allowances than their risk justifies, even with identical spreads. Comparing actual repayment within each band shows this. Error rates at one cutoff check a single line, while allowances change across every band.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because equal spreads look fair. But equal shares in each band say nothing about whether a band means the same risk for both groups.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because error rates are a standard check. But one cutoff is a single line, while allowances change at every band.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because proxies carry bias. But removing inputs does not show whether bands mean the same risk; only outcomes by band and group do.

tips: Eliminate: A reads equal spreads as fairness, and D removes inputs instead of testing outcomes by group.
Final two: C beats B because allowances change at every band, so repayment within each band shows unfairness that one cutoff's error rates miss.
Exam cue: When a score sets graded amounts, check that each score level means the same actual risk for every group.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Rating repair requests
questions.question: A Dutch housing corporation's language model rates tenants' repair requests for urgency; its average ratings match across language groups, though the groups report different faults. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rate the same faults written in each language and compare
options.B: Rate each request several times and compare language-group averages
options.C: Remove tenants' names from requests before the model rates them
options.D: Repeat the comparison on a larger sample covering more faults

questions.key_concept: Equal group averages can hide unequal treatment when groups bring different cases; matched requests differing only in language isolate the effect.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would add to the evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Because the groups report different faults, matching averages can hide a language effect: the same leak may be rated less urgent in one language, offset by other faults in that group. Rating identical faults written in each language isolates whether language alone shifts urgency. Repeated runs show how much ratings vary, but their averages still compare groups reporting different faults.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generated ratings vary between runs. But averaging repeated runs still compares groups reporting different faults, so a language effect stays hidden.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because names can signal group. But the request's language remains, and nothing would show whether it sways ratings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because bigger samples give firmer results. But groups would still report different faults, so the larger comparison can still mask a language effect.

tips: Eliminate: C removes names though the request's language still shows the group, and D enlarges a comparison that the different fault mix still confounds.
Final two: A beats B because matched requests isolate the language effect, while repeated runs only average the same confounded mix.
Exam cue: When groups bring different cases, test fairness with matched inputs that differ only in the group signal.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Deposits for accepted bottles
questions.question: An Estonian deposit-return operator's bottle-recognition model, which pays a deposit for each container it accepts, passed robustness tests with crushed, dirty and wet bottles. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the results, since varied bottles were already tested
options.B: Test it on bottle designs launched after it was trained
options.C: Retrain it on the containers it rejected last year
options.D: Test it with containers altered on purpose to fool it

questions.key_concept: Natural robustness is not adversarial robustness; when a model pays out, test inputs crafted on purpose to fool it.
questions.pre_read: Consider how the model will be used before judging the tests.
questions.correct_explanation: Crushed, dirty and wet bottles test accidental variation, but the model pays money for each container it accepts, so some people may try to fool it on purpose, for example with altered labels or non-deposit containers made to look eligible. Deliberately crafted inputs probe weaknesses chance rarely finds. New bottle designs are a fair test of unfamiliar inputs, but they too are honest containers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because varied bottles were tested. But accidental wear is not deliberate deception, and a model that pays out invites deception.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because unfamiliar designs test generalization. But new designs are honest containers; they do not probe what a person trying to fool it would do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rejected containers show weak spots. But retraining on past rejections tests nothing about inputs crafted to be accepted.

tips: Eliminate: A treats accidental wear as proof against deliberate tricks, and C retrains rather than testing how it can be fooled.
Final two: D beats B because a model that pays out invites deliberate tricks, which honest new designs never test.
Exam cue: When fooling a model earns money, robustness tests must include inputs crafted to deceive it, not just noisy ones.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Choosing among quotes
questions.question: A Hungarian insurance broker's assistant recommends one insurer's quote per client; in validation, the best quote was always listed first, and it picked that quote every time. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add test cases covering more insurers and policy types
options.B: Retest with the same quotes shuffled into different orders
options.C: Have sales staff approve every recommendation it makes
options.D: Accept the validation, since it picked the best quote every time

questions.key_concept: Language models can favor options by position; validation should check that reordering the same inputs leaves the pick unchanged.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the validation could and could not have revealed.
questions.correct_explanation: Language models can lean toward an option because of where it appears, such as first in a list. With the best quote always listed first, a perfect score cannot show whether the assistant judged the quotes or simply took the first. Shuffling the same quotes shows whether its picks hold. More insurers and policy types widen coverage, but if the best still comes first they test nothing new.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because broader cases add coverage. But they do not test whether the order of quotes sways its picks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because people catch errors. But approving every pick does not test the assistant; it adds a reviewer who may defer to it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because every pick was right. But the best quote was always first, so a model favoring the first option would score the same.

tips: Eliminate: D trusts results that favoring the first option would also produce, and C adds approvals instead of testing the assistant.
Final two: B beats A because shuffling reveals whether position sways its picks, while more insurers and policies leave that untested.
Exam cue: When a language model chooses among listed options, test whether changing their order changes its choice.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Photos supplied by applicants
questions.question: A Maltese passport office lets applicants upload their own photos, which border gates later match against travelers' faces. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: A printed photo held up to a border gate's camera
options.B: Poor lighting making genuine travelers fail to match
options.C: A blended photo letting two people match one passport
options.D: Applicants uploading photos taken several years earlier

questions.key_concept: Self-supplied enrollment photos allow morphing: one blended face that matches two people, so both can use one passport at a face-matching gate.
questions.pre_read: Rank the threats by likelihood and impact.
questions.correct_explanation: Because applicants supply their own photos, one can submit an image blended from two faces. Face matching can accept both people against it, so a second person can cross with the first's passport, and nothing looks wrong at the gate. A printed photo held to a gate camera is a known presentation attack, but gates can check for a live face, while the blended photo is genuine to the system.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because presentation attacks are well known. But they happen at a gate that can check for a live face; a blended enrollment photo needs no trick there.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because lighting causes errors. But that is an accuracy problem with honest travelers, not an attack someone exploits.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because old photos match poorly. But aging is an accuracy issue that causes refusals, not a way for someone to cross on another's passport.

tips: Eliminate: B and D describe honest accuracy problems that cause refusals, not threats an attacker exploits.
Final two: C beats A because a blended photo is accepted as genuine at enrollment, while a printed photo must beat the gate's checks.
Exam cue: When people supply their own enrollment images, consider morphing attacks that let two faces share one identity.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An email provider's spam filter
questions.question: A Colombian email provider's spam filter retrains nightly on the mail it blocked; lately, much blocked spam carries long passages of ordinary business wording. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: The filter learning to reject legitimate everyday mail
options.B: Padded spam slipping past the filter to users
options.C: Rival providers copying the filter from its decisions
options.D: Bot accounts flooding the filter so mail arrives slowly

questions.key_concept: Retraining on attacker-shaped data can degrade a model for everyone: spam padded with normal words teaches a filter to block normal mail.
questions.pre_read: Rank the threats by likelihood and impact.
questions.correct_explanation: Each night the filter learns that whatever it blocked is spam. Spam padded with ordinary business wording teaches it that those everyday words signal spam, so it can start blocking genuine invoices and letters for every user; this is availability poisoning. Padding is also an evasion trick, but this mail is being blocked, so the harm comes through retraining, not through spam reaching inboxes.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because padding with ordinary words is a known evasion trick. But this padded spam is being blocked; the harm arrives when the filter retrains on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because decisions can reveal a model. But copying needs many queries nothing here suggests, while the padded spam feeds retraining every night.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because flooding is a real attack. But nothing in the stem points to load, while the padded spam enters training every night.

tips: Eliminate: C needs many queries nothing here suggests, and D is a flood the facts never point to.
Final two: A beats B because the padded spam is already blocked, so evasion is failing, while retraining on it teaches the filter that business words mean spam.
Exam cue: When a model retrains on its own decisions, attackers can shape what it learns; look for inputs built to be learned from, not just to pass.
