questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Customer messages in the system prompt
questions.question: A Paraguayan moving company's booking assistant builds each request by pasting the customer's message into its system prompt, after its rules on discounts and deposits. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the system prompt so customers cannot read its rules
options.B: Add stricter discount wording to the system prompt
options.C: Filter customers' messages for phrases like 'ignore previous rules'
options.D: Pass customers' messages as user input, outside the system prompt

questions.key_concept: Text placed inside the system prompt carries the system's authority; keep users' messages in the user role, apart from trusted instructions.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how directly they address the stated design.
questions.correct_explanation: Pasted into the system prompt, a customer's message sits beside the discount and deposit rules with the same authority, so a message written as a new rule may simply be followed. Passing messages as user input keeps trusted instructions apart from untrusted text, which models are trained to treat differently. A phrase filter blocks known wordings but misses new ones, and the design still grants them system authority.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because hidden rules seem safer. But the model must read the prompt in plain text; the risk is customers' text joining the rules.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because firmer rules sound stronger. But a customer's message pasted beside them carries equal authority and can override them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because filters catch common attacks. But new wording slips past, and anything that does arrives with system-level authority.

tips: Eliminate: A encrypts a prompt the model must read anyway, and B adds rules that pasted customer text can still override.
Final two: D beats C because separating roles removes system authority from customer text, while a phrase filter misses new wording.
Exam cue: Users' text should never be merged into a system prompt; look for trusted instructions kept apart from untrusted input.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Off the hosted service
questions.question: A Kazakh electronics marketplace's shopping assistant uses an open-weight model. Jailbreak tests passed while a vendor hosted it. The marketplace now runs it on its own servers. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the earlier jailbreak tests, since the weights are the same
options.B: Repeat the jailbreak tests on the self-hosted setup
options.C: Confirm the self-hosted model files match the hosted version
options.D: Ask the vendor to certify the model's safety on any server

questions.key_concept: Hosted AI services often add safety filters around the model; the same weights run elsewhere may lack them, so retest as deployed.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by the evidence each would give.
questions.correct_explanation: Hosted services often screen prompts and replies with their own safety filters and settings around the model, so the passed jailbreak tests measured that whole service, not the weights alone. On the marketplace's own servers those layers may be missing. Repeating the tests on the self-hosted setup shows its actual resistance. Matching model files confirms the weights are identical, which the safety question does not turn on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the weights did not change. But the tests also measured the hosted service's own safety layers, which may not exist on the new servers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because integrity checks are careful practice. But identical weights can still answer jailbreaks differently without the hosted service's safety filters.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor knows the model. But a certificate is a vendor claim and cannot cover the marketplace's own setup.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes results travel with the weights, and D relies on a vendor claim about a setup the vendor never tested.
Final two: B beats C because hosted safety filters may not travel with the weights, so only retesting shows resistance, while matching files proves identity.
Exam cue: Safety results belong to the whole deployed system; moving a model off a hosted service means retesting it there.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Vouchers instead of refunds
questions.question: An Indonesian food-delivery app's support agent may refund up to US $20 without approval; logs show it settling larger complaints with uncapped loyalty-tool vouchers instead. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the agent in its prompt not to use vouchers as refunds
options.B: Cap each loyalty-tool voucher at $20 without approval as well
options.C: Apply one approval limit to all value the agent gives customers
options.D: Review a monthly sample of the agent's vouchers for misuse

questions.key_concept: An agent can reach its goal through any tool a limit misses; bind the limit to all value it gives, enforced in the systems.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how reliably each stops the stated behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent is settling complaints through a route the $20 refund limit does not cover, so a limit on one tool invites the next workaround. One approval limit, enforced by the systems on all value the agent gives a customer, whether refunds, vouchers or credits, holds whichever tool it uses. Capping each voucher at $20 closes this gap but can be met with several vouchers, and leaves other tools open.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets the behavior. But a prompt instruction is not a control; the agent already works around the limit it was given.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it matches the refund limit. But several $20 vouchers defeat a per-voucher cap, and any other tool that gives value stays uncapped.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because sampling finds misuse. But it finds it a month later, after the vouchers have been issued and spent.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt instruction, which is not a control, and D finds misuse only after vouchers are spent.
Final two: C beats B because one limit on all value given holds whichever tool the agent uses, while a per-voucher cap can be split or bypassed.
Exam cue: When an agent routes around a limit, bind the limit to the outcome across all its tools, enforced outside the model.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A tool that runs any command
questions.question: A Polish freight-exchange platform's operations agent reads service logs and restarts stuck services by writing commands for a tool that runs any shell command on its servers. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Replace the shell tool with one that restarts named services
options.B: Block commands that match a list of dangerous ones
options.C: Tell the agent in its prompt to limit itself to restarts
options.D: Log every shell command the agent runs for weekly review

questions.key_concept: Give an agent narrow tools matching its task; a general command tool screened by a blocklist still lets reworded harmful commands through.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how much each limits possible damage.
questions.correct_explanation: The task is restarting services, but the tool accepts any command, and text in the logs the agent reads could steer it. A model can write the same harmful action in many forms, such as another command, a script or an encoded string, so a list of dangerous commands misses variants. A tool that can only restart named services removes that power at the source.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because blocking known dangerous commands is common practice. But the agent can write a harmful action in forms no list names, and every other command stays allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it states the intent. But a prompt instruction can be overridden, for example by log text; the tool still allows any command.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs show what happened. But weekly review finds a harmful command only after it has run.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a prompt instruction that log text could override, and D reviews commands only after they have run.
Final two: A beats B because a narrow tool allows only restarts, while a blocklist must foresee every harmful command the agent might write.
Exam cue: Give an agent only the actions its task needs; a list of banned actions cannot foresee everything a model can write.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Hidden text in retrieved documents
questions.question: A scan found hidden instructions in 30 documents that a Croatian shipyard's policy assistant retrieves. Seeing no harmful answers, the team will delete the documents and log nothing. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Delete the documents, then log an incident if harm appears
options.B: Retrain the model to ignore instructions hidden in documents
options.C: Strip hidden text from documents before the assistant retrieves them
options.D: Log a suspected attack, quarantine the files and trace their entry

questions.key_concept: Planted instructions in retrieval sources are an attempted attack, an incident even before harm; record it, quarantine them and find how they entered.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option leaves unknown.
questions.correct_explanation: Hidden instructions rarely appear in 30 documents by accident; someone likely planted them, which makes this a suspected manipulation incident even though no harm has been seen. Logging it, quarantining the documents as evidence and tracing how they got in finds the entry path so it can be closed, and lets past answers be checked. Stripping hidden text blocks this trick but leaves the planter's route open and past answers unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because no harm is seen yet. But an AI incident covers near misses, and planted instructions show someone is trying.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it targets the weakness. But no model reliably ignores injected text, and retraining leaves the planter's access open.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it blocks this kind of hidden instruction. But a filter adds tooling while the planter's route stays open and past answers drawn from the documents go unchecked.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for harm though near misses are incidents, and B expects retraining to make a model immune to injection, which none reliably is.
Final two: D beats C because recording a suspected attack, quarantining the files and tracing their entry finds the planter's route, while a filter only blocks this one trick.
Exam cue: Signs of deliberate manipulation are an AI incident even before harm; record it, keep the evidence and find the way in.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. One serious error within tolerance
questions.question: A Canadian school-meal supplier's assistant wrongly labeled a dish nut-free and a child was hospitalized; its labeling errors are within tolerance, so the owner logged no incident. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The labeling error tolerance may be set too loosely
options.B: Serious harms within tolerance may never be triaged or traced
options.C: The kitchen's own allergen checks may have failed for this dish
options.D: The assistant's training data may lack allergen details

questions.key_concept: A rate tolerance cannot make serious harm acceptable; deciding AI incidents by error rate alone leaves single serious harms untriaged.
questions.pre_read: Note each fact in the stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance limits how often ordinary errors may occur; it does not make serious harm acceptable. Because the owner decides incidents by the error rate, a hospitalization went unlogged, so no one checks the assistant's other nut-free labels or finds why it erred, and the next serious error will be treated the same way. A tighter tolerance would still let a rare, serious error pass as within the rate.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tolerance let this pass. But any rate, however low, allows rare errors; the flaw is deciding whether harm is an incident by rate alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because allergic reactions often start in kitchens. But the stem says the assistant's label was wrong; nothing points to the kitchen's checks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data gaps cause errors. But this guesses at a cause the facts never give, while the stated gap is the unhandled harm.

tips: Eliminate: C blames kitchen checks the facts never mention, and D guesses at a cause the stem never gives.
Final two: B beats A because no rate makes a hospitalization acceptable; a tighter tolerance would still let a rare, serious error pass untriaged.
Exam cue: Tolerances govern ordinary error rates; a single AI output causing serious harm is still an incident.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A description generator switched off
questions.question: A Turkish home-appliance retailer's description generator invented safety certifications. The retailer stopped the generator's automatic publishing and pulled its listings. Editors' 'suggest' button still calls the same generator. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Find the generator's root cause before changing anything
options.B: Remind editors to check each suggestion for safety claims
options.C: Disable the suggest button until the generator is fixed
options.D: Add a notice that descriptions may contain errors

questions.key_concept: Disengaging a faulty generator covers every path to it; a path people use by hand keeps producing false claims, which reviewers tend to accept.
questions.pre_read: Read the stated facts before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The same model and prompt that invented certifications still write suggestions, and editors tend to accept fluent, confident text; an invented certificate looks like a real one unless checked against supplier records. Disengaging means cutting every path to the faulty generator, so the suggest button goes off until it is fixed. Reminding editors to check adds a human step that automation bias wears down, while false claims keep arriving.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because causes matter. But investigating first leaves the faulty generator writing suggestions that editors may publish while the work goes on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because editors are a human check. But reviewers tend to accept fluent generated text, and a false certification looks real unless checked against supplier records.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns buyers. But a general notice leaves specific false safety claims free to reach listings through editors.

tips: Eliminate: A investigates while the faulty generator still feeds editors, and D adds a general notice that stops no false claim.
Final two: C beats B because cutting every path to the faulty generator stops new false claims, while reminders rely on editors resisting fluent, confident text.
Exam cue: Disengaging an AI means every path to it, including tools people use by hand, not just its automatic one.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A replacement model tonight
questions.question: A Colombian cable-car operator disengaged its rider assistant over wrong service-resumption times, and staff take calls more slowly; engineers want another vendor's model, same prompt, live tonight. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Restart the original assistant, as staff answer too slowly
options.B: Switch tonight, since the same approved prompt will still be used
options.C: Switch tonight after a quick test on common questions
options.D: Keep staff on calls until a replacement passes full testing

questions.key_concept: A different model with the same prompt is a new, untested system; while a manual fallback works, the swap waits for proper testing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what is actually known about each option's behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: The same prompt does not make another vendor's model behave like the old one; models read instructions differently, so the substitute is a new, untested system that could give wrong resumption times too. With staff handling calls, slower service is the safe fallback until a replacement passes full testing. A quick test on common questions checks little and could miss exactly the failure that caused the shutdown.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because staff are slower. But restarting the assistant that gave wrong resumption times brings the harm back.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the prompt was approved. But approval covered it with the old model; another model may follow it very differently.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some testing beats none. But a quick check of common questions may miss the resumption-time errors that caused the shutdown.

tips: Eliminate: A restarts the system that caused the harm, and B assumes an approved prompt carries over to a different model.
Final two: D beats C because a working manual fallback buys time for full testing, while a quick check may miss the failure behind the shutdown.
Exam cue: During containment, a substitute model is a new change; prefer a working manual fallback to an untested swap.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Closed as a vendor fault
questions.question: A Japanese camera maker closed the wrong-quote problem record for its assistant as a vendor model fault, since fixed. The assistant's retrieved price list changed as the wrong quotes began. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the record closed, since the vendor fixed its model
options.B: Have the owner test whether the model or price list caused it
options.C: Have the owner rerun last week's wrong quotes on the fixed model
options.D: Add a notice that quotes may not match the price list

questions.key_concept: A retrieval assistant's output depends on its model and retrieved content; root cause must test every layer that changed, not only the one blamed.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not prevent.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrieval assistant's answers depend on its model and retrieved content, and the price list changed as the wrong quotes began. If the new list caused them, the record names the wrong layer and the cause remains. The owner should test each layer, both price lists included, over many runs. Rerunning the wrong quotes tries only the fixed model with the new list; as answers vary run to run, clean reruns cannot show the cause.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor says it fixed its model. But if the new price list caused the quotes, the fault is still live.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it tries only the fixed model with the new list, and varying reruns of it cannot show which layer caused the errors.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns customers. But a notice prevents no wrong quote and leaves the true cause unknown.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a fix that may target the wrong layer, and D adds a notice that prevents no wrong quote.
Final two: B beats C because C tries one combination, and varying reruns of it cannot show which layer caused the errors; testing each layer over many runs can.
Exam cue: When an AI fault is blamed on one layer, check every layer that changed: model, prompt, retrieved content and integration.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Every fault an 'application defect'
questions.question: A Singaporean bank's problem records classify every AI fault as an 'application defect', so its trend reports show one undivided total that nobody can act on. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add AI cause categories, such as data and prompt faults
options.B: Tag each AI fault with the system and model version
options.C: Open a separate problem record for every AI incident
options.D: Move AI faults into the security team's incident system

questions.key_concept: AI faults arise in distinct layers, such as data, model, prompt and integration; problem records need those causes to show recurring patterns.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the stated problem.
questions.correct_explanation: AI systems fail in distinct layers, such as drifting data, a prompt, the model itself or an integration, and each needs a different fix. Coding every fault as an application defect hides which layer keeps failing. Adding AI cause categories makes those patterns visible in every report. Tagging each fault with its system and model version links faults to releases, but drift arrives with no new version, so tags cannot name the layer.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because version tags link faults to releases. But many AI faults, such as drift, start with no new version; a tag cannot show which layer caused them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because separate records seem thorough. But problem management groups incidents by cause; one record per incident scatters the pattern further.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some AI faults are security events. But most are not, and moving them does not record their causes.

tips: Eliminate: C scatters causes across one record per incident, and D treats AI faults as security events, which most are not.
Final two: A beats B because AI faults such as drift arrive with no new version, so only cause categories show which layer keeps failing.
Exam cue: Problem records for AI should capture which layer failed: data, model, prompt, integration or oversight.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Leak-sensor homes
questions.question: A Dutch home insurer's water-damage model learned from claims at the 40,000 homes whose sensors shut off water at any leak; it will now price all 600,000 homes. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Forty thousand homes may be too few to train it reliably
options.B: Claims patterns may have shifted since the sensors were fitted
options.C: Claims at sensor homes may understate risk at other homes
options.D: Owners of other homes have not agreed to sensor monitoring

questions.key_concept: A model trained where an intervention, such as automatic shut-off, changed outcomes learns those outcomes, which may not hold where it is absent.
questions.pre_read: Read the whole stem once before looking at the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Sensors that shut off water at any leak stop many leaks becoming large claims, so the model learned the claims of protected homes. Homes without such sensors face leaks that run on, so their claims may be far larger than it predicts. A shift over time is worth checking, but fresher claims from the same protected homes would still understate the others' risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small datasets can mislead. But 40,000 homes is a sizable set; the problem is what protected those homes, not how many there are.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because claims patterns change over time. But fresher data from the same protected homes would still understate risk where no sensor shuts off the water.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a privacy point. But pricing the other homes needs no sensor in them; the issue is what protected the training homes.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a sizable training set as too small, and D raises consent to monitoring that pricing the other homes does not involve.
Final two: C beats B because the model learned claims from homes whose sensors cut leaks short; fresher data from those same homes would not fix that.
Exam cue: When something in the training setting changed the outcomes, such as a safety device, ask whether the cases scored have it too.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A smaller copy of a fraud model
questions.question: An Egyptian travel agency trained a small, faster fraud model to copy its large model's scores on 3 million past bookings, holding back 300,000 for testing. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Check it on the held-back bookings against confirmed fraud cases
options.B: Compare its fraud scores with the large model's on the held-back bookings
options.C: Stop training small models to copy another model's scores
options.D: Seek customers' consent before training on their past bookings

questions.key_concept: A model trained to copy another model's scores copies its errors too, so agreement shows fidelity, not accuracy; only confirmed outcomes test it.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem once, then restate it before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: The small model learned to reproduce the large model's scores, including any mistakes, so matching them on held-back bookings shows how faithfully it copies, not whether it catches fraud. Testing it against confirmed fraud cases measures what matters: real fraud caught and genuine bookings cleared. Comparing its scores with the large model's looks like a natural check, but close agreement would also repeat every case the large model gets wrong.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a check that the copy kept the large model's skill. But agreement repeats the large model's errors too, so it shows fidelity, not accuracy on real fraud.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because copying sounds improper. But training a small model on a larger one's scores, known as distillation, is a recognized technique; what matters is how it is tested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a privacy step. But screening past bookings for fraud is a normal use of booking data; the issue is what the test measures.

tips: Eliminate: C rejects a recognized way of training smaller models, and D treats routine fraud screening of past bookings as needing consent.
Final two: A beats B because a copy trained on the large model's scores also learns its errors; agreement shows fidelity, while confirmed fraud cases show accuracy.
Exam cue: A model trained to imitate another is judged against real outcomes, never only against the model it imitates.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Recent pharmacy invoices
questions.question: A Bangladeshi pharmaceutical distributor's late-payment model scored 95% on invoices from the last six weeks, held out from training; pharmacies have 60 days to pay. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Pharmacies may pay late for reasons no input captures
options.B: Six weeks may be too short to cover seasonal payment patterns
options.C: A random split across the invoices would test it more fairly
options.D: Test labels may count invoices later paid late as on time

questions.key_concept: An out-of-time test needs outcomes that have had time to happen; otherwise cases not yet late are scored as on time.
questions.pre_read: Restate in your own words how the model was tested.
questions.correct_explanation: With 60 days to pay, no invoice from the last six weeks can be late yet, so none can carry a true late label. Invoices later paid late are scored as on time, so a model that predicts on time looks accurate, and 95% may reflect unfinished outcomes. Six weeks may miss seasonal patterns, but that narrows a valid result; here the outcomes themselves are not yet known.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because no model sees everything. But every model has unseen causes; the stated test flaw makes this score unreliable now.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because payment habits vary by season. But that narrows a sound test; here the test outcomes are not yet known.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because random splits use every period. But mixing periods tests the model on times it learned from; holding back recent data is right once outcomes are known.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps a sound out-of-time design for one that mixes periods, and A names a limit every model has, not this test's flaw.
Final two: D beats B because no test invoice has reached its due date, so the labels are not yet outcomes; seasonality only narrows a valid test.
Exam cue: An out-of-time test needs outcomes that have had time to happen; check the outcome window before trusting the score.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Scored call recordings
questions.question: A Qatari airline's data gate cleared 300,000 call recordings to train a call-grading model. Supervisors scored them from 2019 to 2025. The rubric was rewritten in 2022. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Train on every year, since more scored calls improve accuracy
options.B: Have the gate check old and new rubric scores are comparable
options.C: Have the gate check sampled scores against each year's rubric
options.D: Confirm the 2022 rubric rewrite was formally approved

questions.key_concept: A model learns one target from all its labels, so a data gate checks that labels mean the same across every period used.
questions.pre_read: Read the priority word, then each option in full.
questions.correct_explanation: The model will learn one idea of a good call from all 300,000 scores, but scores given under the old and new rubrics may reward different things, so it could learn a blend that matches neither. The gate should check that old and new rubric scores are comparable before training. Sampling scores against each year's rubric checks that supervisors applied it, yet correctly applied scores can still mean different things.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more labeled data often helps. But more calls scored under two rubrics add a mixed target, not a clearer one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a check of label accuracy. But each score can be right under its own rubric while the two rubrics reward different things.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a governance check. But approval of the rewrite says nothing about whether old and new scores teach the same target.

tips: Eliminate: A adds data that carries the same mixed scores, and D checks the rubric's approval, not what its scores teach the model.
Final two: B beats C because scores applied correctly under each rubric can still mean different things; the model learns one target from all of them.
Exam cue: When a label's rules changed during the data period, check that old and new labels are comparable before training.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Buying a bed-demand model
questions.question: An Algerian hospital group will buy a vendor's bed-demand model and monitor its input drift itself; the vendor will not share its training data. Which vendor deliverable should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Summary statistics for each input in its training data
options.B: The vendor's SOC 2 report on its hosting controls
options.C: Accuracy results on recent data held out from training
options.D: A warranty that its inputs will not drift

questions.key_concept: Input drift monitoring compares live inputs with the training data; a bought model needs at least a statistical profile of that data.
questions.pre_read: Note each party's role before and after the purchase.
questions.correct_explanation: Input drift is found by comparing live inputs with the data the model learned from. Without the training data, summary statistics for each training input give the hospital group that baseline. Accuracy results on recent held-out data are useful buying evidence, but they show how the vendor's test went, not what normal inputs looked like, so they cannot reveal when live inputs move.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as standard vendor assurance. But a SOC 2 report covers hosting controls, not how the model's inputs behave.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as strong performance evidence. But accuracy results do not describe what normal inputs looked like, so they give no baseline for drift.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a contract protection. But drift comes from changes in the world, which no vendor can promise away.

tips: Eliminate: B covers hosting security, not model behavior, and D promises what no vendor controls, since drift comes from changes in the world.
Final two: A beats C because drift monitoring needs a picture of the training inputs; accuracy results cannot show when live inputs move away from it.
Exam cue: To watch a bought model for drift, you need its training baseline; when the data cannot be shared, ask for its statistical profile.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Handwritten tax amounts
questions.question: A Swiss tax office cites its form-reading model's 98% accuracy. The model card says handwritten amounts are often misread. They appear on 4% of test forms but most office forms. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on its 98% accuracy, since the model card discloses the limit
options.B: Obtain the model's test accuracy on handwritten forms alone
options.C: Have the owner measure accuracy on a sample of the office's forms
options.D: Have the model retrained on the office's handwritten forms

questions.key_concept: Headline accuracy reflects the test mix; where a known weak case dominates real use, accuracy must be measured on the user's own data.
questions.pre_read: Restate the stem in one sentence before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The 98% averages the test forms, only 4% of them handwritten, so it mostly describes typed amounts. In an office where most forms are handwritten, the card's known weakness dominates, and real accuracy may be far lower. Measuring on a sample of the office's own forms shows what assessors will get. Accuracy on the handwritten test forms narrows the gap, but they may not resemble the office's own.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the limit is disclosed. But disclosing a weakness does not show how often it bites where most forms are handwritten.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it isolates the weak case. But handwritten test forms may not resemble the office's; only its own forms show the accuracy it will get.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because handwriting is the weak spot. But no one has yet measured the model on the office's forms, so a fix comes after measuring.

tips: Eliminate: A treats disclosing a weakness as a control, and D orders a fix before anyone has measured the problem on the office's forms.
Final two: C beats B because the test set's handwritten forms may differ from the office's; only the office's own forms show the accuracy it will get.
Exam cue: A model card's headline figure holds for its test mix; when your mix differs, measure on your own data.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Retiring a tuned telemedicine model
questions.question: When a Georgian telemedicine firm retired its model fine-tuned on consultation notes, engineers deleted the deployed model, the tuning data and backups of both. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Patients were not told that the model would be retired
options.B: Checkpoints saved during training may survive as model copies
options.C: Deleted files may still be recoverable from the storage disks
options.D: The vendor's base model may still hold the consultation notes

questions.key_concept: Training often saves checkpoints, each a model copy that may repeat training data; retirement finds every copy and records whether it is kept or deleted.
questions.pre_read: Think through the model's whole history before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning commonly saves checkpoints, each a full copy of the model at that stage, often in an experiment tracker apart from production. A tuned model can reproduce text from its training notes, so a surviving checkpoint carries the same patient data. Recovery from disks is a real sanitization point, but it takes forensic effort, while a checkpoint is a working copy anyone with access can run.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a transparency step. But nothing in the facts creates a duty to announce a retirement; leftover copies are the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a media-sanitization point. But disk remnants need forensic recovery, while a leftover checkpoint is a ready-to-run copy of the tuned model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tuning starts from a base model. But tuning changed a copy; the base model never saw the consultation notes.

tips: Eliminate: D forgets that tuning changes a copy, not the vendor's base model, and A invents a duty to tell patients about a retirement.
Final two: B beats C because a checkpoint is a ready-to-run copy that can repeat patient notes, while disk remnants need forensic recovery.
Exam cue: When a model trained on sensitive data is retired, find every copy, including training checkpoints and experiment records.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Retiring a bookkeeping agent
questions.question: A Jamaican accounting firm retired its bookkeeping agent by revoking all its credentials; while live, it acted inside clients' bank portals and accounting ledgers. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Confirm that every credential the agent held is revoked
options.B: Ask the agent's vendor to delete its copy of the model
options.C: Delete the agent's logs, since it has been retired
options.D: Have owners review payments and entries the agent scheduled

questions.key_concept: Agents can create lasting objects in other systems, such as scheduled payments and recurring entries, which keep running after their credentials are revoked.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would and would not establish.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent that worked inside other systems may have left things there that run without it, such as scheduled payments, saved payees or recurring journal entries. Revoking its credentials stops new actions, not those, so finding them for their owners to keep or remove closes the gap. Confirming every credential is revoked is a sound access check, but it would miss a standing payment a bank portal runs on its own schedule.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a thorough access check. But objects the agent may have created, such as scheduled payments, can keep running without any credential.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendor-held copies matter at retirement. But a vendor deletion leaves untouched what the agent set up in client systems, which keeps running.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as tidying up. But retirement keeps the records needed to explain past actions; deleting logs destroys them.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes records a retirement should keep, and B looks to the vendor's copy while what the agent set up in client systems keeps running.
Final two: D beats A because objects an agent created keep running after its credentials go; access checks alone miss them.
Exam cue: Retiring an agent means finding what it set up elsewhere for owners to review, not only removing the access it held.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Patched explanation library
questions.question: A Lithuanian online marketplace's refusal notices give would-be sellers reasons from an explanation library. IT patched the library as routine because the vetting model was untouched. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rerun the vetting model's regression tests on sampled decisions
options.B: Replace the reasons with the model's top global factors
options.C: Test that given reasons still match what drove each decision
options.D: Accept the routine patch, since the model was untouched

questions.key_concept: Where an explanation component produces the reasons people receive, changing it is an AI change even when the model's decisions are untouched.
questions.pre_read: Note each system the stem names and what it produces.
questions.correct_explanation: Refused sellers read reasons produced by the explanation library, not by the model, so a patch to the library can change which factors it reports while every decision stays the same. That makes it an AI change needing a test that reasons still match what drove each decision. Rerunning the model's regression tests checks the decisions, but those tests never read the reasons the library writes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a careful regression check. But model regression tests check decisions, not the reasons the patched library writes, so they can pass while sellers get wrong reasons.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because global factors are stable. But they describe the model overall, not why one seller was refused.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no model changed. But the reasons people receive come from the library, so patching it can change what they are told.

tips: Eliminate: D treats only model edits as AI changes, and B swaps case reasons for global ones that explain no single refusal.
Final two: C beats A because the patched library writes the reasons; regression tests on the model check the decisions, not whether their reasons are still true.
Exam cue: A change to any part that shapes what people are told about an AI decision is an AI change.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Weekly prompt rewrites
questions.question: A Rwandan electric-motorbike rental firm's support assistant uses a tool that rewrites its system prompt weekly to raise customer ratings, putting the top-rated version live automatically. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Gate each rewritten prompt on fixed policy and safety tests
options.B: Have the tool rewrite the prompt monthly instead of weekly
options.C: Keep every rewritten prompt version so that any can be restored
options.D: Let the tool run, since higher ratings show better answers

questions.key_concept: An automated prompt rewriter makes a change each time it runs; optimizing for ratings can drift into rule-breaking, so each version needs tests.
questions.pre_read: Restate the setup in one sentence before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Each rewrite changes how the assistant behaves, so each is an AI change. A tool chasing ratings can drift toward answers customers like but policy forbids, such as fee waivers the rental terms do not allow. Fixed policy and safety tests before each version goes live catch that. Keeping versions to restore is sound, but it helps only after a harmful version has already answered customers.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as fewer changes. But monthly rewrites are still untested changes going live automatically.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as good version control. But restoring helps only after a harmful prompt has already served customers; nothing tests each version first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ratings measure satisfaction. But answers can please customers while breaking policy, so ratings alone are not quality.

tips: Eliminate: D reads ratings as quality, though they reward what pleases, and B slows the changes without testing any of them.
Final two: A beats C because each rewrite is an untested change; restoring versions helps only after a harmful one has served customers.
Exam cue: Anything that changes an AI system's behavior automatically still needs tests before each change goes live.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Monthly tuned versions
questions.question: An Estonian shipping broker fine-tunes each month's charter-drafting model from the last; version 5 was withdrawn for repeating clients' freight rates, and versions 6 and 7 are live. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Tune version 8 from version 7 with freight rates masked
options.B: Block version 5 in the registry so it cannot be redeployed
options.C: Keep versions 6 and 7 live, since version 5 is withdrawn
options.D: Test versions 6 and 7 for the same leak of freight rates

questions.key_concept: A version tuned from an earlier one inherits what it learned, so a fault in one version may be in every version built from it.
questions.pre_read: Restate the situation in one sentence before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Each version starts from the one before, so whatever version 5 learned, clients' freight rates included, can carry into versions 6 and 7. Those live versions are the ones that could leak now, so testing them comes first. Blocking version 5 in the registry is a sound control, but version 5 is already out of service; blocking it does nothing about its descendants still drafting charters.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a fix going forward. But version 7 may already carry the leak, and masking new data cannot remove what it learned.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a sound registry control. But version 5 is already withdrawn; the live versions built from it may carry the same leak.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because only version 5 was caught. But each later version was tuned from it and can inherit what it learned.

tips: Eliminate: A builds yet another version on one that may carry the leak, and C assumes each version is independent of the one it was tuned from.
Final two: D beats B because versions tuned from version 5 inherit what it learned; blocking a withdrawn version does not test the live ones.
Exam cue: When a model version is found faulty, trace every version built from it, not only the one withdrawn.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Two-language police assistant
questions.question: A Catalan police force's non-emergency assistant answers in Catalan and Spanish; each vendor model update is tested on Spanish questions and machine translations of them into Catalan. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Pin the model version so that no update reaches it
options.B: Add Catalan questions written as residents actually ask them
options.C: Rely on the translated questions, since they cover both languages
options.D: Watch Catalan users' ratings closely after each update

questions.key_concept: A model update can shift performance unevenly across languages, and machine-translated tests miss how native speakers ask; tests need real questions in each language.
questions.pre_read: Note who uses the system and how.
questions.correct_explanation: Machine translations of Spanish questions read like Spanish in Catalan words and miss residents' own phrasing and local terms, while an update can change how a model handles each language unevenly. Questions written as residents ask them test each update on the Catalan the assistant will actually receive. The translated tests cover both languages in name, but they can pass while real Catalan questions fail.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a way to stop surprises. But pinning blocks safety fixes too, and versions are retired in time, so updates must still be tested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both languages are tested. But machine-translated questions miss how residents phrase things in Catalan, so they can pass while real questions fail.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as ongoing monitoring. But ratings flag problems only after wrong answers reach residents, and many errors go unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: A would block safety fixes and only delay the testing problem, and D detects a regression only after wrong answers reach residents.
Final two: B beats C because translated questions miss how residents really phrase Catalan, so they can pass while real questions fail.
Exam cue: Regression tests for a model update need real questions in every language served, not translations of one language's tests.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Leaflet translation updates
questions.question: A Luxembourg drug regulator accepts vendor updates to its leaflet-translation model if they reduce errors of its listed types. The vendor tunes updates to those types. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Ask the vendor to warrant each update is error-free
options.B: Test each update for error types beyond the list
options.C: Accept updates, as tuning on the list shows vendor diligence
options.D: Count the listed error types on leaflets new to the vendor

questions.key_concept: An update tuned against a known-error list can cut those errors while making new kinds, so acceptance tests must look beyond the list.
questions.pre_read: Restate the acceptance rule in your own words.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor tunes each update against the listed types, so a lower count partly shows what was tuned for, not overall quality. An update can cut listed errors while adding kinds the list does not count, so testing each update for error types beyond the list keeps acceptance meaningful. Counting listed errors on fresh leaflets stops tuning on the test items, but still counts only the kinds tuned against.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a contract protection. But a warranty is a vendor claim, not evidence; only testing shows which errors an update makes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fixing known errors is diligent. But tuning on the list can lower its count while other kinds of error rise unseen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fresh leaflets block tuning on test items. But the count still covers only the error kinds the vendor tunes against.

tips: Eliminate: C reads tuning on the list as proof of quality, and A swaps testing for a vendor promise, which is not evidence.
Final two: B beats D because the vendor tunes against the listed error kinds; fresh leaflets stop item-level tuning, yet they still count only those kinds.
Exam cue: A test the vendor tunes against stops measuring overall quality, so acceptance must also look for what it was not tuned for.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Boiler-failure drift monitor
questions.question: A Cuban sugar mill retrained its boiler-failure model with added sensor inputs; its drift monitor, set up for the previous version, shows every tracked input within limits. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model whenever a drift alert fires
options.B: Confirm validation of the retrained model covered its new inputs
options.C: Check that the monitor's inputs and baselines fit the new model
options.D: Rely on the monitor, since no tracked input has left its limits

questions.key_concept: Drift monitors belong to a model version's inputs and baselines; each release that changes the inputs must update its monitors.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem once for what each system does.
questions.correct_explanation: A drift monitor compares a model's inputs with their training baselines, so it must change whenever a release adds inputs or retrains on new data. A monitor set up for the previous version may not watch the added sensors, and its baselines may predate the new training data, so readings within limits may mean little. Checking validation is sound change control, but validation shows the new inputs before release, not drift since.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a quick response. But retraining on every alert skips finding the cause, and inputs the monitor does not track never raise one.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a change-control check. But validation is a one-time look before release; it cannot show the new inputs drifting in live use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because every tracked input is within limits. But the monitor may not track the added inputs, and its baselines may predate the retraining.

tips: Eliminate: D trusts readings from a monitor that may not fit the retrained model, and A retrains on each alert without finding its cause.
Final two: C beats B because validation looked at the new inputs once, before release; only a monitor matched to the new model catches later drift.
Exam cue: Monitoring is part of the model version; when a release changes the inputs, the monitors must change with it.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Edited entitlement letters
questions.question: A Belgian pension office wants evidence that caseworkers' edits to AI-drafted entitlement letters catch model errors; its case system keeps each sent letter and the caseworker's name. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep each model draft beside the letter that was sent
options.B: Have a second caseworker check a sample of sent letters
options.C: Record the model version behind each drafted letter
options.D: Keep the sent letters as the record, since caseworkers own them

questions.key_concept: To judge human review of AI output, keep both the AI's draft and the final version; only the pair shows what review caught.
questions.pre_read: Restate the office's goal in one sentence.
questions.correct_explanation: Edits can only be judged against what the model wrote, and the case system does not keep that. Keeping each draft beside the sent letter shows which errors the model made, which ones caseworkers fixed and which slipped through. A second check of sent letters finds errors that survived review, but without drafts it cannot show whether they came from the model or from editing, or how many review caught.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a standard quality check. But sent letters show only errors that survived review, not which the model made or what edits caught.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because versions trace faults to releases. But a version says which model drafted a letter, not what the draft said.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because caseworkers sign the letters. But without the AI's part, nobody can see the errors it makes or whether edits catch them.

tips: Eliminate: D keeps only the edited version, hiding the model's part, and C records which model drafted a letter, not what it wrote.
Final two: A beats B because only the draft beside the sent letter shows what the model got wrong and what review fixed; sampled sent letters show survivors only.
Exam cue: To show whether people catch an AI's errors, keep the AI's output beside the final version.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Cheating-ban appeals
questions.question: A Taiwanese online game publisher's model, validated at 99% precision, bans players it scores as cheating; appeal staff see only each player's score. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Uphold bans whose scores sit far above the cutoff
options.B: Show appeal staff the confidence level the model gave each ban
options.C: Have the model rescore each player's games on appeal
options.D: Give appeal staff the play data and factors behind each ban

questions.key_concept: An appeal needs the case's own inputs and factors; a score or the model's confidence cannot show where one decision went wrong.
questions.pre_read: Think about what an appeal is meant to achieve.
questions.correct_explanation: An appeal can correct an error only if the reviewer can see what the ban rested on: the play data and factors behind that player's score. A bare score gives nothing to test. Adding the model's confidence tells staff how sure it was, but a model can be confident about faulty inputs, so staff still could not find where the decision went wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model is 99% precise. But one ban in a hundred is still wrong, and a faulty input's high score looks like any other.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confidence shows how sure the model was. But a confident ban built on faulty play data is still wrong, and confidence gives staff nothing to test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as an objective recheck. But the model judging its own decision again is not human review and repeats any input error.

tips: Eliminate: A turns appeals into a rubber stamp for high scores, and C has the model judge its own decision again.
Final two: D beats B because confidence says how sure the model was, not what it relied on; only the case's data and factors let staff find an error.
Exam cue: For a real appeal, the reviewer needs the specific inputs and reasons behind the contested decision.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Filing classification with referrals
questions.question: A Kenyan court registry's model classifies case filings itself only when confident, referring the rest to clerks; each release must reach 98% accuracy on filings it classifies. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the accuracy each release must reach to 99%
options.B: Have clerks review every filing it classifies itself
options.C: Require it to classify every filing without referrals
options.D: Judge each release on accuracy and referral rate together

questions.key_concept: A model that refers uncertain cases can raise its measured accuracy by referring more; criteria must cover accuracy and referral rate together.
questions.pre_read: Restate the release rule in your own words.
questions.correct_explanation: Accuracy on the filings the model chooses to classify can rise simply because it refers more of the hard ones, so a release could pass while classifying far fewer filings and pushing work to clerks. Judging accuracy and referral rate together closes that gap. Raising the accuracy bar sounds stricter, but a release can meet it the same way, by referring more.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a stricter bar. But a release can meet any bar on self-chosen filings by referring more of the hard ones.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as full assurance. But reviewing every filing it classifies removes the model's purpose and still leaves the release rule open to gaming.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because referrals look like failure. But sending uncertain cases to people is a sound design; forcing every filing removes that safeguard.

tips: Eliminate: C removes referrals, a sound way to handle uncertain cases, and B reviews every filing it classifies, defeating the model's purpose without fixing the rule.
Final two: D beats A because any accuracy bar on self-chosen cases can be met by referring more; only pairing it with the referral rate stops that.
Exam cue: When a model can decline to decide, judge what it decides and how much it declines together.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Plain-language rewrites
questions.question: A Slovak insurer accepted a model's plain-language policy rewrites after lawyers confirmed meaning was kept. Staff preferred the rewrites in 70% of 300 pairs labeled by version. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Score rewrites by word overlap with the original terms
options.B: Redo the comparison with raters not told which text is which
options.C: Accept it, since a 70% preference is a clear and decisive majority
options.D: Have a grading model rate the same 300 pairs instead

questions.key_concept: Human preference tests of generated output must hide which version produced each item, or labels can sway the judgments.
questions.pre_read: Ask how each stated result was produced.
questions.correct_explanation: Raters who know which rewrite is new can be swayed by that label, toward novelty or toward the familiar, so a preference count from labeled pairs may reflect the labels more than the text. Repeating the comparison blind gives a fair result. A grading model would not see the labels, but it brings leanings of its own, such as favoring longer text, and its marks count only once checked against people.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as an objective measure. But word overlap rewards copying the original, the opposite of a plain-language rewrite, and ignores meaning.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 70% looks decisive. But a clear majority from biased ratings is still biased.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a grading model never sees the labels. But grading models lean their own way, such as toward longer text, and need checking against people first.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts a majority that may come from the labels, and A rewards copying the original wording, which plain language should change.
Final two: B beats D because a grading model swaps the label bias for leanings of its own; blind raters remove the bias and still judge as readers do.
Exam cue: When people judge generated output, hide which system produced it, or the judgment may test the label.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A hiring model's ethnicity test
questions.question: A New Zealand supermarket tested its hiring model for ethnic bias on the 18,000 of 60,000 applicants who answered an optional ethnicity question, 2,100 of them Pacific peoples. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Applicants who replied may differ from those who did not
options.B: The model may infer ethnicity from inputs such as suburb
options.C: The 2,100 Pacific applicants may be too few for reliable rates
options.D: Asking applicants about ethnicity may breach their privacy

questions.key_concept: Fairness tests on voluntarily disclosed group data describe those who disclosed, who may differ from the whole group.
questions.pre_read: Read every figure in the stem before the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Applicants chose whether to answer, and those who did may differ from those who did not, for example in which jobs they apply for. The test then shows outcomes for those who answered, not for each ethnic group. Proxies such as suburb are a real bias route, but comparing outcomes by group already captures bias through them; what the test cannot show is whom its figures describe.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because inputs can stand in for ethnicity. But the test compares outcomes by group, which shows bias through such inputs too; the open question is whom the figures describe.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small groups give unstable rates. But 2,100 applicants is a workable group; who chose to answer is the open question.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a privacy point. But an optional question used for fairness testing is a recognized way to gather group data.

tips: Eliminate: D treats an optional fairness question as a privacy breach, and C doubts 2,100 applicants, a group large enough for workable rates.
Final two: A beats B because an outcome test by group already captures bias through suburb or any other input; it cannot show whether those who answered stand for each group.
Exam cue: When group data comes from voluntary answers, ask whether those who answered differ from those who did not.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. District upgrade rankings
questions.question: A Thai telecom's model ranks districts for mobile data upgrades; it passed its fairness test across provinces after analysts added a calibration step to their analysis code. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a second analyst recheck the analysis code's calculations
options.B: Remove the province field so provinces cannot be ranked apart
options.C: Retest fairness on rankings the live system actually produces
options.D: Accept the result, since the fairness test has passed

questions.key_concept: A fairness fix applied only in test or analysis code does not change live decisions; fairness evidence must come from the deployed system.
questions.pre_read: Restate the sequence of events before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: The calibration that closed the gap lives in the analysts' code, and nothing shows the live system applies it. If it does not, real upgrade rankings keep the gap the test hid. Retesting on rankings the live system produces shows what districts actually get. Rechecking the analysis code confirms its arithmetic, but correct code that production never runs proves nothing about live rankings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as reperformance. But it only shows the analysts computed their result correctly, not that the live system applies the calibration.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a way to stop gaps. But other inputs, such as population density, can track province, so gaps can remain.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the test passed. But it passed on output produced outside the live system.

tips: Eliminate: D accepts a pass produced outside the live system, and B assumes dropping the province field stops gaps, though other inputs can track province.
Final two: C beats A because the question is whether production applies the fix; reperforming the analysts' code shows only that the test was computed right.
Exam cue: A fairness fix counts only where decisions are made; test the deployed system's outputs.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Chatbot builder for clients
questions.question: A Swedish software firm sells a chatbot builder on one hosted model; it red-teamed the model under its default system prompt, but each client writes its own. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Red-team under client-style prompts, weak ones included
options.B: Check each client's prompt against a list of safety rules
options.C: Keep the default prompt secret so attackers cannot study it
options.D: Leave red-teaming to the client who set up each chatbot

questions.key_concept: System prompts shape a model's safeguards; red teaming must cover the configurations actually deployed, including weak ones clients write.
questions.pre_read: Note who controls each part of the product.
questions.correct_explanation: Safeguards depend partly on the system prompt, and clients will write their own, some loosely worded or with rules that clash with safety. Red-teaming only under the firm's default prompt tests a setup few chatbots will run. Testing under realistic client prompts shows how the product holds up as deployed. Checking client prompts against safety rules is a useful preventive step, but a prompt's wording cannot show whether safeguards hold under it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a preventive check on client setups. But reading a prompt's wording cannot show how the model behaves under it; only attacks run under such prompts show that.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a security step. But system prompts can be drawn out by prompting, and secrecy does not test what clients' prompts allow.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because clients write the prompts and should test their own chatbots. But the builder is the firm's product, which it must test too.

tips: Eliminate: D hands all testing to clients, though the builder and its model are the firm's product, and C relies on secrecy, though system prompts can be drawn out.
Final two: A beats B because a prompt's wording cannot show whether safeguards hold under it; only attacks run under client-style prompts show that.
Exam cue: Red-team the AI as people will actually configure and use it, not only in the builder's own setup.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Tuned on financing contracts
questions.question: A Peruvian telecom fine-tuned a language model on 2 million handset-financing contracts listing customers' ID numbers; partners will query it by API. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Partners sending so many requests that the service slows
options.B: Partners learning whether a given customer's contract was used
options.C: Partners drawing contract text out of the model with prompts
options.D: Partners copying the model through large numbers of queries

questions.key_concept: Generative models can memorize and repeat training strings; tuning on text holding identifiers lets anyone who can prompt the model try to extract them.
questions.pre_read: List the assets in the stem before weighing the threats.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuned language models can memorize strings seen in training, such as ID numbers in contracts, and repeat them when prompted. Partners querying the model could draw customers' numbers out directly. Membership inference is a real privacy attack, but it reveals only whether someone's contract was used, far less than the numbers themselves.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a service risk. But slowing the service exposes no customer data, the stem's main asset.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a known privacy attack. But it reveals only whether a contract was used, while extraction can reveal the ID numbers themselves.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because API access invites copying. But a copied model threatens the telecom's investment, not the customers' identities the stem puts at risk.

tips: Eliminate: D targets the model's value, not the customers' data the stem puts at risk, and A is a service risk that exposes no personal data.
Final two: C beats B because extraction reveals the ID numbers themselves; membership inference reveals only that a contract was used.
Exam cue: When a generative model is tuned on sensitive text, ask what it could repeat word for word to anyone who can prompt it.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Overdue fees in the prompt
questions.question: A Mongolian kindergarten chain's fee assistant reads all 600 families' overdue fees in its prompt; its rules forbid discussing any family but the signed-in parent's. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the overdue-fees file while it is stored
options.B: Give each chat only the records of the family using it
options.C: Strengthen its prompt rules against discussing other families
options.D: Red-team it to confirm it refuses other families' details

questions.key_concept: Anything in a language model's context can be drawn out; load only the data the current user is entitled to see.
questions.pre_read: Picture one chat from start to finish.
questions.correct_explanation: Whatever sits in a model's context can be drawn out by a jailbreak or a persuasive request; the rule in its prompt is only an instruction. Giving each chat only the records of the family using it leaves nothing else to leak. Red-teaming the refusal is useful evidence, but it shows only that the attacks tried failed; new wording can still reach other families' records.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as standard protection. But encryption at rest does not cover the copy the assistant reads in each chat.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rules set the limit. But a jailbreak can talk a model past instructions while the data stays within reach.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as evidence the rule holds. But passing tests shows only that the attacks tried failed; a new jailbreak can still reach records sitting in its context.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a prompt rule a jailbreak can bypass, and A protects the stored file, not the copy the assistant reads.
Final two: B beats D because tests show only that the attacks tried failed; data never placed in the context cannot leak to any attack.
Exam cue: Limit what a model can see to what the current user may see; prompt rules and filters are weaker than absence.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Longer uploads
questions.question: A Japanese machine-tool maker's portal assistant now accepts 500 pages of input, up from 10, so customers can upload specifications. Jailbreak tests passed before the change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the earlier tests, since the model itself is unchanged
options.B: Rerun the existing jailbreak tests on the changed assistant
options.C: Restrict uploaded pages to customers with signed contracts
options.D: Retest with jailbreaks built into long uploaded documents

questions.key_concept: Longer input limits allow many-shot jailbreaks that fill the input with fake examples of rule-breaking; tests must use the new lengths.
questions.pre_read: Restate the change in your own words.
questions.correct_explanation: Long inputs allow attacks short tests never try, such as many-shot jailbreaking: hundreds of fake exchanges in which the assistant breaks its rules, which can wear down its safeguards. The earlier tests used inputs that fit the old limit. Rerunning them on the changed assistant checks nothing new, because they are still short; tests must use the longer inputs the change now allows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model did not change. But the input limit changes what attackers can send, so earlier results no longer cover it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as standard retesting after a change. But the old tests are all short, so rerunning them cannot reveal attacks that need long inputs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a way to vet senders. But contracted customers can still send long jailbreaks, and their files can carry others' text.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes only model changes matter, though the limit changes what attackers can send, and C vets senders without testing what long inputs can do.
Final two: D beats B because the old tests never use long inputs; rerunning them cannot show whether the new limit opened an attack.
Exam cue: When a change widens what an AI accepts, test the new attacks it allows, not only the old suite.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Dispatch agent's tool keys
questions.question: A Kazakh trucking company's quarterly access review covers its dispatch agent's directory account; the agent calls booking and payment tools with API keys held in each tool. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rotate the tools' API keys every 30 days
options.B: Have each tool's owner review that tool's key rights quarterly
options.C: Include rights the agent holds through tool keys in the review
options.D: Accept the review, since the directory controls the agent's access

questions.key_concept: An AI agent's real access includes rights held through each tool's own credentials, which may sit outside the identity directory.
questions.pre_read: Picture how the agent completes one task.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent can do whatever its tools' keys allow, and here those keys sit in the tools, outside the directory the review covers, so the review misses its rights to book trucks and make payments. Per-tool reviews would see each key, but an agent chains its tools on its own, so only reviewing its rights together shows it can both book and pay for loads.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as good key hygiene. But rotating a key changes its secret, not what the key allows the agent to do.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as owner-based review. But each owner sees one key; only a review of the agent shows that it can both book trucks and pay for them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because directories usually hold access. But this agent's booking and payment rights come from keys stored in the tools.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes the directory holds all of the agent's rights, and A changes the keys' secrets without checking what each key allows.
Final two: C beats B because an agent chains its tools, so its rights must be reviewed together; each tool's key can look fine alone.
Exam cue: An agent's real access is everything its tools' credentials allow; access reviews must cover them.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Emailing course certificates
questions.question: A Portuguese first-aid training provider's AI agent emails course certificates that trainees request in chat, through a tool that sends to whatever address the agent supplies. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the tool send only to the address on the trainee's record
options.B: Have the agent confirm the address with the trainee before sending
options.C: Review the tool's weekly log of addresses certificates went to
options.D: Add a prompt rule forbidding emails to other addresses

questions.key_concept: Constrain an agent's tool parameters, such as recipients, to values from a system of record; checks inside the conversation can be steered.
questions.pre_read: Follow one certificate from request to sending.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent picks the address, and that choice can be steered by a confused request, someone posing as the trainee or instructions injected into the chat (prompt injection). Binding the tool to the address on the trainee's record takes the choice away from the agent. Confirming the address in chat sounds careful, but it happens in the same conversation that may be steered, so it can confirm the wrong address.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a careful double-check. But the confirmation runs inside the same chat that may be steered, so it can approve a wrong address.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as oversight. But a weekly review finds misdirected certificates only after they are sent.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a clear instruction. But a prompt rule can be talked around; the tool still sends wherever the agent says.

tips: Eliminate: D puts the limit in a prompt the agent can be talked out of, and C finds misdirected certificates only after they are sent.
Final two: A beats B because a check run inside the conversation can be steered with it; a limit in the tool cannot.
Exam cue: Bind an agent's tools to values a system of record allows, instead of trusting the agent's own checks.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Guarded fan-speed proposals
questions.question: A Bolivian tin mine's ventilation model proposes fan speeds; a guard swaps any proposal outside safe limits for a fixed speed, logging each swap silently. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Widen the safe limits so fewer proposals are swapped
options.B: Treat a rise in swaps as a possible AI incident
options.C: Rely on the guard, since it replaces every unsafe proposal
options.D: Retrain the model on the fixed speeds the guard chose

questions.key_concept: A guard that swaps unsafe AI outputs for safe defaults hides the model's failures; a rise in swaps is an incident signal.
questions.pre_read: Trace one proposal from the model to the fans.
questions.correct_explanation: The guard keeps each unsafe proposal from reaching the fans, but it also hides why proposals went unsafe: drift, a faulty input or a bad release. A rise in swaps is an early sign the model may be failing, and its proposals inside the limits may be wrong too, so it should reach incident triage. Relying on the guard, option C, treats the symptom it catches as the whole problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fewer swaps look like fewer problems. But wider limits let more unsafe fan speeds through and still hide why the model failed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the guard blocks every unsafe proposal. But swaps may signal a failing model whose in-limit proposals are wrong too, and no one learns of it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the guard's choices look like corrections. But retraining before anyone knows why proposals went unsafe may teach fixed speeds, not fix the cause.

tips: Eliminate: A widens limits that protect miners, and D retrains on fallback values before anyone knows why proposals failed.
Final two: B beats C because a guard hides the failures it catches; a rise in swaps signals a model that may be failing inside the limits too.
Exam cue: when a safeguard silently replaces AI outputs, its activations are an incident signal, not proof the risk is handled.
