questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Wiring answers reported
questions.question: A Quebec electrical-safety board's public-facing assistant answers electricians' wiring questions; its IT service desk alone rates reported answers for severity, using a checklist of system faults. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rate answers by how many users reported each one
options.B: Rate every reported answer as high severity
options.C: Add wrong-answer categories to the service desk's checklist
options.D: Have a licensed inspector help rate reported answers

questions.key_concept: Rating the severity of a generated answer needs domain expertise; plausible wrong answers can be dangerous in ways non-experts miss.
questions.pre_read: Picture the most serious report this desk could receive.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether a wiring answer is dangerous depends on electrical knowledge: a fluent reply can give the wrong cable size or skip an isolation step. IT service desk staff cannot judge that from a checklist of system faults, so a qualified inspector should help rate reported answers. Wrong-answer categories would help sort reports, but staff still could not tell which wrong answers could cause a fire or injury.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because volume shows reach. But one dangerous answer can cause serious harm, however few report it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as cautious. But rating everything high is no triage, and serious reports get lost among minor ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because categories improve sorting. But staff still lack the knowledge to tell a harmless slip from dangerous wiring advice.

tips: Eliminate: A rates by report count, which misses a single dangerous answer, and B rates everything high, which ranks nothing and so is not triage.
Final two: D beats C because the severity of a generated answer depends on domain knowledge; better categories do not give the desk that knowledge.
Exam cue: Triage of harmful AI output needs someone who can judge the harm in that field.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Queued meter bills
questions.question: A Finnish gas distributor switched off its meter-reading vision model after a faulty update. Staff confirm 600 queued bills before sending, using only the figures the model read. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Delete the queue so no faulty bill can be sent
options.B: Let staff confirm each queued bill in their usual way
options.C: Send the queue, since the model is now switched off
options.D: Hold queued bills until each is checked against its photo

questions.key_concept: Disengaging a model does not stop outputs it already produced; containment holds queued and cached outputs for recheck.
questions.pre_read: Trace the stem's events forward one day.
questions.correct_explanation: Any of the 600 queued bills may carry a misread from the faulty version. Holding the queue and checking each bill against its meter photo stops wrong bills reaching customers and keeps the queue as evidence. The usual confirmation, option B, works from the read figure alone, which is the model's own reading, so a misread passes it unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a clean stop. But deleting the queue destroys evidence and any bills that were correct.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because staff already confirm each bill. But they confirm from the read figure, the faulty model's own reading, so a misread still passes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model is off. But switching it off does not recall what it already produced.

tips: Eliminate: C treats switching the model off as recalling what it already produced, and A deletes evidence along with any correct bills.
Final two: D beats B because the usual check reads only the model's own output; only the photos can show a meter was misread.
Exam cue: Containment covers the faulty AI's outputs still in flight, not just the model.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Export quotes after a devaluation
questions.question: After Sri Lanka's rupee fell 40% in a month, a Colombo rubber exporter's quote-pricing model began underquoting orders. Engineers plan to roll back to last year's approved version. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The rollback may overwrite evidence of the current version's fault
options.B: Last year's version also learned from prices before the fall
options.C: A rollback needs fresh approval from the change board
options.D: Last year's version may be slower at quoting each order

questions.key_concept: Rollback contains a faulty release, not drift; when conditions shift, earlier versions trained before the shift may fail the same way.
questions.pre_read: Note what each party in the stem plans to do.
questions.correct_explanation: The fault comes from a market shift, not a bad release: last year's version also learned from prices before the devaluation, so it would likely underquote orders the same way, and the rollback would contain nothing. Preserving the current version as evidence matters, but it can be saved before any switch; it does not make the plan stop the underquoting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because evidence matters in an incident. But the current version can be saved before any switch; the plan's flaw is that the older version would underquote too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as change discipline. But returning to an approved version is a planned containment step; the problem is that this version predates the fall too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting as a service point. But quoting speed is not the harm here; the older version's view of prices is.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a planned rollback to an approved version as needing fresh approval, and D worries about speed when the harm is underquoting.
Final two: B beats A because the older version predates the fall too, so the rollback stops nothing; evidence can be saved before any switch.
Exam cue: Before a rollback, ask whether the earlier version would fail the same way; drift affects every version trained before the shift.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Copied answers in a wiki
questions.question: Staff at a Czech university pasted the help assistant's answers into wiki pages that it reads, spreading a wrong VPN step. The problem record blames those pages. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the record name copied answers as the root cause
options.B: Have the assistant cite the wiki page behind each answer
options.C: Close the record once IT corrects the wrong wiki pages
options.D: Retrain the model so it stops giving the wrong step

questions.key_concept: When an AI's outputs flow back into its own sources, errors can reinforce themselves; root cause covers how generated content enters those sources.
questions.pre_read: Restate the stem's facts in order before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: The wrong step spread because the assistant's own answers became pages it later draws on, so an error can feed on itself and look like a trusted source. Blaming the pages records the symptom; naming the copying of answers as root cause lets the owner control that path, such as review before posting. Closing the record once IT corrects the pages, option C, fixes today's pages but leaves the loop open.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as traceability. But citations would point to the copied pages, making the wrong step look sourced; the path that let answers into the wiki stays open.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the pages gave the wrong step. But they went wrong because answers were copied in; closing on corrected pages leaves that path open.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model gave the step. But it repeats what it retrieves, so retraining leaves the wrong wiki pages in place.

tips: Eliminate: D retrains a model whose wrong step comes from pages it retrieves, and B adds citations that would point to the copied pages.
Final two: A beats C because the wrong pages are a symptom; the loop from the assistant's answers back into its sources is the cause.
Exam cue: When an AI's output can flow back into its own sources, treat that loop as a root cause to control.

questions.question: A Romanian news app trains its alert model on readers' opens. Its problem record ties complaints about alarming crime alerts to that signal and proposes blocking those alerts. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model on this month's alert opens
options.B: Have crime alerts blocked, then confirm crime complaints fall
options.C: Have the owner add complaints and opt-outs to training
options.D: Close the record, as readers chose to open the alerts

questions.key_concept: A model pursues whatever its training signal rewards; blocking one harmful output leaves the reward in place, so the fix belongs in the signal.
questions.pre_read: Restate the stem in one sentence before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The record has found the cause: training on opens rewards alarm. Blocking crime alerts removes one topic, but the reward stays, so the model may simply favor other alarming stories, such as disasters or health scares. Adding complaints and opt-outs to training changes what the model is rewarded for, which removes the cause. Confirming crime complaints fall would only show that the blocked topic went quiet.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting as a refresh. But retraining on opens alone teaches the same preference again.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a quick control outside the model. But the reward for alarm stays, so the model may shift to other alarming topics while crime complaints fall.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because opens show interest. But complaints about the alerts show readers object, so opens are not approval.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains on the same signal that caused the fault, and D reads opens as approval despite readers' complaints.
Final two: C beats B because the cause is what training rewards; a crime block treats one symptom, and the model can find other alarming stories.
Exam cue: When a training signal rewards harm, fix the signal; blocking one output leaves the cause in place.
